en: Now begins the third chapter: "The vow pertaining to the three Vedas consists of practicing [service] under a guru for thirty-six years;
or half of that, or a quarter, or even until [the Veda] has been mastered. (3.1)

Two types of *brahmacārin* were previously established: the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student) and the *upakurvāṇa* (temporary student). By the verse, "He who serves his teacher until the completion of his body" (MDh 2.244), *naiṣṭhika* celibacy is described. By the phrase, "until the return [home]" (MDh 2.108), another alternative is also indicated. In that regard, for the *naiṣṭhika*, the specific limit is easily understood through the very acquisition of his name, which possesses a causal basis. He goes to the end (*niṣṭhā*), that is, completion; thus he is a *naiṣṭhika*. The time is prescribed by the scripture itself as "until completion. As for the *upakurvāṇa*:
By this sequential method: "The entire Veda is to be mastered through various specific forms of austerity and vows prescribed by rule" (MDh 2.165). "By this sequential method" (MDh 6.85).

Thus, since neither the number nor the specific desire for a particular branch is intended to be expressed, the study of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or more branches—which would otherwise be undertaken according to one's capacity—is here regulated.

The *traivedika* vow is to be observed. The term *trivedī* refers to the collection of the three Vedas; the purpose of that [study] is the *traivedika*. The act of acquisition (*grahaṇa*) is included within the term "observance" (*vrata*), because the mastery of the Vedas has already been prescribed previously. A *vrata* is the entire set of duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). It is *carya*, meaning it is to be practiced. The *kṛtya* suffix is used here in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Since it might thus follow that the sequence beginning with "fetching" (āharaṇa) ends with "grasping" (grahaṇa), he says: "lasting thirty-six years. Even when the Veda has been grasped, the time must still be completed.

If the duty [dharma] is for the sake of the injunction to study one's own recitation (svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi), and if that injunction for recitation ceases upon the grasping [of the text], then for what purpose is the observance of vows continued for twelve years after the grasping?

This is stated too narrowly. Even in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, this must be said regarding those subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) that follow the primary offerings such as the Āgneya; for it is only when the performance of all the subsidiaries—endowed with the [remotely] beneficial (*ārād-upakāraka*) and other types of auxiliaries and possessing a specific sequence—is understood to be accomplished through the meaning of the injunction (*vidhy-artha*), that the injunction is established precisely from the word of the original impulsion (*paricodanā-śabda*).

Now, there are alternative options that are lighter than the great [twelve-year vow], ranging down to its half or even a quarter; since these exist, one might ask: who indeed would undertake such a great effort and such an extremely long period as the twelve-year observance?

To this we reply: those who desire an abundance of results will perform the greater number of auxiliary practices (*aṅga*). As it has been said: "From a distinction in effort, there must be a distinction in the result."

But surely, apart from the comprehension of meaning, there is no other fruit for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) than its apprehension. For thus they say: "The venerable ritualists do not declare that the mere recitation of it is its fruit. Likewise, in the *Śabara-bhāṣya* [it is said]: "For its visible purpose is indeed the comprehension of ritual action" (ŚBh 1.1.1). And yet, no distinction is observed in that regard.

If this were so, then even at the time of initial acquisition (*grahaṇa*), there would be the consequence that the performance of the recitation could occur without the observance of the rules of the vow (*vrata-dharma*). And who says that "the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) is for the purpose of understanding the meaning"? The injunction for Vedic study has its own inherent purpose; there is no evidence for one thing having the purpose of another. For the comprehension of the meaning arises from the very nature of the thing once the [text] has been acquired, not from the injunction itself. Now, if it is argued that this injunction is for one who desires results such as heaven, how will that be possible?
What, then, is the meaning of this expression: “by way of a specific fruit”?

This is the logical reasoning regarding the statement. First, this injunction for the refinement (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) has the private study (*svādhyāya*) as its primary object, because it arises in relation to that act of studying. Furthermore, injunctions for refinement do not by themselves merit an independent qualification (*adhikāra*); rather, they enter into another injunction that possesses such a qualification by means of the object to be refined. For example, in the injunction "one threshes the rice," the act of threshing experiences a connection with the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) through the medium of refinements—such as the removal of the husks and chaff from the rice—which serve as the means for the *puroḍāśa* cake and other offerings used in the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices within the scope of the New and Full Moon sacrifices' qualification. It is not independent of those [sacrifices]; rather, it is understood precisely as something to be performed. In this way, the status of the Veda as the object to be refined cannot be established elsewhere than in its entirety. The comprehension of meaning is observed to follow immediately after the study of the private recitation (*svādhyāya*). Therefore, this study extends until the comprehension of meaning, just as threshing extends until the production of rice grains. However, there is this distinction: because it is studied within a specific ritual context (*prakaraṇa*), threshing quickly attains a connection with another injunction possessing a qualification; but this [study of the Veda], because it is studied outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), results in comprehension of meaning and is understood as a qualification (*adhikāra*) by virtue of its utility for the performance of all actions that yield fruits. Thus, the very fulfillment of the purpose of the injunction is intended as the specific fruit. For the fact that an injunction serves the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is understood through linguistic convention; whether that occurs directly or through a succession of steps makes no difference. And because its qualification is thus understood, this injunction is indeed independent and compels its own performance, even though the comprehension of meaning is useful in the case of injunctions for obligatory (*nitya*) or optional (*kāmya*) rites.

However, as for those who maintain that [the study of grammar] shares the same purpose as the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices by way of understanding the meaning, and who claim that the excellence of that very result arises from a specific effort—what wrong has been done to them by the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), such that its sharing the same purpose is so strenuously denied? If you say, "It would result in the Veda being non-authoritative," let it be so. One cannot abandon a meaning established by the force of reasoning simply because it lacks a [practical] purpose; rather, a reasoning is sublated by another, more powerful reasoning.

If, however, this [injunction] had the same purpose as the injunction for appointing a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), its very nature as an injunction would be lost, because its own meaning would not be intended to be expressed. This is equally the case even when it enters into the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices.
But when this injunction is independent and enforces its own performance—standing on the same footing as them—it is then performed joined with its own specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

In this regard, among those optional alternatives (*kalpa*)—whether they be lighter or more burdensome—the performance of the more burdensome ones when the lighter one has already been established serves only to bring about a specific distinction for the sake of the injunction (*vidhyartha*). For example, regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), we have: "One [cow] should be given, three should be given, twelve should be given," and so forth (VārŚ 3.2.3.45). Once this injunction has been performed, whether the alternative is explicitly heard (*śruta*) or merely implied (*pratīyamāna*) by its own capacity, this constitutes a difference in the means of knowledge (*pramāṇabheda*), not a difference in the relationship (*sambandhabheda*). In every respect, we cannot escape being touched by both [alternatives], provided that the injunction compels the performance of its own meaning and serves as an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites.

But surely, why is this being prattled, which is contradictory from beginning to end? Previously it was stated that the injunctions for purificatory rites (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) are not directly connected to the qualification (*adhikāra*); yet now it is claimed that this injunction is independent and enforces its own purpose. Just as this [qualification] is not connected with a specific [text] that is explicitly heard (*viśeṣa-śruta*), so too the qualification understood by implication is not inconsistent even with the injunctions for purificatory rites. This is not a distinction if the performance of this [study] is intended to belong to the portion concerning the comprehension of meaning (*arthāvabodha*) when it is impelled by the injunction. Since the mere recitation is impelled by the teacher’s injunction, the connection of the injunctions for purificatory rites with the qualification would have to be accepted. If, on the other hand, the performance is impelled because it assists another injunction, then the study would belong to one who is already qualified, and there would be no qualification for one who has merely studied the Veda. In that case, the qualification of a *śūdra* would be difficult to prevent. Furthermore, the hearing of the Vedic meaning would not necessarily follow immediately after the study; for at whatever time something is incidentally learned from somewhere—such as "the ritual named Jyotiṣṭoma is Vedic and has heaven as its fruit"—at that very time one would learn its procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and would study at that same time the *yajamāna*-mantras useful for it.

On this point, some resolve the difficulty by the principle of the *āśrayin* (the dependent) [PMS 4.1.18]. For just as the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such offerings are of a dual nature—being both acts of refinement (*saṃskārakarma*) and acts for the sake of a result (*phalavat karma*)—so too the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*), following its application through direct denotation (*abhidhāna-viniyoga*) and because it is observed to result in the comprehension of meaning, is both an act of refinement and an act for the sake of a result. Therefore, its status as having a specific qualification (*sādhikāra*) is established. But who is the qualified person (*adhikārī*)? We reply: it is the initiated boy (*māṇavaka*) of the three higher castes. For this is traditionally taught among the duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*). Indeed, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth convey the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) whose purpose is an agent (*niyojya*) who is invariably connected to it. When there is a requirement for a specific qualification, that qualification is sometimes provided by the words themselves, as in: "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* as long as he lives. Sometimes, even if not explicitly heard, it must be inferred by the force of the capacity of the connected denotation (*anvitābhidhāna*), as in the case of the *viśvajit* sacrifice and others. Sometimes it is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*), from the inherent capacity of the thing itself (*vastusāmarthya*), or by considering other injunctions. All of these factors are present here. The religious student is the subject under discussion; and the comprehension of meaning arises through the inherent capacity of the thing. And that comprehension is useful in all injunctions, since only one who possesses knowledge is qualified [to perform them].

Others do not accept this view. They maintain that its status as a subordinate topic (*adhikāra*) is perceived solely through its nature as a purificatory injunction (*saṃskāra-vidhi*). This is because purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*) are performed for the sake of that which is to be purified (*saṃskārya*). Furthermore, if no specific distinction were observed in the object to be purified, then—like the *saktu* offering—it would lose its character as a purificatory act. However, in this case, there exists a specific distinction characterized by the comprehension of fruitful ritual action. As for the argument that it is "like the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other such offerings," that is correct insofar as it possesses a dual nature, since it lacks the quality of being understood through the analysis of roots and suffixes (*prakṛti-pratyaya-vijñāna*).

Therefore, it is established that this injunction is independent with respect to the student; and for this reason, it is to be performed by himself alone, and not through the implication of the mandate of qualification for the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, as is the case with threshing and similar acts.

In this same way, the study of multiple Vedas is also to be understood. For even there, since the purpose of the injunction is accomplished by means of a single Veda, why study multiple Vedas? It is justified, however, by the abundance of results. And the result is as previously stated, not merely the milk, curd, and so forth mentioned in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*). This being the case, for one who studies a single Veda, the study of those mantras useful for ritual acts that are not recited in his own branch (*svaśākhā*) is permitted by implication at the time of performing the rites, due to their functional necessity. Even though the qualification for one who has studied the Veda is expressed by the word "studied" (*adhīta*).

Others, however, consider that in the statement, “The Veda with its six auxiliary limbs is to be studied by a Brāhmaṇa as a duty without motive” (*PMS* I.1.1), the term “without motive” (*niṣkāraṇa*) functions as a word that establishes the qualification (*adhikāra*). “Without motive” means without aiming at any specific purpose; it must be performed like an obligatory rite (*nityakarman*). For, unless it serves to establish a qualification, its syntactical connection cannot occur through the medium of the subject matter (*viṣaya*), nor as a factor of action (*kāraka*), nor as a qualifier thereof, and so on. Therefore, even though it is an injunction for a preparatory act (*saṃskāravidhi*), there is no contradiction in its having either an implied qualification or an explicitly stated qualification.

Others, however, consider the lack of *adhikāra* (qualification for ritual agency) to be superior, because this is a rule concerning a *saṃskāra* (consecratory rite). For *adhikāra* is postulated for the sake of obtaining a specific performance; but here, that is established simply by the observation of the specific object to be consecrated. Rules concerning *saṃskāras* require a purpose. In this case, the fruit of the action itself is what is to be accomplished by the injunction. And that, being situated in the object (*karman*) and characterized as "grasping," is clearly seen and is not contradictory.

Since no division is explicitly stated, the understanding of the division is derived from another Smṛti: "Brahmacarya for twelve years for each Veda" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.36). Which three Vedas are intended here? The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda. Now, what about the Atharvaveda? Who says this? However, in this context, as it is heard [in the text], the performance of the injunction is attained through its focus on the comprehension of meaning for the sake of fulfilling the requirements of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). For comprehension is useful for the performance of all ritual acts (*karman*). And the Atharvaveda contains many instructions on malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the like; therefore, rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are not enjoined therein, nor is anything subsidiary to them found there. The completion of all those subsidiaries, such as the duties of the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ priests, is accomplished by the Trayī (the three Vedas) alone. Furthermore, the originative injunctions (*utpatti-vidhi*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other primary rites exist only in the Trayī. The office of the Brahman priest (*brahmatva*) is also found only in the Trayī. Moreover, the word *tri* denotes a number. Numbers do not function without depending on some single property (*dharma*). Therefore, only those things which are intent upon the instruction of their specific functions can be designated by the word *tri*. The Atharvaveda does not enter into those functions. Therein, there are no originative injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, nor are there injunctions for their subsidiaries. In malevolent sacrifices such as the Śyena, the same officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the same procedure (*itikartavyatā*) apply. Even the specific details that differ are taught only in the Trayī. Thus, because the Ṛg, Yajus, and Ṛk-Sāmans cannot coexist in a single ritual, the designation "Trivedī" (Three Vedas) would be untenable if the Atharvaveda were included. Nevertheless, since the term *svādhyāya* (one's own study) refers to the Atharvaveda, its inclusion within the scope of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) is not contradictory.

"Half of that": the number thirty-six is being referred to here. Half of that is eighteen years. Here too, the division is conceived as six years. Here again, "one-quarter": a quarter is that same number divided into four parts, which is nine years. A fourth part. Three for each Veda. But how can a Veda be mastered in three years?
There may be someone who is most exceptionally intelligent.

Another says: Dharmas are not prompted by the essential nature of the learning (*grahaṇa*) itself; rather, they are prompted by the injunction (*vidhi*) concerning that object. In that case as well, once the learning has been completed, if the observance of the rules (*niyama*) is performed for certain days during the period of study, the purpose of the scripture is indeed accomplished. For the sake of the injunction regarding Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), the performance of the auxiliary components (*aṅga-kalāpa*) is fulfilled by that much alone. For one whose learning is not yet complete, the designation "one who has bathed after the vow" (*vrata-snātaka*) occurs upon the cessation of those specific vows. Therefore, the prescription of a specific time is logical: one does not become a *vrata-snātaka* without three years [of observance]. Although some Smṛti texts state, "The bath [of graduation] occurs upon the completion of the Veda," nevertheless, even upon the completion of the vows for that purpose, the usage is indeed stated figuratively (*upacārāt*).

That is incorrect. Even if [the observances] are prompted by an injunction, it is logical that the observances last only as long as the study [of the Veda], for they are enjoined in connection with the study. They ought to endure for the duration of the study. For if this were a separate statement, then by the force of the words alone, the three-year period of observances would apply even prior to the acquisition [of the Veda]. However, if it is a single statement meaning "until the acquisition [of the Veda]," then there is no cessation of the observances once the Veda has been acquired. By the use of the particle *eva* (only), they favor this very position.

If there is no cessation of that [duty] when the Veda has not been grasped, how then is there a distinct designation as "one who has bathed after the vows" (*vratasnātaka*) and "one who has bathed after the Veda" (*vedasnātaka*)?
We shall explain this in the fourth [chapter].
Having studied the Vedas— either all four, or two, or even one— in the proper order,
and having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.

The study of three Vedas has been prescribed. The study of one or two Vedas, which was not previously established as an option, is now provided as an alternative. It has been explained that the word "veda" refers to a *śākhā* (branch). One should study three *śākhās*, or two, or one, from each Veda, but not from only a single [Veda]. For it is recited that "the Trayī is the Trividyā."

Having studied and mastered the Veda according to the prescribed observances of the vow, one should dwell in the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*). The author will describe the nature of the householder’s stage in the passage beginning with, “A twice-born man should marry a wife” (MDh 3.4). He should “dwell” (*āvaset*), which means he should practice [it]. Verbal roots have multiple meanings; here the prefix *ā-* denotes a limit. By convention, one who has taken a wife is called a *gṛhastha* (householder); the word *gṛha* refers to a wife, and he dwells therein. The collection of prescribed matters consisting of injunctions and prohibitions pertaining to him is designated by the term *āśrama*. For example, for one who has been initiated, there is the student’s stage (*brahmacaryāśrama*) until his return home (*samāvartana*), and for one who has performed the marriage ceremony, there is the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*).

One whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is unviolated and unbroken—that is, who has desisted from sexual union with women—is described in this way. A syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) should be recognized here: "He shall be one whose celibacy is unviolated, and he shall enter the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*). If it were a single sentence, then in the event of a violation, his very eligibility for the householder's life would be lost. However, since it is prescribed here as a human duty (*puruṣārtha*), upon its transgression one is subject to expiation (*prāyaścitta*), but he does not cease to be eligible [for the householder's life].

In the injunction "having studied, one should settle down," only the sequence of priority (*paurvāparya*) is intended, not that marriage must occur immediately after study. This is because the suffix *-lyap* (in *adhītya*) prescribes a sequence, and immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not the literal meaning of the word. Consequently, it follows that between the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) and marriage, there is room for the study of sciences such as grammar for the purpose of understanding the meaning of the Veda. For only a learned person is qualified for the life of a householder (*gārhasthya*), not an ignorant one as might be implied by the rule for Vedic study. Although during childhood a boy possesses qualities similar to those of animals and is incapable of understanding his own qualification, he is nevertheless made to perform his duties by his father or teacher. In reality, the qualification belongs to these two alone. Since the injunction regarding the procreation of offspring is fulfilled by the father’s instruction of his child, the father has the authority over the child’s education. Education consists in establishing the child in both the spheres of what is enjoined and what is prohibited. In this regard, even if the child does not understand while being instructed, he is guided by the hand like a blind man. Just as he is held back from touching fire or falling into a well by a firm grasp of the hand, so too is he restrained from drinking liquor and other such acts that have unseen consequences (*adṛṣṭa*). Or, just as he is made to take medicine against his will, so too is he engaged in scriptural matters. When he has attained some degree of proficiency, he should be directed thus: "You ought to do this and that. This being the case, once the Veda has been studied, the young student (*māṇavaka*) must be enlightened by his father or teacher in this way: "You have mastered the Veda; you are now qualified to desire to know its meaning, and therefore you ought to hear its auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). By this much, the father’s obligation regarding the procreation of offspring is completed. As it has been said: "To what extent is a son considered 'procreated'? To the extent that he becomes one who has personally understood his duty."

Therefore, this is established: marriage does not take place merely after one has finished the formal study [of the Veda], as long as the meaning of the Veda has not been mastered. And thus the construction of the words should be made as follows: even when the study is completed (*adhītya*), one should remain one whose *brahmacarya* (celibacy) is unimpaired. Since the cessation [of study] has already occurred, the repetition [of the word *adhītya*] is intended to signify the cessation of other restrictive rules (*niyama*) such as the avoidance of honey and meat. Consequently, all these rules must be observed for as long as the study lasts; however, once the study is finished and during the time of understanding the meaning, only the cessation from women is to be practiced—sexual intercourse with women is not to be undertaken. Although the word *brahmacarya* is derived in that context as the undertaking of vows for the sake of grasping the *Brahman*, we shall demonstrate that its usage there is nevertheless directed solely toward the cessation from women.

In due order: by that very sequence of recitation which is well-known among students; first the *catuḥṣaṣṭi*, and then the *brāhmaṇa* which begins with the continuous account of one's lineage, such as one's father, grandfather, and so forth. For regarding such a matter, speakers do not say, "not by family, nor by character, nor by sequence. By this it is established: that very branch (*śākhā*) which was studied by one's ancestors must not be abandoned. (3.2)
One should first honor with a cow that son who is well-known for his own duty, who inherits the father's Vedic legacy, and who is seated upon the couch wearing a garland.

One should first honor with a cow that person who inherits the *brahmadāya*. He is called a *brahmadāyahara* because he takes—that is, appropriates—both *brahman* and *dāya*. *Dāya* means wealth, as it is given; *brahman* means the Veda; and *haraṇa* means acquisition. Having acquired the Veda and having been divided [in his inheritance] by his father, he enters the householder's state (*gārhasthya*), for one who lacks wealth has no entitlement [to it]. However, if the father is without wealth, then he should acquire wealth through the duty of providing progeny (*sāṃtānika*) and cause him to marry.
Others, however, consider this to be a restatement of the previously mentioned rule, interpreting *brahmadāya* as "the *brahman* itself is the *dāya*" (the inheritance). This refers to the father.

But surely, the teacher’s authority (*adhikāra*) regarding the instruction of the student has already been stated; why then is it said here that "the father is the one who receives the inheritance of the Veda" (*brahmadāyahara*)?

It is replied: for one whose father exists, that very person is the teacher. In the absence of the father, or if he is incapable, another has the authority. By the appointment of another teacher, the father’s authority indeed ceases. Whether he teaches himself or by means of appointing another makes no difference. As for what they say—that because a fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed as a constant rule in the initiation (*upanayana*), the act must necessarily be performed by another—[that is not so].

That is incorrect. For this rule—"the *vara* is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)"—applies specifically to the initiation (*upanayana*). And the initiator is either the father or the teacher; both of them, when engaged in their respective duties, do not require anything else for the purpose of bowing down (*ānamana*). Indeed, the giving of the fee is for the sake of inducing respect. However, for one already engaged in another duty, such respect is not required. Therefore, since the term *dakṣiṇā* lacks the sense of inducing respect here, it should be understood by implication as signifying a gift for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), like the giving of gold. Furthermore, the father himself must become the master of the boy with such wealth that the granting of the *vara* is accomplished for him.

Now, if this insistence is held—that the term *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) cannot logically apply except in the sense of a gift, and that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not permissible when a primary sense is available—then in that case, the rule regarding the sacrificial fee will apply to one who initiates himself, like Satyakāma, provided he has neither a father acting in his stead nor a teacher. For it has been established that even such a person, having somewhat outgrown childhood, possesses the qualification for self-purification.
Therefore, the father’s qualification exists in both ways: either when initiating himself or when employing another as his teacher.

"Pratītaḥ" means one who has become present for the undertaking of the householder's stage of life (*gṛhāśrama*), but not one who is *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate), even if he has completed the purpose of the rules for Vedic study, when returning to the village. "Wearing a garland" (*sragviṇam*) is intended to illustrate all those duties whatsoever that have been prescribed by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* for the ritual of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). "Seated on a couch" (*talpa āsīnam*) means seated upon a costly bed or sofa; it refers to one who is lying down as one entitled to the honor of worship. "With a cow and the honey-mixture" (*gavā madhuparkeṇa*): since this procedure is prescribed as optional (*pākṣika*) regarding the honey-mixture, the word "cow" here indicates the specific ritual act for which the cow is the means. "He should honor" (*arhayet*) means he should worship. By virtue of the context, it is either the father or the teacher [who performs this]. "First" (*prathamam*) means prior to the marriage. The phrase "in accordance with his own duty" (*svadharmeṇa*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*); there is no difference in meaning whether one connects it as "the receiver of the Brahman-inheritance according to his own duty" or "he should honor him according to his own duty. (3.3)
Having bathed with the permission of his teacher and returned home according to the prescribed rule,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who is endowed with auspicious marks.

Even when the completion of the Vedic study and vows has occurred, he should bathe once permitted—that is, authorized—by his teacher. By the word "bath" (*snāna*), a specific sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* is indicated; it marks the end of the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). How this term functions as an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) has been explained previously. On that very day, having undergone a certain sacramental rite consisting of the worship with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) as prescribed by the authors of the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, he is described as "one who has returned" (*samāvṛtta*) from the teacher’s house back to his father’s house. All of this is already established as a supplement to the injunction "he should marry" (*udvahet*); however, the "returning home" (*samāvartana*) is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the marriage itself. Therefore, for one who has studied the Vedas while remaining in his father’s house, marriage certainly takes place even though the formal "returning home" is impossible.

Some consider the *samāvartana* (the returning home) to be the ritual bath (*snāna*) that is an integral part of marriage. If it is argued that a distinction [between the two] is understood from the use of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*), then [we reply]: in that case, he will describe the *samāvartana* as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of a bath that is an auxiliary to marriage; for there, the bath is indeed prescribed with specific details in such passages as "by one who is a *snātaka*," and so forth.

Alternatively, the statement regarding "returning" (*samāvṛtti*) has the intention of referring to the abandonment of restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*). The meaning is that one who has returned has entered back into his previous state, which is devoid of such restraints. Furthermore, the statement regarding the abandonment of restraints intends a specific distinction: for the restraints and observances of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) are of a superior degree, whereas those of the subsequent stages are not so.

"According to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*) means "in accordance with his own duty" (*svadharmeṇa*). "A twice-born man should marry a wife" (*udvaheta bhāryām*): the term "should marry" (*udvaheta*) refers to the ritual procedure of marriage. Marriage is a sacramental act (*saṃskārakarma*), as indicated by the use of the accusative case in the word "wife" (*bhāryām*). Now, there is no such thing as a "wife" established prior to marriage for whom the sacrament of marriage could be performed—just as one cannot apply the ritual of collyrium to an eye that does not yet exist. What, then, is brought into being by marriage? Just as in the expression "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*), that to which the preparatory rites such as cutting are applied is called a "sacrificial post," so too it is through marriage itself that one becomes a "wife."

By the word *vivāha* (marriage), the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is meant; and that is the primary element here. For thus they record in tradition: "Marriage is the act of taking a wife, the taking of the hand. Here too, [the author] will say: "The sacrament of taking the hand" (MDh 3.43), which has the *lājā-homa* and other rites as its constituent parts. And all of that is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Because of the use of the term "maiden" (*kanyā*) in the rule, "One should not marry a tawny maiden" (MDh 3.8), this is a sacrament for a maiden and not for every woman. Furthermore, we shall explain that in this context the word "maiden" refers to a female who has not yet engaged in sexual intercourse with a male.

"Of the same caste" means belonging to the same class. "Endowed with *lakṣaṇas*" means possessed of those marks—such as color, lines, and moles—which, as understood through the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), indicate freedom from widowhood, progeny, and wealth; thus, the meaning is "endowed with auspicious marks. Although there are also marks that indicate undesirable things, one should nevertheless marry such a girl according to the very scriptures that describe them; therefore, she should be understood as "possessing marks" (*lakṣaṇavatī*) in the sense of having praiseworthy marks. In common usage, the word *lakṣaṇa* is employed specifically to indicate what is intended [to be auspicious]; for instance, when one says "this man is *salakṣaṇa*" or "this woman is *salakṣaṇā*," it is only she who possesses auspicious marks who is so described.

In this regard, an investigation into the qualification (*adhikāra*) must be undertaken. Because it is a rite of consecration (*saṃskāra-vidhi*), its performance is established just like the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*); for just as the establishment of the fires is performed for the sake of accomplishing the *āhavanīya* and other fires—which are auxiliary to both obligatory and optional rites by serving as their medium—so too is marriage. This is because marriage, by means of producing a wife, serves both visible and invisible human goals. To explain: when a man’s inclination toward sexual gratification would otherwise result in a mere pursuit of women in general, the prohibition against approaching maidens or the wives of others ensures that the lustful man finds satisfaction only within his own wife. Furthermore, through the injunction "One should practice dharma together [with her]" (*Śabara-bhāṣya* 6.1.17; cf. *Gautama-dharma-sūtra* 4.7), she shares in the qualification for all religious duties; thus, the attainment of the invisible human goal (*adṛṣṭa-puruṣārtha*) is dependent upon her.

On this point, some reflect as follows: those possessed of passion perform marriage of their own accord for the sake of accomplishing what has been seen [in worldly experience], according to the manner previously described. For those who have performed marriage, that marriage may serve the purpose of accomplishing the performance of ritual acts (*karma*), by virtue of its being prescribed as a duty for the twice-born (*dvijāti*). However, for one whose attachment to women has somehow ceased, there is no marriage. Since there is no entitlement to ritual acts in the absence of marriage, and since there is no fault in the non-performance of duties by one who lacks such entitlement, it is not contradictory for even one who is not in a stage of life (*anāśramin*) to remain without performing the practices aimed at human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

This is incorrect. Just as desire (*kāma*) is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), so too is duty (*dharma*) a motivator for the status of being a human goal; indeed, everyone acts for the sake of accomplishing some human goal. If this were not the case, such statements as "having remained without an order of life (*anāśramī*) for a year" (cf. Medhātithi on 6.87) would be untenable. We shall determine this precisely in the sixth [chapter] during the discussion on the optionality of the orders of life (*āśrama-vikalpa*). 3.4.
He now shows what kind of maiden is to be married:
"She who is not a sapinda of the mother and not of the same gotra as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the rites of marriage for sexual union. (3.5)

A woman who is a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother and belongs to the same *gotra* as the father is recommended for marriage. The mention of *sapiṇḍa* is intended to indicate the maternal relatives (*mātṛbandhu*). For the *sapiṇḍya* of women according to another *smṛti* extends up to the third generation from the mother; however, marriage beyond three generations of the maternal kin is not permitted, but rather beyond the fifth. Thus Gautama recites: "Beyond the seventh [generation] from the paternal kin and beyond the fifth from the maternal kin" (GDh 4.3–5). Therefore, since there is no literal consistency with the text [of Manu], the absence of *sapiṇḍya* must be explained by way of maternal connection according to other *smṛtis*. By this it would be stated that a wife born from the lineage of the mother is not [permissible]. And the limit is indeed that of Gautama. Consequently, a girl born in the lineage of the maternal grandfather or the maternal great-grandfather should not be married until the fifth degree, because of the proximity of kinship within the line of the son's progeny. Hence, there is a prohibition against all those born in the lineage of the maternal grandmother and her daughters, as well as those born in the lineage of the maternal great-grandmother, because there is no difference in their status as kin.

"And one who is not of the same *gotra* as the father. *Gotra* is traditionally defined as a lineage such as Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Garga, and so forth. Those of the same *gotra*, such as the Vasiṣṭhas, do not marry among themselves, nor do the Gargas marry among themselves. However, in the case of a Vasiṣṭha, there is a prohibition even against one who is of the same *gotra* as the mother: "Having married a woman of the same *gotra* or likewise the same *pravara*, a twice-born man should abandon her and perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
As well as the daughter of one's maternal uncle and likewise one who belongs to the same lineage as one's mother.

Gautama, however, recites: "Marriage [is permitted] with those who do not share the same *pravara*" (GDh 4.2). In that case, even if there is identity of *gotra*, if there is a difference in *pravara*, marriage is appropriate. That is incorrect, because in another *smṛti* both are prohibited: "One born from a lineage (*ārṣa*) and *gotra* different from one's own" (YDh 1.53). *Ārṣa* and *pravara* have the same meaning. But how can there be identity of *ṛṣi* (*samānārṣeya*) when there is a difference of *gotra*, if it is so recorded in tradition? This matter is based on the authority of *śruti* and *smṛti*; it is not within the scope of direct perception such that a contradiction would arise. What, then, are these things called *pravara*? This is stating too little. This must also be explained: what indeed is this thing called "Brahminhood," and likewise, what is this thing called "lineage" (*gotra*)? Just as there is a distinction such as Brahminhood despite the commonality of being human, so too, despite the commonality of Brahminhood, there is a division of lineages such as Vasiṣṭha and others; and for each lineage, there are shared *ṛṣis*. One whose *gotra* is this must perform the invocation of the *pravara* by means of those names. The same applies to the prohibition of marriage. And the authors of the *sūtras* record the *pravara*s in connection with the division of *gotra*: "For one whose *gotra* is this, these are the *pravara*s. However, the division of *gotra* is known only by those born of that *gotra*. It is recorded: "We are Parāśaras; we are Upamanyus. Although they record the *pravara*s just like the *gotra*s, nevertheless, because of their multiplicity, they might perhaps forget them; thus, taking the *gotra* as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), the recording of the *pravara*s was composed. They do, however, remember the *gotra*. And for that, there is no further defining characteristic such as: "He who is of such a form, his *gotra* is this. That is all there is to the memory in that regard: as far as the *gotra* extends, there is a commonality of species within the lineage.

Furthermore, this distinction between *gotra* and *pravara* applies to Brāhmaṇas, not to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. For thus says the author of the Kalpasūtra: "Because of their service as domestic priests, [the *pravara* of] Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas [is determined]. Although this statement regarding the *pravara* section would be appropriate even as a prohibition of what was otherwise obtained when there is a designation of a specific *gotra*, they do not possess a traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*) of their *gotras*. What, then, is the rule for the limit of kinship even in the marriage of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas?

It is said: this [rule] regarding "beyond the seventh from paternal kinsmen" (GDh 4.3) pertains to all castes. Here too, she must be of a different *gotra*; and because of the word "and" (*ca*), she must also be one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*. Thus, the term *sapiṇḍa*, being carried over [from the previous rule], serves—as before—to indicate a relationship by kinship. By this, the prohibition is established for women descended from the father's sister, as well as other women in the lineage of the great-grandfather, up to the seventh person. For it is recorded in tradition that *sapiṇḍas* extend to the limit of the seventh person.

Others, however, say that *gotra* means lineage (*vaṃśa*). In that case, there is no requirement for a specific limit; as long as it is known that "we belong to one and the same lineage," there is no marriage. Even under this view, the phrase "and not a *sapiṇḍa*" continues to apply. Consequently, as before, there is a prohibition against marrying the daughters of one's father’s sister and others. However, under this view, a prohibition against those of the same *ṛṣi* and *gotra* would be difficult to establish, for in their case it is not the case that "we belong to one and the same lineage."

It is said: they support this with historical observation. For therein they describe: "The seer (ṛṣi), such as Vasiṣṭha and others, is the original founder of the lineage; those born from him belong to that *gotra*, and the *pravara*s are his sons and grandsons. These [ancestors] became most renowned through their possession of qualities such as excellence in austerity and learning. This very rule is established by another *smṛti* text.

However, this point must be examined here: regarding the phrase "with those who have the same *pravara*," the identity [of *pravara*] is based on name and not on number. As for the identity of names, does the prohibition apply only where all [names] are identical, or even when just one is identical? In that regard, if *pravara-hood* belongs to the collection [of names] as a whole, then when one [name] is the same but another is different, a different collection has arisen; thus, because the *pravara* is not identical, there would be no prohibition. In this way, marriage would be permitted between the Upamanyus and the Parāśaras. Their lineage (*gotra*) is distinct: one group is the Upamanyus, the others are the Parāśaras, and according to the aforementioned principle, there is a difference in *pravara*. The *pravara* of the Upamanyus is Vasiṣṭha, Bhāradvāja, and Ekapāt; that of the Parāśaras is Vasiṣṭha, Gārgya, and Pārāśarya. Alternatively, if *pravara-hood* belongs to each individual [name], then there is a prohibition even when only one is the same. For example, as in the case of the rule "beans should not be eaten," they are not eaten even when mixed together.

What, then, is the correct position here? That each one individually possesses the status of being a *pravara*. For thus is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) observed: "He chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three. Thus, it is understood that there is one [lineage]. Even when those are equal, it says: "There is no intermarriage among these."

The mention of the "twice-born" (*dvijāti*) is for the sake of illustration; for even in the case of a Śūdra, there is [the rule]: "up to the seventh [generation] from the father and the fifth from the mother. "Taking a wife" (*dārakaraṇa*) means the act of taking a wife, the rite of marriage. In this context, "praiseworthy" (*praśastā*) means prescribed by way of praise. "Sexual" (*maithunī*): that which exists in sexual union (*mithuna*) is "sexual"; that which is not sexual is "non-sexual" (*amaithunī*). This is connected with "of the father," meaning she is produced solely from the father's seed as soon as she is born. Since *niyoga* (levirate) is prescribed, there is no prohibition for one produced thereby by the aforementioned qualifications. Therefore, she is prohibited separately as "non-sexual. Consequently, one produced by *niyoga* should not be married at will because she is sexual.

Others, however, read "amaithune" (not for sexual intercourse). [The bride] is praised for the purpose of dharma in the act of taking a wife, but not for sexual intercourse. And this is a praise, not a prohibition. Such a wife, even though there be sexual intercourse, exists solely for the sake of dharma. (3.5)
Even if they are great and prosperous in cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain—one should avoid these ten types of families in forming a marriage alliance. (3.6)

This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the prohibition that is about to be stated. *Samṛddhi* means prosperity; *dhana* means wealth or power. The word "even" (*api*) implies "even though they are great" or "even though they are excellent. He says "cows, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain" (*go'jāvidhanadhānyataḥ*) as a qualification of "wealth. The suffix *-tasi* is used here in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*). Thus, it means "by means of cows, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain. The mention of "wealth" (*dhana*) serves to qualify the cows, goats, and so forth; it refers to those cows, goats, etc., which constitute wealth. For grain is indeed a form of wealth. *Strīsaṃbandha* means marriage; it is a connection for the purpose of obtaining a wife. (3.6)

Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic desire, those with hairy anal folds, and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy—[these should be avoided]. (3.7)

In that family where the rites such as the *jātakarma* (birth-rite) and other sacraments (*saṃskāras*) have been abandoned, and where the obligatory five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) and so forth are not performed; where it is devoid of males—that is, where only women give birth, and generally daughters are born rather than sons; where there is no Vedic study (*niśchandaḥ*); where there is excessive hairiness or hemorrhoids (*romaśārśasam*); where there is consumption (*kṣaya*), which is the disease of pulmonary tuberculosis (*rājayakṣmā*); where there is chronic illness (*āmayāvī*), meaning a weak digestion in whom the food eaten does not properly digest; epilepsy (*apasmāra*), which causes impairment of memory and other faculties; vitiligo (*śvitra*), which is a white, cutaneous discoloration on the body; and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), which is well known—all these words from "hairiness" onwards denote specific diseases and are indicated with possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*). The ancient commentators have described the basis for this prohibition: "Children imitate the two-footed [ancestors]. Therefore, the offspring of those who have abandoned the rites and so forth would also possess that same character. Furthermore, diseases are contagious. Thus it is stated in medical science (*vaidyaka*): "All diseases are contagious, with the exception of dysentery (*pravāhikā*). (3.7)
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.

The previous prohibition was based on family lineage; this one, however, is based on physical characteristics. A woman whose hair is tawny (*kadru*) or golden in color is called *kapilā*. One with extra limbs is one who has six fingers (or toes). A sickly woman is one afflicted by many diseases or seized by a malady difficult to treat. The suffix *-in* is used here either in the sense of abundance or in the sense of constant connection. One without hair is one without body hair; "hair" (*loman*) refers to both body hair and head hair. This refers to the total absence of hair on the middle of the arms or on both shanks. A talkative woman speaks excessively and harshly even when there is very little to be said. A *piṅgalā* is one whose eyes are circular due to eye disease, or one whose eyes are tawny-brown. (3.8)

One should not marry a girl whose name is that of a lunar mansion, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one with a terrifying name. (3.9)

*Ṛkṣa* is a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); [names] derived from that are *Ārdrā*, *Jyeṣṭhā*, and so forth. A tree (*vṛkṣa*) is one named after a tree, such as *śiṃśapā* or *āmalakī*. A river (*nadī*) is the Gaṅgā or Yamunā; [names] derived from those are likewise. The compound *ṛkṣāṇi ca vṛkṣāś ca nadyaś ca* (lunar mansions, trees, and rivers) is a *dvandva*; "names of those" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Then, with the second word *nāma*, there is a compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). Names ending in [the suffix] *-ī* include *barbarī*, *śabarī*, and so forth. Mountains (*parvata*) are the Vindhya, Malaya, and others; the suffix is applied as before to form the compound. A bird (*pakṣin*) is one named after a bird, such as *śukī* or *sārikā*. A snake (*ahi*) is a serpent; [names] derived from that are *vyālī* or *bhujaṅgī*. A servant (*preṣyā*) is a female slave, a maid, or a handmaid (*ceṭī*, *daranī*). *Bibhiṣaṇa* means "fear-inducing"; [names] such as *ḍākinī* or *rākṣasī* [fall under this category]. (3.9)

One should marry a woman whose limbs are free from defects, who has an auspicious name, who walks with the gait of a swan or an elephant, whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft. (3.10)

"One whose limbs are unimpaired" (*avyaṅgāṅgīm*): she whose limbs (*aṅgāni*) are unimpaired (*avyaṅgāni*) is so described. Although the word *avyaṅga*—like words such as *pravīṇa* or *udāra*—is etymologically derived as "one whose limbs are not deficient" (*avikalāny aṅgāni yasya*), nevertheless, because it is more appropriate for the second word *aṅga* to denote the whole (*avayavin*), the term *avyaṅga* refers here to the perfection of physical form. "Gentle" (*saumyam*) means sweet; this is shown in the verse: "That which is easy for women to utter" (MDh 2.33). She walks like a swan or like an elephant; that is, her gait possesses the graceful, slow movement characteristic of swans and elephants. The word *tanu* does not mean "small," but rather refers to a moderate dimension. She is called *tanvaṅgī* who is neither too stout nor too thin. She is one whose limbs are soft, pleasant to the touch, non-hard, and non-rough. He should marry such a woman; since the context concerns maidens, he should marry a maiden.

If this is so, then the prohibition beginning with "not one who has no pubic hair" is redundant, since the non-marriageability of a woman who does not possess such characteristics is already established by this very injunction.
True, it is so; however, when a single meaning is presented through both the mode of affirmation and the mode of negation, it is understood more clearly.

In this context, the word *kanyā* (virgin) refers, by virtue of the subject matter, to women who have not experienced sexual intercourse. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "One should take as a wife a suitable woman who has not experienced sexual intercourse" (VaDh 8.1). Furthermore, one who has been consecrated by one [man] cannot be consecrated again by another, because that which has already been done cannot be done again. Therefore, in the case of a married woman whose union with her husband has not yet occurred—who becomes unchaste (*svairiṇī*) due to some cause such as her husband's absence—there is no marriage with another even though she retains the status of a *kanyā*. It is for such a case that the statement of Vasiṣṭha cited above was placed in the middle [of the discussion]. It is also stated elsewhere: "One should marry a woman who has belonged to no other [man before], who is younger [than oneself], and who has brothers" (cf. YDh 1.52). || 3.10 ||
But a wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother or whose father is unknown, for fear that she may be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter). (3.11)

One should not marry her who has no brother, due to the suspicion of her being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), that is, due to the suspicion that she might be an appointed daughter. This means: "Perhaps the status of an appointed daughter was once conferred upon her by her father"—it is out of this suspicion, this doubt, [that one should not marry her]. And how does this suspicion arise?

If the father is not known—whether he has gone abroad or is deceased—and she is given away by her mother or by the father’s *sapiṇḍas*, it is recorded in the *smṛti* that when the time has arrived and the father is absent, she may be given away even by these others. We shall demonstrate this *smṛti* passage later. However, as long as the father is known to be alive, there is no suspicion of her being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), for he himself says, "Whether she is [already] given or not. The word "or" (*vā*) should be understood here in the sense of "if" (*cet*). If the father is not known to be alive, then the girl must not be married.

Others, however, maintain that these two negations are independent. If it were not known [that she was born] from a father, then the prohibition would apply to one secretly born (*gūḍhotpannā*). And the connection is as follows: one should not marry a girl who has no brother, for fear that she might be an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). In this context, the phrase "it should not be known" is not connected with the clause "for fear of her being an appointed daughter."

In this context, where there is no prohibition based on direct perception—as in the verse, “and she who is not a sapinda” (MDh 3.5)—if that [prohibition] is transgressed, the very essence of marriage is not accomplished. Therefore, even if a marriage with a woman of the same *gotra* or similar prohibited kin has been performed, it is as if it were never performed. Because marriage, like the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), consists in the comprehension of the injunction, it ceases to exist upon the transgression of that injunction. Just as in the rite of establishing the sacred fires, if any subsidiary element is not known and thus absent, the *āhavanīya* fire and others do not come into being; likewise, a woman of the same *gotra* does not attain the status of a wife. Consequently, such a woman must be abandoned, even if she has undergone the formalities of that sacrament. The venerable Vasiṣṭha and others also prescribe penance for such a marriage. Although the deficiency resulting from the transgression of a prohibition regarding a subsidiary part of a ritual belongs to the rite itself and not directly to the person, nevertheless, penance is prescribed by explicit scriptural statement. Alternatively, approaching a woman of the same *gotra* is forbidden; therefore, the penance mentioned applies to one who engages in the act intended for that purpose.

However, as for the prohibition against those deficient in ritual acts and so forth, because that is rooted in the observation of visible [worldly] consequences, the marriage is annulled; she does not become his wife, and there is no abandonment of her. It is for this very purpose that the verse beginning with "even great" (MDh 3.6) is recited as a distinction from the preceding prohibition, for the sake of praise. And such indeed is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*): one may sometimes marry a woman who is deformed, for example, but never one of the same lineage (*sagotrā*). 3.11.
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] are permissible in order of descending rank. (3.12)

Regarding the rule, "A twice-born man shall marry a wife" (MDh 3.4), although there is an accusative case ending indicating the wife as the primary object (*pradhāna*) and the marriage as a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*), the singular number of the word *bhāryām* is intended to be significant. This is because it is an object of reference (*uddeśya*) within a restatement (*anuvāda*), just as in the injunction "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*). When something whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is already known from another source is restated elsewhere for the purpose of prescribing a different function, the restatement refers to that very nature as it was previously understood; for example, "he cleanses the house" (*gṛhaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). Since a restatement depends on prior knowledge, the cups (*graha*) have their number already determined by such sentences as, "The Adhvaryu priest takes these ten cups at the morning libation," and their function is likewise known from the statement, "He offers oblations with the cups" (*grahair juhoti*). Therefore, because the word *graha* depends on this prior understanding, its singular number is not intended to be significant. In the present case, however, the entity characterized as a "wife" is not established through any other source and must be understood from this very sentence. Consequently, it is perceived exactly as it is heard in the text; like the meaning of the nominal stem itself, the singular number is also intended to be significant. This will be explained in detail with logical reasoning in the fifth book (*pañcama-adhyāya*).

When the intention to specify a number is established, even if a second marriage is performed, she does not attain the status of a wife; just as when there is already an *āhavanīya* fire, a second *āhavanīya* fire does not exist. Yet, the taking of another wife is desired under certain circumstances; for that purpose, this [rule] is commenced. With this very point in mind, it is stated in the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra*: "If one's wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring, one should not take another; but if either of these is lacking, one may take another. (ĀpDh 2.11.12).

A *savarṇā* is one of the same caste. She is recommended first and foremost for one who has not previously taken a wife of a different caste. However, if after marrying a *savarṇā*, he by some chance finds no pleasure with her, or if his purpose regarding offspring is not accomplished, then—regarding activity motivated by desire—these following women of lower castes than the *savarṇā* are to be known as superior from the scripture. Thus, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of singleness and the restriction to a *savarṇā*.

But surely, in the case of marriage with a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*), dependence is understood; it is not plurality that is intended for a woman of the same caste. At least, the transgression of the number one is perceived [in the rule]. If it is argued that this has already been superseded by the permission to marry women of different castes (*asavarṇā*), then who would prohibit marriage with a woman of the same caste? Likewise, Gautama has stated without qualification: "But when either of these is lacking, he should marry" (*anyatarāpāye tu kurvīta*). Furthermore, in the subsequent verse, the phrase "she and his own" (*sā ca svā ca*) indicates that marriage with a woman of the same caste exists. (3.12)

A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as a wife for a Śūdra; she and one of his own [caste] are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and one of his own for a Kṣatriya; and those three and one of his own for a Brāhmaṇa. (3.13)

When there is a difference in caste, the restriction to a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is established. Just as for a Brāhmaṇa, three [wives] beginning with the Kṣatriya are permitted, so too for a Śūdra, wives of lower castes such as washerwomen or carpenters would be obtained; therefore, this rule regarding a wife of the same caste is stated. However, a woman of a higher caste was not previously obtained, because of the mention of "succession" (*krama*) in the preceding [verse].

And for a Vaiśya, those two—the Śūdra and his own [Vaiśya wife]—are permitted; and for a Rājanya, those two—the Vaiśya and the Śūdra—and his own [Rājanya wife]. Thus it is for the *agrajanman*, the Brāhmaṇa. Although the exposition should have been made according to the order of the Brāhmaṇas, the fact that it is presented starting from the Śūdra serves to reinforce the very point previously stated: "The option follows the sequence [of castes]; there is not necessarily a conjunction. (3.13)
For it is taught that, even in times of distress, a Śūdra woman is not prescribed as a wife for either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, regardless of the circumstances. (3.14)

Even if a Śūdra woman is exceedingly beautiful, and the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya are of heroic nature such that they might reach even the tenth stage of life, nevertheless, they must not marry a Śūdra woman. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). It is taught—that is, described—not in any account whatsoever, nor even in any historical narrative or legend. [This applies] in the event of a most severe calamity, that is, in an extreme emergency.
Since she was permitted previously but is now prohibited by this [text], there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two.

Now, one might object: when two scriptural injunctions (*śāstralakṣaṇa*) meet upon a single subject, an option (*vikalpa*) is appropriate—such as the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—but this is not the case here with respect to an activity characterized by passion (*rāgalakṣaṇā*) being prohibited. Furthermore, marriage with a Śūdra woman is not characterized by scripture; rather, the meaning of the preceding rule is that such an inclination toward her arises solely from passion and is not itself prohibited. The prohibition, however, pertains to what is characterized by scripture; thus, a Śūdra woman is certainly not to be married. Intending exactly this, Yājñavalkya stated: "As for that which is said regarding the taking of a Śūdra wife by the twice-born—that is not my opinion" (YDh 1.56).

To this it is replied: In every case, an option (*vikalpa*) is resorted to precisely because an injunction would otherwise be purposeless. If there were an absolute prohibition against Śūdras, then only the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas would be the subject of the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding permission in times of distress. Both the scriptural counter-exception (MDh 3.13) and this prohibition would be rendered useless, since [marriage with] a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is already established by rule. Therefore, this permitted [rule] and the prohibition, being mutually contradictory, are to be treated as optional alternatives.
But surely there is freedom of choice regarding optional rites, since they are established precisely by way of counter-exception (*pratiprasava*); thus, no prohibition need be stated. [Response:
It is not as one pleases regarding the marriage of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, but it is not so for a Śūdra woman; except in times of distress, [marrying her] is more serious.

However, it is proper to understand this: since the exclusion of non-Savarṇa women is already established by implication through the restrictive rule regarding Savarṇa women, the specific mention of the exclusion of Śūdra women indicates that the exclusion of non-Savarṇa women is not absolute. And because it is not absolute, this understanding arises—that in times of distress or when a Savarṇa woman is unavailable—a Śūdra woman must not be married, but others may be. (3.14)
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth, swiftly reduce their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras. (3.15)

This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serving as a supplement to the preceding prohibition. "Of low caste" refers specifically to the Śūdra, because that alone is the subject under discussion, and because of the concluding statement: "they [lead] their lineages to the state of Śūdras. These twice-born men, through delusion—that is, through lack of discernment born of greed for wealth, or due to the motive of desire—cause their families to descend into the state of Śūdras. The sons born of such women become Śūdras, and so too do their sons and grandsons. Now, it is said: "together with their lineages. A lineage (*saṃtāna*) is the continuous succession of offspring, consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth. (3.15)
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her. (3.16)

"He who marries a Śūdra woman"—that is, he who takes her in marriage—"he falls," meaning he becomes like an outcast (*patita*). Atri was the son of Utathya; this is their opinion, according to Upaskara. This half-verse is a supplement to the preceding prohibition. According to Śaunaka, [the prohibition applies] because of the birth of a son. This is another scriptural tradition (*śāstrāntara*); having permitted approaching a Śūdra woman during her season (*ṛtu*), it prohibits it by specifying the consequence of procreation, for the birth of a son occurs on even nights during the season. The meaning is: "One should not approach a Śūdra woman during her season. According to Bhṛgu, it is due to the status of being her offspring. This too is another Smṛti text. He whose offspring are those very ones born of a Śūdra woman is *tadapatya*; the state of being such is *tadapatyatā*. This is the opinion of Bhṛgu: one may approach women of higher castes even during the season, provided the offspring is already established. And the statement regarding his falling is merely a censure here, not an indication that he is subject to the legal status of an outcast, as in the passage beginning with "The water of those who have fallen... (MDh 11.182). We shall explain this further. 3.16.
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood. (3.17)

This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). If one procreates a son through her, he then falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa; thus, it is a mere censure that the offspring lacks Brāhmaṇahood. Furthermore, because of the masculine gender used in the word *suta* ("son"), even though the phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*) is the same, the phrase *sutotpattiḥ* ("procreation of a son") is intended to mean specifically "the birth of a son. This is demonstrated by the statement: "The even nights are to be avoided. (3.17)
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are dominated by that [greed], neither the ancestors nor the gods will eat; he does not go to heaven. (3.18)

This prohibition is absolute. Even if, for some reason, a Śūdra woman is married, these rites—those in which she is the primary agent—must not be performed. The meaning is that she has no entitlement to participate in religious duty (*dharma*) alongside him as a woman of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) does. Since entitlement would arise from her status as a wife, this is a prohibition. Therefore, when he employs wealth for his own religious duties, her permission is not required, as it is in the case of women of the twice-born castes. However, in matters other than *dharma*—namely, in regard to wealth and pleasure—she is certainly not to be disregarded. Her employment in tasks like a servant is not forbidden; thus, there would be no fault in having her perform work such as husking grain during a *śrāddha* ceremony and the like. But she must not be made to perform tasks such as serving food.

In this context, *daiva* (divine) action refers to rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, as well as the feeding of Brahmins with a deity in mind, as explained under the rule "one who observes a vow" (MDh 2.189). *Pitrya* (ancestral) action refers to *śrāddha* ceremonies, water libations (*udakatarpaṇa*), and so forth. *Ātitheya* (hospitality) refers to the honoring of a guest through food, water for the feet (*pādya*), and other services.
But is there not already a prohibition [against marrying] in the verse, "with another woman of the same caste who is established [as a wife]" (MDh 9.87)?

Not at all. For it is heard there [in the text]: "by one who is present. If a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) who is in her season (*ṛtumatī*) is somehow not present, [the act] would apply to a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman. Furthermore, this is not a prohibition regarding eligibility (*adhikāra*); rather, it concerns the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth. It is prescribed as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) that "the clarified butter is to be inspected by the wife. In the word "wife" (*patnī*), when it comes to ritual purposes, a performance by whichever woman is available occurs without restriction. Just as among several wives of the same caste, the act is performed by whichever wife of the same caste is available, so too, this prohibition is for the purpose of ensuring that it is not done by one of a different caste (*asavarṇā*). Primacy [is attributed to the wife] because of her status as the one eligible [for the primary role].

"The ancestors and gods do not eat from him"—thus he states the fruitlessness of his ritual action. Nor does he go to heaven; even if a guest eats, the fruit thereof, such as heaven and so forth, does not accrue to him. The mention of "heaven" is intended to indicate the fruits of honoring a guest in general, and it serves as a restatement of what was said in passages such as, "It brings wealth and fame" (MDh 3.106). 3.18.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a *vṛṣalī*, who has been defiled by her breath, and who has even begotten a child upon her, no atonement is prescribed. (3.19)

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). *Vṛṣalīphena* means the saliva from the mouth of a *vṛṣalī*; it refers to one by whom that has been drunk. The inversion of the word order [in *vṛṣalīphena*] is like [the compounds] *palāṇḍubhakṣita* and so forth. There is an alternative reading: *vṛṣalīpītaphenasya*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that whose foam has been drunk" (*pītaḥ pheno yasya*); thus, it is "the foam drunk by a *vṛṣalī*" (*vṛṣalyā pītaphenaḥ*). The compound is formed by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "after a word ending in the third case" (*tṛtīyā*, Pāṇini 2.1.30). Alternatively, in the analysis "the foam drunk by him" (*pītaḥ pheno 'nena*), it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*, Pāṇini 2.2.8) with *vṛṣalyāḥ*. However, the meaning remains the same in all these grammatical operations (*vṛtti*s). When two people are engaged in sexual union, kissing the lower lip and so forth necessarily occurs; by this concomitant attribute (*sahacāridharma*), the connection to sexual intercourse is indicated. Furthermore, because of the context, this is a supplementary rule to the prohibition of marriage and not an independent sentence. For if it were an independent statement, the duty of ritual appointment (*niyoga*) would be highly esteemed as excluding kissing and the like. Therefore, one who approaches a Śūdra woman while avoiding kissing and such acts does not transgress any purpose of the scripture.
And "of one born of her" means of one who approaches her during her season; "there is no atonement" means there is no purification—this is an expression of extreme censure. [72] 3.19.
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women among all four social classes, which lead to welfare or harm both in this world and after death. (3.20)

This is a brief introduction to what is about to be explained. "Beneficial and non-beneficial": some are beneficial, others are not. "Eight" is the specification of the number. "Summary" means a concise statement. "Marriages for the purpose of consecrating women" refers to the marriages of women (*strīvivāhāḥ*). But what, then, is this thing called "marriage"? It is the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) performed with its constituent parts and procedures for the purpose of making her a wife of the girl who has been obtained through the proper means; it is characterized by the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) and extends as far as the sighting of the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*). (3.20)
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, the Āsura, the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest. (3.21)
These are the names of those indicated as eight by number [73]. The mention of "inferior" (adharma) is for the purpose of censuring the Piśāca marriage. 3.21.
I shall declare to you all that which is the righteous duty of each caste, as well as the virtues and faults belonging to each, and the merits and demerits pertaining to procreation.

"Lawful" (*dharmya*) means not departing from the Dharma; that is to say, it is prescribed by the scriptures. Regarding the marriage, its "qualities and defects" (*guṇadoṣau*) consist in being the cause of desirable or undesirable results. "In offspring," meaning in the birth of children, there are qualities and defects—where "qualities" refers to virtues and "defects" to vices. For the groom alone, these qualities and defects consist in [attaining] heaven, hell, and so forth; their purpose is, by implication, heaven and the like. Since such [marriages] are indeed of this nature, they state again what has already been explained for the sake of further comprehension. (3.22)

One should know that for a Brahmin there are six [kinds of marriage] in succession, and for a Kshatriya four, starting from the lower ones; for a Vaishya and a Shudra, however, one should know those same [four] as lawful and not Rākṣasa.

There are six forms of marriage for a Brāhmaṇa in their proper order. "Order" means sequence; it is the enumeration of names in successive order. For the Kṣatra—the word *kṣatra* being a synonym for the Kṣatriya—one should know that the four inferior ones following [the first two], namely the Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca, are permitted. For the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, those same [forms] are permitted, excluding the Rākṣasa. (3.23)
The wise know that the first four [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone for a Kṣatriya; and the Āsura for both Vaiśyas and Śūdras. (3.24)

This prohibition of the Āsura and Gāndharva forms applies to the Brāhmaṇa because of the prescription of the Brāhma and other forms for him. Likewise, for the Kṣatriya, only the Rākṣasa form is permitted, not the Gāndharva or Āsura; for the Vaiśya and Śūdra, only the Āsura is permitted. There is an option (*vikalpa*) among those forms that are both prescribed and prohibited. Consequently, when that which is prescribed as obligatory (*nityavat*) is absent, one proceeds to the options. If a man, regardless of the absence of his specifically prescribed marriage form, were to proceed first to those forms that are both prescribed and prohibited, the author of the *Śāstra* has shown that the man would incur sin and undesirable offspring would be produced—by means of the verse beginning with "and the merits and demerits in the offspring" (MDh 3.22)—but this does not mean the cessation of the essential nature of the marriage itself, as is the case with marrying a *sapiṇḍa* woman. (3.24)
Of these five, three are considered lawful and two unlawful in this world;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura rites must never be performed.

This Smṛti rule concerns Kṣatriyas and others, not Brāhmaṇas, because it contradicts [the rules for] the Rākṣasa form of marriage; for a Brāhmaṇa ought not to perform killing or wounding, since this practice is logically applicable only to the domain of Kṣatriyas and others. Among the five forms of marriage, three beginning with the Prājāpatya are lawful (dharmya); two are not to be performed—the Paiśāca and the Āsura. Although the Prājāpatya is not prescribed for Kṣatriyas and others, it is here ordained for them, as is the Rākṣasa for Vaiśyas and Śūdras. There is a prohibition against the Āsura and the Paiśāca.

The established rule here is as follows: there are six forms of marriage for a Brāhmaṇa. Among them, the *brāhma* is the best of all; inferior to that are the *daiva* and *prājāpatya*; even inferior to those is the *ārṣa*; then the *gāndharva*; and even inferior to that is the *āsura*.
