For those who hold the view that this verse refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas, they maintain that even the *rākṣasa* form is permissible for a Brāhmaṇa who has adopted the conduct of a Kṣatriya. Furthermore, they consider that even for one engaged in improper acts (*vikarmastha*), provided he undergoes penance for killing or wounding, the *rākṣasa* is not excluded from being a valid marriage.

In this regard, the superiority of the *brāhma* marriage is demonstrated by its fruit alone. The inferiority of the other three is established by the absence of a prohibition, precisely because their fruits are stated to be diminished. Furthermore, since the *āsura* marriage is prescribed for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is understood through the principle of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) that it does not apply to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. The statement "six" is a general injunction (*vidhāna*). Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*), and that is determined by specific circumstances (*vyavasthayā*). The recourse to that [option] is equal when the others are impossible. Indeed, an option is established—just as in the case of rice and barley—and because multiple forms of marriage are enjoined, their simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*) is impossible. Even if such a combination were possible, that [marriage] would yield inferior results in terms of both spiritual merit (*dharma*) and offspring.

Now, regarding the Kṣatriya, the Rākṣasa form is primary because it is prescribed by four verses as an alternative. By the word "four," the Āsura, Gāndharva, and Paiśāca forms are also included; however, these are prohibited for the Kṣatriya by the rule, "The Rākṣasa alone for the Kṣatriya" (MDh 3.24). Therefore, they are merely alternatives and not primary. Furthermore, because the context refers specifically to the Rākṣasa, the rule prescribes that single form alone. There is no such restrictive enumeration (parisaṃkhyāna) regarding the Prājāpatya. Consequently, for the Kṣatriya, the Prājāpatya is equal to the Rākṣasa.

In this manner, for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra as well, the *prājāpatya* rite is traditionally taught as obligatory and is not prohibited. However, the *āsura* and *paiśāca* rites are both prescribed and prohibited for them. As for the *rākṣasa* rite, it is prohibited by the rule "not [those] other than the *rākṣasa*" (MDh 3.23), yet it is prescribed by the rule "three are lawful" (MDh 3.23).
For a Brāhmaṇa, the *paiśāca* does not exist at all; for Kṣatriyas and others, the *brāhma*, *daiva*, and *ārṣa* rites are established as permissible. (3.25)
Whether performed separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.

The phrase "separately" (*pṛthak pṛthak*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since this is already established by what precedes. The term "mixed" (*miśrau*) is the actual injunction (*vidhi*), because the other two forms of marriage, the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa, are prescribed as independent options. This statement regarding mixing is made because it was not otherwise obtained, much like the case of rice and barley (*vrīhi-yava*). Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" or "with barley," there is an option (*vikalpa*) rather than a mixture, because the substances are prescribed for the performance of a single sacrifice as being mutually independent. For if there were a mixture, the purpose of the scriptural rule for rice would not be fulfilled, nor would the purpose of the scriptural rule for barley. Likewise, here, when a single girl is to be taken [as a wife], two means that were not previously applicable are simultaneously enjoined.

Its scope is as follows: when a maiden in her father’s house somehow comes within the range of sight of a prince staying there, and having been introduced by a female messenger, she likewise desires him; yet, being dependent on others, she does not obtain union with him. Then, having made an agreement with the suitor, she causes herself to be led away, saying, "Lead me from here by whatever means possible. And he, through his superior strength, carries her off after killing and cutting [her relatives]. In that case, there exists both the form of the *gāndharva* marriage, according to the rule "union through mutual desire" (MDh 3.32), and the form of the *rākṣasa* marriage, according to the rule "having killed and cut" (MDh 3.33).

These two marriages belong only to the Kṣatriya; they are lawful for the Kṣatriya, as previously enjoined—this is a restatement. Others, however, say: when a Kṣatriya takes many wives, he may marry one by the Gāndharva rite and another by the Rākṣasa rite; this is the view of mixed forms. Or else, he may marry all of them by either one of these two [rites] separately. By this it is understood that for the Kṣatriya there is no restriction regarding these two alone, whereas among the Prājāpatya and the others, she must be married by whichever rite was first employed. (3.26)
Now he describes their essential nature:
"Having covered [the girl] and honored her, and having invited one who is learned and virtuous, the giving away of the daughter by oneself is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite. (3.27)

"Having clothed" (*ācchādya*): a specific kind of clothing is intended here, since other garments would be obtained by their very nature. Having dressed [the bridegroom] with excellent clothing—according to the place, according to what is available, and with a garment that is appropriate; having honored him (*arhayitvā*). By this, it is meant that after performing worship with ornaments such as bracelets, earrings, and so forth, along with special marks of affection and special hospitality, both [the bride and the groom] should be provided for, because there is no evidence [in the text] that the gift of clothing and honor applies to either the bride or the groom alone. To one who possesses learning and good character (*śrutaśīlavate*). Other qualities of the bridegroom mentioned in other Smṛtis should also be observed: "He should be young, wise, beloved by the people, and carefully tested as to his virility" (YDh 1.55). He has not previously asked for her himself (*svayaṃ prāgayācitaḥ*). Having summoned the bridegroom by sending his own men and brought him to a nearby place, whatever the gift given, that is the Brāhma form of marriage (*dharmah*). Although the word *dharma* is used in a general sense, it should be understood here as referring specifically to that [marriage], because it is required by the preceding context. The definition of the Brāhma marriage is: "The acquisition [of the bride] without asking, preceded by honoring, is the Brāhma marriage."
But is it not improper to say that marriage is for the purpose of taking a woman as one's own?

This gift extends up until the marriage; the purpose of the gift does not cease before the marriage is performed. For that [marriage] is the time for her formal acceptance (*pratigraha*). And a gift is not completed in the absence of acceptance. A gift is not merely the cessation of one's own ownership; rather, it culminates in the acquisition of ownership by another. As he will state: "But their completion should be understood by the wise at the seventh step" (MDh 8.227). Thus, the girl must be given away precisely at the time of the marriage. Accordingly, the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra* demonstrates the ritual rules (*kāṇḍikadharma*) for the Brāhma marriage at that very time. As for the gift prior to the marriage, that is merely a statement of agreement (*upasaṃvādana*). For if that [agreement] is not made, the marriage will not necessarily take place at the intended time. Someone might not give after having previously agreed, or the other might sometimes not accept. Therefore, an agreement should be made before the marriage: "In this case, she is to be given by you, and she is to be wedded by me. Just as a sacrifice that has begun but lacks its constituent parts is excluded from its purpose because that purpose is not achieved, even though it was enjoined.

However, those who think that just as the giving of a substance such as a cow—which is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*)—is accomplished through a reception preceded by a mantra, so too this statement "and thus in the case of duties involving giving" was made; and that here marriage stands in the place of the mantra for reception; and that consequently "taking in hand" (*upayamana*) and "marriage" (*vivāha*) have the same meaning, and that "taking in hand" means making one's own; and that the venerable Pāṇini indeed records: "The root *yama* with the prefix *upa* is used in the sense of making one's own" (Pāṇ 1.3.56); therefore, marriage has the purpose of accepting the girl.

That is incorrect. Marriage is for the purpose of making her one's wife; there is no injunction stating that "one should accept [her] by means of this rite. Furthermore, the marriage mantras (*vaivāhika-mantra*) are not of the nature of a formal acceptance (*pratigraha*), unlike mantras such as "I accept you with the permission of the God" (*devasya tvā pragṛhṇāmi*). As for the statement that it is "the act of making her one's own" (*svakaraṇa*), that is not contradictory; for marriage also possesses the character of making her one's own. When mere ownership (*svatva*) has been established through the act of giving, a specific form of ownership is created by the marriage. This is not a form of property like cattle or other goods, to be employed according to one's will, but rather as a wife (*jāyātvena*). For the relationship characterized as husband and wife is indeed a specific kind of owner-possessed relation. And so he will show: "For the sake of auspiciousness, the *svastyayana*... at marriages, the act of giving is the cause of ownership" (MDh 5.152). || 3.27 ||
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest is performing his duties,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) form of marriage.

In an extensive sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, once the ritual procedure has been commenced, there is the giving of a daughter to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), specifically the *adhvaryu*, who has performed that rite. The phrase "having adorned her" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because every form of giving a maiden is of this nature. This is a general injunction: "One should marry her off after clothing and adorning her. Now, it may be objected: cows, horses, mules, and so forth are prescribed in the scriptures as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the priests; nowhere is the giving of a maiden enjoined as being for the sake of the sacrifice.

What is the purpose here of [defining it] as being for the sake of the sacrifice? When the sacrifice has commenced, that which one gives to the officiating priest is the *daiva* marriage. And there exists even a trace of benefit, insofar as he performs that [act]. Even when given without reference to the ritual act itself, it certainly produces a specific inference in one who is engaged in performing that act. On account of this connection with benefit, the *daiva* is inferior to the *brāhma*. (3.28)
Having taken one or two pairs of kine from the bridegroom according to the law, the giving away of the daughter according to the rule—this is called the Ārṣa rite. (3.29)

A cow and a bull constitute a pair; having accepted one or two from the bridegroom, the giving away of the girl is the Ārṣa rite. "According to Dharma" means that this is indeed Dharma; the intention is that no notion of a sale should be entertained here, because there is no repayment of a high or low debt. (3.29)
Having addressed the words, "May you both perform your duty together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite. (3.30)

The *prājāpatya* [form of marriage] is that gift which is made after establishing a formal agreement (*paribhāṣā*) by restricting [the bridegroom] with the words, "Dharma must be practiced by you two together. The mention of "dharma" is for the sake of illustration (*upalakṣaṇārtham*). The meaning of this statement of agreement is that there shall be a commonality of purpose, security, and well-being regarding dharma, artha, and kāma. Only the word "dharma" is uttered: "Let dharma be practiced together," and not "dharma, artha, and kāma together. However, that word "dharma" is explained as being illustrative of artha and kāma on the authority of other Smṛtis. When a contract has been made such as, "If you do not transgress her in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, then she is given to you," then at the time of the wedding, the formula "let them practice dharma together" should be recited in that very context. Even though companionship in artha and kāma is intended, it is not explicitly uttered because it is not the primary subject under discussion. And so says Gautama: "In the *prājāpatya*, the mantra is 'let them practice dharma together'" (GDh 4.7). By the use of the term "mantra," he shows that it should be employed in its authorized form, like a mantra. For it is not proper to stipulate companionship in matters of artha and kāma for great-souled men; however, such a meaning is understood from other Smṛtis.

By this very [use of the] word *saṃvid* (agreement), there is a deficiency here due to a fault: for in this case, there is on the part of the giver a desire to obtain a favor (*upakāra*). This is expressed by the word *vāk* (speech); however, this is not a restriction of the speech to the giver alone. For since this is already established by the word *anubhāṣya* (having repeated after), the word *vāk* would be redundant, as the organ of speech is the instrument for repeating. Thus says the author of the Gṛhyasūtra: "Having said, 'This is the truth for you,' he should cause the giver to say, 'This is the truth for us. And the prefix *anu-* expresses the determination by speech of that which has already been obtained. 3.30.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability, the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma. (3.31)

The Āsura marriage consists of giving the woman's property (*strīdhana*) to the girl’s paternal relatives, such as her father and others, and to the girl herself, and then taking the girl away; it is called "taking" because she is brought [home]. By the phrase "out of one's own will" (*svācchandyāt*), meaning out of one's own desire and not according to the scriptures, he states its distinction from the Ārṣa form. For in that case, there is a scriptural injunction as a regulator: "a pair of cattle. Here, however, the choice depends on the qualities of the girl, such as her beauty and good fortune. (3.31)
The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through desire, arising from passion for sexual intercourse, is to be known as the Gāndharva form. (3.32)

And by the will of the man and the maiden, out of mutual affection, there is a union—a coming together in one place. This is its censure: "born of sexual intercourse" (*maithunyaḥ*), meaning arising from desire. It is called *maithuna* because it has sexual union as its purpose; that which is conducive to this is *maithunya*. This very same meaning is made explicit by the phrase "born of desire" (*kāmasaṃbhava*). It is called *saṃbhava* because it originates from this; thus, desire is its source. (3.32)
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she cries out and weeps, after having slain, wounded, or broken down [her guardians], is called the Rākṣasa rite. (3.33)

What is intended here is simply that the forcible abduction of a maiden from her family circle by means of violence constitutes the *rākṣasa* form of marriage; the words "having killed" (*hatvā*) and so forth are merely descriptive restatements (*anuvāda*). If there is some obstacle encountered by one who desires to carry her off by force, then killing and the like are indeed already implied. However, if [the groom], recognizing the superior strength of the assailant, should remain indifferent out of fear for his own life, then it remains a *rākṣasa* marriage even then; killing and the like need not necessarily be performed.

Having struck her with a wooden staff or similar object; having cut her limbs into pieces with blows from a sword or other weapons; having broken through walls, fortresses, and so forth—[this refers to taking] a maiden who is crying out and weeping against her will. This is the distinction from the *gāndharva* form of marriage. "I am being carried off helpless; save me!"—making such loud cries is "crying out. Weeping is the shedding of tears. This is the rule regarding a woman who is terrified. (3.33)
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged, that is the most sinful among marriages; it is known as the Paiśāca, the lowest of all.

The lack of consent is equal for both the Rākṣasa and the Paiśāca [forms of marriage]. In the Rākṣasa, there is killing; in the Paiśāca, there is deception. "Asleep" means overcome by sleep; "intoxicated" means drunk or under the sway of liquor; "negligent" means one whose consciousness is lost due to the agitation of wind. He who approaches her in secret—that is, in private—and engages in the act of sexual union, that is the Paiśāca marriage; it is the most wicked of all marriages and a cause of sin. From it, offspring in accordance with dharma is not produced.

In this context, because the Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca forms are used in grammatical coordination with the term "marriage" (*vivāha*), it is held that their mere union, seizing, or approaching—without dependence on the sacramental rite of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*)—constitute marriage.

For them, since the terms "giving" (*dāna*) and "marriage" (*vivāha*) are also used in coordination even in the case of the Brāhma and other forms, the sacramental rite would be excluded; however, it has been shown how it is not so excluded. By figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "marriage" is applied to the act of giving when its purpose is marriage.

Regarding the Gāndharva form of marriage, however, it was described by the venerable Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana in the *Duṣyanta-Śakuntalā-saṃgamana* as being "without fire and without mantras. By the observation of that [text], there exists the sacramental rite of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa-saṃskāra*), though it is devoid of mantras and the like.

Regarding the *paiśāca* [form of marriage], however, they dispute as follows: the primary factor is the act of approaching (*upagamana*). Yet, her status as a maiden (*kanyātva*) does not depart, because that is revoked by the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). Consequently, since the prohibition—"The mantras of the taking of the hand are established only for maidens" (MDh 8.226)—does not apply here, there is indeed a connection with the sacramental rites accompanied by mantras. Furthermore, that prohibition was made for the purpose of prohibiting the sacramental rites; for she, having been consecrated by the mantras, has lost her status as a maiden. For this very reason, even if the approach occurs first, there is no fault of her being a non-maiden (*akanyā-doṣa*). Thus is the view that Karṇa is the son of a maiden (*kānīna*). If, however, her status as a maiden were to depart through sexual intercourse with a man, how could this expression "the son of a maiden is *kānīna*" be possible? But if "maiden" is said to mean one who is unconsecrated (*asaṃskṛtā*), then it is logical that "Karṇa and others are sons of an unmarried woman. When the approach is taken in its primary sense, the birth of offspring from a maiden is possible; indeed, such a marriage is described in the epics and other histories. Now, if the connection of pleasure has already occurred due to intoxication from wine and the like, what is the purpose of the sacramental rite?

To this it is replied: although the status of being a woman and a man has ceased and the prohibition against approaching a maiden has been transgressed, nevertheless, for the sake of her qualification [for ritual acts] together with him, and so that there may not be a "approaching of a maiden" again upon subsequent intercourse, the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is performed. Furthermore, this marriage is censured as being for the benefit of the man, due to its connection with the transgression of the prohibition against approaching a maiden.

That is incorrect. For in common usage, this word *kanyā* denotes a woman who has not had sexual intercourse with a man, regardless of whether she depends upon the state of having undergone sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). Even those who have not undergone the sacramental rites are not designated as *kanyā*s if their virginity (*yoni*) has been violated by men. Furthermore, there is no fault of violating a *kanyā* when one approaches women who have taken up the life of courtesans (*veśaśritā*). Even though the words *kumārī* and *kanyā* are accepted as denoting the first stage of life, nevertheless, in the context of marriage rites, they refer specifically to a woman who has not yet been enjoyed sexually. Thus, when someone seeks as a wife a girl wearing the dress of a maiden (*kumāra-veśa-dhāriṇī*) whose sexual intercourse with men has not become publicly known, others perceive her as: "This is not a *kumārī*; her maidenhood (*kaumāra-bhāva*) has perished."

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction of the ritual injunctions (*saṃskāra*). For the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) must be performed with the recitation of mantras, such as "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb" (RV 10.184.1). Once [the womb] has been prepared, it is impossible to perform that preparation again; thus, in that case, the application of the mantra would be ineffective. Nor is there the application of mantras for an unmarried woman in the Paiśāca form of marriage, because such [mantra] recitation is heard [only] in the context of a married woman. Furthermore, it is neither stated nor logical to assume that [the mantra] applies to marriages other than the Paiśāca, since the scriptural injunction is heard without qualification.

Therefore, many such defects follow from the position that [sexual] intercourse (*upagama*) is the primary meaning. Consequently, in activities such as embracing, hugging, and kissing, which have intercourse as their purpose, the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *upa* should be understood [in this sense] due to association (*sāhacarya*) and because it serves that purpose (*tādarthya*). As for the expression "the maiden-born son" (*kānīnaḥ putraḥ*), since the primary meaning is impossible there, one understands through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) the absence of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). As for the observation of sacramental rites in certain cases—such as the rule, "A woman who is pregnant, whether her condition be known or unknown, may be married"—there, the one who has had intercourse is not the same as the one who performs the rite; yet this is not the *paiśāca* form of marriage. For in the *paiśāca* marriage, she is given to the very person by whom she was enjoyed, and he alone performs the rite for her. However, the sacrament for a pregnant woman is based on a specific scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). All of this will be explained more precisely again in the ninth chapter.
Others think: "The primary sense is indeed approaching; for if it were not primary, the prohibition of 'going' would be untenable."

For if "approaching" (*upagama*) were taken in its primary sense, then that alone would constitute marriage, because no other form exists according to the reasoning just stated. Consequently, there would be no scope for that prohibition, since the *gāndharva* [marriage] occurs by mutual consent, the *rākṣasa* by force, and the *paiśāca* otherwise; nor is there any other mode by which that prohibition could find its scope. However, it does have a scope: where there is an approach in secret by force, or where a girl is given by her parents but not consecrated with the sacramental rites. This is not a *gāndharva* marriage, because of the absence of the maiden’s consent. For this very reason, even the husband does not incur the sin of approaching a maiden, since a different category of case is possible.

Therefore, because the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is prohibited for those whose virginity has been lost, because [the act] serves as a means (*upāya*) just like the *brāhma* and other forms, and because the term "marriage" (*vivāha*) is applicable to them in that same way, the meaning of "approaching" (*upagama*)—by virtue of the force of the context—is indeed figurative (*gauṇa*). And their distinction is as follows: the *brāhma* form is that which comes unasked, like land, gold, and so forth; the *daiva* is distinguished by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); the *ārṣa* is by means of a pair of cattle; the *prājāpatya* is by means of a request or non-request, according to the established rule of the formula, "May both of you perform dharma together"; and the distinctions of the remaining forms are easily understood.

This is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix applied to words such as *brāhma* in the sense of "belonging to"; and the connection with Brahmā and the others is superimposed by way of praise. This applies to all [the other languages] as well. *Paiśāca* means "this is appropriate for the Piśācas," which is a form of censure. (3.34)
For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is prescribed as the most distinguished; for the other castes, however, it is by mutual desire. (3.35)

Regarding the giving of a daughter (*kanyādāna*) by those who give a daughter—namely, the foremost of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇas—the gift is praised as being performed with water alone. When one gives a daughter to a Brāhmaṇa, one should give her with water alone. But how is water the instrument of the gift? For there is no gift without them, according to the rule: "In the case of alms-giving and other religious duties, one should indeed give the gift after having addressed it with water preceded by the word 'namaḥ'. Alternatively, by the restrictive phrase "with water alone," he excludes the *ārṣa*, *āsura*, and *prājāpatya* forms of marriage. For in those cases, water alone is not the cause; rather, there is also the taking of property such as a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*), as well as a formal agreement (*saṃvit*). Therefore, this is what is meant: just as when property such as a cow or gold is given, nothing is stipulated—such as, "This cow must be tended by you alone" or "Such grasses must also be provided"—in the same way, the daughter should be given, and the son-in-law should not be subjected to stipulations out of affection for a daughter. Nor should wealth be accepted from him.

But for Kṣatriyas and the others, [the giving occurs] through mutual desire—that is, by the reciprocal wish of both parties. If there is a mutual longing between the bride and the groom, then the giving should be performed; not otherwise, as is the case with the Brāhma marriage. Others, however, explain that "having taken wealth, or even with water alone"—this is the meaning of "mutual desire. According to this view, it is made known that for a Brāhmaṇa, [all forms of marriage] are permissible. (3.35)
O Brahmins, listen as I correctly proclaim all those virtues which Manu has declared for each of these forms of marriage. (3.36)

He recalls what was stated in [Manu Smṛti] 3.22: "And whatever virtues and defects belong to whom... Since many points were promised to be discussed, this restatement is appropriate for the sake of specific knowledge, indicating that this particular matter is being addressed by the verses that follow.

"In these marriages" (eṣām vivāhānām) is a genitive used for specification (*nirdhāraṇe*). Thus, O Brahmins, listen to all those qualities of whichever marriage has been proclaimed by the Teacher Manu. Bhṛgu addresses the great sages: "Proclaim," that is, speak, correctly—that is, without error—and without confusion. (3.36)
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who performs meritorious deeds liberates ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin. (3.37)

"Ancestors" refers to those of the preceding lineage, such as the father, grandfather, and so forth; "descendants" refers to those of the subsequent lineage, such as the son, grandson, and so forth. He "liberates them from sin," meaning he raises them up from the torments of hell and other such states. This applies if the son born of a woman wedded by the *brāhma* form of marriage is a performer of good deeds—that is, a doer of merit. The term "ancestors" (*pitṛn*) refers to those who have departed to the other world; this word *pitṛ* is a synonym for *preta*, for otherwise the designation "ancestor" would not be applicable to the progeny of sons and the like. The word "ten" (*daśa*) is connected with each of the terms "preceding" and "subsequent," as indicated by the expression "twenty-one" (*ekaviṃśakam*).

This is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). Therefore, one should not ask how he can liberate those who have not yet come or have not yet been born. However, it will be explained in the section on ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) that for ancestors, liberation from sin indeed occurs through the merit performed by their offspring, such as *śrāddha* offerings. Thus, what is meant by "he liberates ten generations from sin" is based on the following premise: that ten persons are born sinless within a particular family. (3.37)
A son born of a woman married according to the Daiva rite delivers seven generations before him and seven after;
a son born of a woman married according to the Ārṣa rite delivers three before and three after; and a son born of a woman married according to the Kāya rite delivers six before and six after.

One who is married according to the *daiva* rite is called *daivoḍhā*. One born of her is *daivoḍhājaḥ*. A son (*suta*) is a child (*putra*). Who is *kaḥ*? He is Prajāpati. That marriage which has him as its deity is *kāya*. Even though there is no actual connection with a deity in the sacramental rite characterized by the taking [of the hand], the status of Prajāpati as the deity is superimposed through figurative usage (*bhakti*). Furthermore, although there is a *prājāpatya* sacrifice there, it is common to all forms of marriage and is not the cause for the designation *kāya*. Moreover, there would be no application [of this term] in the case of the *āsura* and other marriages, for there is no sacrifice associated with *āsura* marriages. The shortening in the form *kāyoḍhaja* is according to Pāṇini 6.3.63: "The elision of *ṅī* and *āp* occurs diversely in technical names and in the Veda."

But surely, whatever has a lesser fruit is mentioned later; therefore, it would be logical for the *ārṣa* rite to be mentioned after the *prājāpatya*. There is, however, a reason why the *prājāpatya*, which yields a greater fruit, is mentioned later: because in the verse, "Of the five, three are lawful" (MDh 3.25), the inclusion of the *prājāpatya* is intended, whereas otherwise it would have been the *ārṣa*. (3.38)
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, performed in their proper order, sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born. (3.39)

It was stated [in MDh 3.22]: “And [he should consider] the merits and defects in procreation. This is that [which follows]. *Anupūrvaśaḥ*: this term is used by the authors of the Smṛtis in the sense of *ānupūrvyeṇa* (in due order). *Brahmavarcasa* is the honor and renown resulting from the excellence of Vedic learning, study, and understanding. Those who possess this are *brahmavarcasinaḥ*; this word ends in the suffix *-in*. They are those approved and authorized by the learned (*śiṣṭas*), not censured, not disliked—that is to say, beloved. Furthermore, because the word has the sense of "approval" (*amati*), it does not fall under the scope of Pāṇini 3.2.188 (*matibuddhi...*), and thus there is no prohibition of compounding by virtue of Pāṇini 2.2.12 (*ktena ca pūjāyām*). And when the general relationship is intended to be expressed, the genitive case is used. || 3.39 ||
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned, possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years. (3.40)

"Form" means a captivating appearance. "Sattva" refers to a quality (*guṇa*) which will be explained in the twelfth [chapter]. "Endowed with these" means possessed of them. "Wealthy" means possessing riches. "Famous" means renowned for qualities such as learning and valor. "Possessing abundant enjoyments" means constantly provided with an unimpaired set of instruments of pleasure, such as garlands, ointments, song, and instrumental music. "Enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is the non-separation from the aforementioned instruments of pleasure; those whose enjoyment is "abundant"—meaning uninjured and complete—are "possessors of abundant enjoyments. "Devoted to the practice of dharma" means most virtuous (*dharmiṣṭha*). The word *dharma* is, for some, a term denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*); therefore, the superlative suffix (*ātiśāyika*) is applied according to the rule *guṇavacanāt*. They live for a hundred years. (3.40)
But from the remaining improper marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of the Veda and dharma are born. (3.41)

Regarding marriages other than the *brāhma* and others—such as the *gāndharva* and so forth—they are called "speakers of cruelty and falsehood" (*nṛśaṃsānṛtavādinaḥ*). "Cruelty" (*nṛśaṃsa*) refers to harsh, abusive speech directed toward one's mother, sister, and others; "falsehood" (*anṛta*) is well known. "Cruelty and falsehood" (*nṛśaṃsānṛte*) refers to these two together. The etymology of the word is: those whose habit is to speak such things are "speakers of cruelty and falsehood. They hate or revile the "duty of Brahman" (*brahmadharma*), which is the duty of the Veda or the meaning of the Veda, or they simply do not have faith in it. For this very reason, there is a censure [of them] in the phrase "in ill-arranged marriages" (*durvivāheṣu*). (3.41)
Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they are blamed by men. Therefore, one should avoid those who are blameworthy. (3.42)

This is a summary showing the results of the various forms of marriage. Those marriages which are prescribed for a man are blameless; the offspring—characterized as sons and so forth—of those who have married according to them becomes blameless, meaning it is praiseworthy. By means of blameworthy, that is, prohibited, marriages, the offspring is blameworthy, meaning contemptible. Therefore, lest the offspring become partakers of suffering, one should avoid the blameworthy forms. (3.42)
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste; this following rule is to be known for the act of marriage with women of a different caste. (3.43)

The rite called *pāṇigrahaṇa* (taking of the hand) is a sacrament prescribed by the authors of the Gṛhya-sūtras; it is taught, ordained, and established as something to be performed when women of the same caste (*savarṇā*) are being married. Regarding marriages with women of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), this following rule is to be understood. || 3.43 ||
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden, and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste. (3.44)

When being carried by a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow held in the Brāhmaṇa’s hand, because the arrow is prescribed in place of taking the hand. A goad causes distress to oxen, by which they are pained while being driven, just as a hook does for elephants. A Śūdra woman should take hold of the hem of the garment—that is, the cloth—during the *vedana*, which is the marriage ceremony, with men of superior castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. (3.44)

He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may approach her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days. (3.45)

Marriage has been described. Now, once that has been completed and the status of being a wife has been attained, this [section] is commenced to prevent the possibility of approaching her at will on that very same day, which would otherwise be permitted.

One should not go [to one's wife] immediately after the marriage on that very day; rather, one should wait for the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*). However, the authors of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* have stated: "From this point forward, the couple shall eat food free from pungent salt, remain celibate (*brahmacārin*), and sleep on the ground—either for three nights, twelve nights, or a year" (ĀśG 1.7.11). In that case, even if the fertile period occurs during the interval of the year, there is no intercourse. Likewise, after this period has elapsed, there is no intercourse even if the fertile period occurs. In this way, these two Smṛti texts are not contradictory. As for the option between three nights and so forth: intercourse may take place for those who are intensely tormented by passion, whereas for those who possess self-control (*daiyavat*), there is celibacy.

*Ṛtu* is defined as a specific state of the female body, characterized by the appearance of menses, during which she is capable of conceiving; it refers to a particular period of time. Because the appearance of menses is merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*), even when this has ceased, the period remains subject to the times to be described hereafter. The time of that [period] is *ṛtukāla*. Alternatively, by association, the time itself is called *ṛtu*. Thus, there is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*). One whose vow (*vrata*) is to approach [his wife] during the *ṛtukāla* is *ṛtukālābhigāmī*. The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.20 (*vrate*)—as in examples such as *sthaṇḍilaśāyī* ("one who sleeps on the bare ground") or *aśrāddhabhojī* ("one who does not eat at a funeral feast"). The meaning of *syāt* is "should be" or "must be. Although the injunctive suffix (*vidhivibhakti*) is directed toward the verb *asti* ("to be"), it nevertheless prescribes the act of approaching; thus, "he should be one who approaches" means "he should approach. For one who does not approach cannot be said to be "one who approaches."

What, then, is this vow (*vrata*) like? Is it that one must approach [the wife] only during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), or must one approach her only during the fertile period? This is what is being asked: is this a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) or an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)? But surely, by the very definition of the term "vow" according to the scriptures, it is called a restriction; moreover, the suffix *-ṇini* occurs precisely in that sense. Therefore, how can an exclusive specification be suspected here? It is replied: we shall demonstrate that even in the case of an exclusive specification, there exists both scriptural authority and the nature of a restriction. What, then, is the difference between these two?
A specific rule is a restriction (niyama). Now, what is a rule (vidhi)?

A word that makes known what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) is, for example, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice. For, without this statement, there would be no understanding of the *agnihotra*'s being something to be performed from any other source. A restrictive rule (*niyama*), on the other hand, occurs where there is an optional possibility (*pākṣikī prāptiḥ*) of performing an act for the sake of accomplishing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) even without the statement; as in "One should sacrifice on level ground. Since the injunctions for sacrifices such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* imply a location in general, no performance of a sacrifice is possible without resorting to some location. Location is of two kinds: level and uneven. When one sacrifices on level ground, then this statement is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). But when, due to the unrestrained nature of desire, one wishes to sacrifice on uneven ground, then this statement is purposeful by enjoining level ground; once level ground has been enjoined, uneven ground is not resorted to because it was not enjoined. By implication, its exclusion follows. For when the performance is based on an injunction, why would one do what is not enjoined? Indeed, if one were to do so, the performance would not be accomplished exactly as prescribed.

And in this regard, there is this example from the Smṛti: "One should eat food facing the east. For one who is eating, the act of eating might occur by chance while resorting to any direction whatsoever; in that case, sometimes the east is reached and sometimes some other direction. Since when the east is reached, another is not, and when another is reached, the east is not, the statement "one should eat food facing the east" serves as an injunction (*vidhi*) for the alternative that was not otherwise established. By transgressing this, one abandons the purpose of the scripture.

Thus, in this case, approaching [the wife] at will and not approaching during the fertile period (ṛtu), while the approaching prescribed for one half of the month is not performed, would result in the transgression of the sacred law (śāstra). Just as other matters enjoined by the sacred law become causes for penance when they are transgressed, so too is the failure to approach [the wife].

Now, when approaching [one's wife] out of passion occurs both during the fertile season (*ṛtu*) and outside of it, the injunction "one should approach her during the fertile season" is sought as follows: one should approach her only during the fertile season and not go to her outside of it. Just as in the case of the statement "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," where the purpose of warding off hunger leads to the possibility of eating even among the five-nailed animals such as the hare, and even among others such as monkeys; and since there is no restriction of application by turn there—because they might be eaten simultaneously—this statement "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten" results in being for the purpose of excluding the others (*parisaṃkhyā*). So too here, it is an exclusion.

But surely they declare that *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) possesses three defects; for three defects would manifest therein: the abandonment of its own primary meaning (*svārthatyāga*), the assumption of a foreign meaning (*parārthakalpanā*), and the sublation of what is already established (*prāptabādha*). When, in the statement "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," eating with respect to five-nailed animals is understood through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then that [eating] is abandoned, because the sentence is intended to prohibit what is other than those. Furthermore, the prohibition is not explicitly heard [in the text], hence there is the assumption of a foreign meaning. And since there is a desire [to eat], the eating which was established as having a universal scope is sublated. Thus, by this, there are three defects in *parisaṃkhyā*.

This is not the core point. When there is a purpose and the literal sense of the Vedic text is impossible, it is not contradictory for the sentence to have that [purpose] as its intent, so that it may not be rendered meaningless. "An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when [an action] is absolutely unestablished; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when it is optionally established;
and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) applies when it is established both there and elsewhere, as in the case of the fingernails" (TV 1.2.42).

What, then, is the correct interpretation here? It is *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusion), because the definition of *parisaṃkhyā*—namely, "the attainment [of a result] both there and elsewhere"—is present. For intercourse is established as occurring both during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and outside of it; however, it is not the case that what occurs during the fertile period does not occur outside of it. Just as when there is a desire to eat, the restriction regarding food is that one eats "not at a funeral feast" (*aśrāddham*), yet this does not mean that one remains eating only non-funeral food by abandoning all other food; so too here, when there is distress (the desire for offspring), the restriction regarding intercourse is understood as "one should not go outside the fertile period. Since intercourse is already prompted by desire, it is logical that the purpose of the statement is solely to prescribe the proper time. Otherwise, a matter not previously undertaken would be taught. Furthermore, since the injunction to procreate applies to one who has already married, and intercourse is possible during the fertile period, such intercourse is already established. Moreover, for one who has already produced a son, the production of a second son is not mandatory. This is because, if the singular number in the injunction "one should produce offspring" (*apatyam utpādayet*) is intended, the purpose of the injunction is fulfilled by that single act. Nor can intercourse itself be enjoined as having an invisible spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because the injunction pertains to the purification of the wife (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) and the fulfillment of the duty (*adhikāra-grahaṇa*), and because it is impossible to assume an unseen result where the injunction to procreate already implies intercourse during the fertile period. If the phrase "one should approach her during the fertile period" were intended to prohibit intercourse outside the fertile period, then it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), and the *parisaṃkhyā* would apply. For in that case, the statement retains its utility through the indication of another meaning (i.e., the exclusion of non-periodic intercourse).

And by establishing it thus, there is no contradiction with the Gautamiya [text]. For it is stated there: “One should approach [the wife] during her season (*ṛtu*), or at all times, except for those occasions that are prohibited” (GDh 5.1–2). This alternative, expressed as “or at all times,” is intended to permit acting according to one’s desire; it does not, however, establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that applies at all times, both during and outside the season. If, in the preceding clause, “one should approach during the season” were a restrictive rule, then in the phrase “or at all times,” the word *upeyāt* (should approach)—being supplied from the previous context—would necessarily function as a restrictive rule due to the uniformity of the discourse structure. Indeed, it is not logical that the same word, when not explicitly repeated, should have a different meaning. Furthermore, it has already been stated that a restrictive sense is not possible for a time other than the season. Therefore, the statement regarding approaching during the season is for the purpose of prohibiting it outside the season. In this regard, for one who has not yet fathered a son, the rule is indeed restrictive because of other injunctions; however, one who has already fathered a son may act according to his desire.

Regarding intercourse during the non-season (anṛtu) or when it is otherwise prohibited, the following counter-exception is stated: "He should approach her according to her wish, except on the forbidden days (parvan), being one who observes that vow. Here, "that" (tat) refers back to the wife. "One who observes that vow" (tadvrataḥ) means one whose vow consists of capturing her heart. The meaning is that even without the desire for sexual pleasure, whether for the sake of offspring or when a son has already been born, or even if no son has yet been born, he should approach her during the season or at other times out of a desire for sexual union, provided he is observing that vow toward her, and not out of his own personal whim.

Alternatively, the word *tat* (that) is also to be understood here in connection with *ratikāmyayā* (through the desire for pleasure), because this is a work of Smṛti scripture. Thus: "Through the desire for pleasure, he may go [to another woman] even on other occasions, excluding the sacred festival days (*parva*). In this case, a phonetic elision (*akāraśleṣa*) is to be observed; the remainder of the sense is "not through the desire for pleasure for himself. However, according to the explanation already given, there is no need for such an elision here, nor is there any lack of connection for the word *tat*, which is subordinate within the compound. He will state the festival days later: "The new moon, the eighth day, the full moon, and the fourteenth day. "Devoted to his own wife" (*svadāranirataḥ*): he should be devoted to his own wife, intent on cultivating affection for her. Alternatively, he delights only in his own wife and does not take pleasure in the wives of others; thus, it is a prohibition against the wives of others. This vow is to be maintained always, throughout one's life.

Therefore, this is established: there are three statements here. "He should approach his wife during her season" is the first. The second is a restatement of a rule for one who has not yet produced a son: "When impelled by his wife, he should go to her during her season, except on the forbidden days, and even outside the season, but not out of a desire for sexual pleasure. The third is: "He should be devoted to his own wife. And the construction of these words is as follows: "He should approach her during her season for the sake of offspring; but if he desires sexual pleasure, he may go to her while observing that vow; and he should be devoted to his own wife. (3.45)
The natural menstrual period of women is recorded as sixteen nights, together with four other days that are censured by the virtuous. (3.46)

This verse is for the purpose of indicating the characteristics of the seasons; this matter is to be understood from medical and other sciences, and is not based solely on scriptural injunction. The same applies to these two verses, including "In even [lunar nights] sons are born" (MDh 3.48).

Those sixteen nights constitute the natural menstrual period (*ṛtu*) for women month after month. Because it is based on another authority, even though it is not explicitly stated in the verse, the phrase "month after month" is understood. "Natural" (*svābhāvika*) means that which occurs in the state of nature; it refers to what happens in those whose constitution is healthy. Due to disease or other causes, the period may fail to occur for some woman even when the time has arrived; conversely, through the use of medicines such as ghee and sesame, or by the power of sexual passion, it may occur even out of season. Therefore, those nights are called the "natural menstrual period. "With four others": these are the four days which are censured by the virtuous, during which touching or conversing with a woman is prohibited; and these begin from the first appearance of blood. The use of the word "day" (*ahar*) is intended to indicate a full day and night (*ahorātra*). Together with those [sixteen nights], [there are twenty days]. (3.46)
Of these, the first four, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights, however, are praised. (3.47)

Among those nights, the first four following the initial appearance of menstrual blood are censured; there is no approaching [the wife] during them. During those three, even physical contact is forbidden due to impurity. On the fourth night, although she has become pure after bathing, sexual union is not permitted according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, because all four nights have been declared contemptible. Furthermore, the eleventh and the thirteenth nights are also censured; thus, approaching her on these is prohibited. The eleventh and thirteenth nights are counted starting from the onset of the menses, not according to the lunar dates (*tithi*). The word "among them" (*tāsām*) refers to the nights as the subject of selection, and it is understood that what is being selected must be of the same class, as in the expression, "the black cow among cows that yields abundant milk. This prohibition against approaching her for six nights is for the sake of an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). The remaining ten nights are praised; since the six have been prohibited, the excellence of the ten is already established and is merely restated here. (3.47)
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one who desires a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night. (3.48)

Among those ten nights, the even ones—the sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, fourteenth, and sixteenth—those are the nights upon approaching which sons are born; on the odd nights, daughters are born. Therefore, for the sake of ensuring the birth of a son, one should approach and have sexual intercourse with a woman during her fertile period (ṛtu) on the even nights. This is a restatement; it is also a restrictive rule (niyama): that one who has not yet fathered a son must not approach her on the odd nights. 3.48.
A male is born when the male seed is in excess; a female is born when the female seed is in excess.
When they are equal, a neuter is born, or a male and female twin; when they are diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs. || 3.49 ||

The semen of the man is the *śukra* (vital seed), and that of the woman is the *śoṇita* (blood). It has been stated by the venerable Vasiṣṭha: "Man is born from the combination of semen and blood" (VaDh 15.1). When the male seed (*puṃbīja*) is superior to the female seed (*strībīja*), a son is born even on uneven nights; likewise, when the female seed is superior, a girl is born even on even nights. This [rule] is intended for one seeking a son to engage in intercourse on uneven nights as well. This teaches that when a man considers himself well-nourished and possessed of superior virility through the use of aphrodisiac foods and practices, while the woman’s [seed] is somehow diminished, then he who seeks a son should approach her. Furthermore, "superiority" here does not refer to quantity, but rather to quality (*sāra*). If the two are equal, there is a male or a female; some say "apumān" means a hermaphrodite (*napuṃsaka*), while others read "sāmye" [in this sense]. When both are equal, it is indeed a male, or else a male and a female. When the wind, during conception, divides the mixed semen and blood equally—placing a portion in one place and exactly as much in another—then twins are born. Even in that case of equal division, if the female seed is superior, a girl is born; if the male seed is superior, a boy is born. If the seed is deficient in quality, the result is the opposite: either failure of conception or the birth of a hermaphrodite. (3.49)
Avoiding women on the eight censured nights and the other [inauspicious] nights, he remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) he inhabits. (3.50)

If, avoiding women during the six censurable nights and the other eight non-censurable nights, he approaches them on the two remaining nights—provided it is not during the *parvan* days—he remains indeed a *brahmacārin* and attains the fruit of celibacy, regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) he inhabits. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). It does not, however, grant permission for sexual intercourse during those nights in the stages of life such as the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), because the subduing of the senses is prescribed for all stages of life other than the householder’s; furthermore, the repetition [of the term] is justified as being merely explanatory. These nights are to be avoided not necessarily in sequential order; rather, the permission for two nights is granted so that one may engage in intercourse at will, provided it does not occur on the *parvan* days. What, then, is the fruit of celibacy? Since no specific result is mentioned, it is heaven. However, it is heard in some places: “The *brahmacārin* does not fall,” meaning he is not defiled by minor transgressions. (3.51)
A wise father of a maiden shall not accept even the slightest bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring. (3.51)

This is a prohibition against *śulka* (bride-price) among the Asuras, because later on [in verse 53], the "acceptance of wealth for the sake of the maiden" (*kanyārthasaṃgraha*) is mentioned. A wise man—one who knows the defects of planetary influences—should not accept even a small amount of wealth or property from the father of the girl. By accepting it, he incurs the fault of selling his offspring. But what is this so-called *śulka*? It is that which is taken from the groom preceded by verbal agreement (*ābhāṣaṇa*). However, where there is bargaining over high or low stakes, and the determination of a price based on the qualities of the girl, that is indeed a purchase (*kraya*). In this case, however, even for a girl of great qualities, only a small amount of wealth is given; or it is accepted without prior verbal agreement. Since this is not the nature of a sale, it is censured by superimposing the status of a sale upon it. (3.51)
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property—whether it be her vehicles or her clothing—are sinners who go to a downward state. (3.52)

This is a supplement to the preceding [verse]. Wealth derived from women refers to those things received from a groom at the giving away of a daughter; it also refers to those relatives, such as fathers and others, who live off them out of delusion, as it has been said: "Having given wealth to his kinsmen" (MDh 3.31). This includes gold, silver, and other forms of wealth, as well as female vehicles—vehicles being horses and the like—or clothing. Not even this much should ever be lived upon, such as clothing, vehicles, and so forth, let alone more. He declares the consequence for those who do live off such things: being sinful, they go to a downward state, that is, to hell, because of practicing what is forbidden by the scriptures. Alternatively, he will show in the ninth chapter that these are "women's properties. Those relatives—fathers and their kin, husbands and their kin—who live off them out of delusion, [live off] the vehicles and so forth, and likewise the clothing. Because of their proximity in the mind of women, a verbal proximity is to be inferred, just as in the case of "Whose man is the king’s? [The man] of the king. (3.52)
Regarding the rite of the seers (ārṣa), some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price; but that is surely false.
Whether it be small or large, even so, it remains nothing other than a sale. (3.53)

A cow and a bull constitute a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*). Some say that this may be accepted; however, Manu’s opinion is that this is indeed false—that is, it is incorrect. It means it must not be accepted. The same applies even to a small amount. "Small" refers to one who possesses few means; in such a case, he becomes great [in merit]. The sale remains exactly as much [as it was]. (3.53)
When the kinsmen do not take a fee for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely an honoring of the maidens and an act of pure compassion. (3.54)

Is the acquisition of wealth from a bridegroom a sale? We say: no. When relatives, having authority over the maiden, take or receive wealth for their own sake, then that is a sale. The acceptance of wealth for the sake of the maiden is her *arhaṇa*—it constitutes her honor and worship. It engenders great esteem in the minds of the maidens: "We are such that we are to be married after being given wealth. Furthermore, they become objects of respect elsewhere as well, [thinking], "These women are fortunate. Or, with that wealth, ornaments and the like should be made; thus, they become highly esteemed and beautiful. This is compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) and freedom from sin; there is not even the slightest scent of unrighteousness. Therefore, by means of this explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), the acceptance of wealth for the sake of the maiden is enjoined. (3.54)
These women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant prosperity for them. (3.55)

Not only should [the bride] be given by the groom’s relatives after receiving the gift, but she must also be given by the girl’s relatives. Because of their association with the father, the word *pitṛ* (father) refers here to the grandfather, paternal uncles, and so forth; hence the plural number. Alternatively, the plural is used in reference to individual persons. Similarly, it applies to the husbands, such as the fathers-in-law and others, either collectively or in reference to individuals. *Devaras* are the husband’s brothers. They are to be honored. On festive occasions such as the birth of a son, they are to be honored with respect through invitations, providing shelter, great esteem, and offerings such as food. They are to be adorned, meaning they should be decorated with garments, ornaments, ointments for the body, and the like. The fruit of this is stated to be "those desiring much auspiciousness. "Auspiciousness" (*kalyāṇa*) means desirable things, such as the attainment of sons, wealth, and other prosperities, health, and freedom from humiliation. From the word "much," it follows that this applies to all such things. Thus, this is an injunction for one who seeks a result, for those who desire to obtain and wish to attain these benefits. (3.55)
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual actions there become fruitless. (3.56)

The deities rejoice, are satisfied, and become gracious. Being gracious, they endow their masters with the very fruits they desire. However, where they are not honored, all those rites—such as sacrifices, oblations, and gifts—and those offerings made with the intention of propitiating the deities, are fruitless; such is the meaning of this explanatory praise (arthavāda). [3.56] [121]
Where the female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes; but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever. (V 3.57)
Those houses which female relatives, when not properly honored, pronounce a curse upon,
perish on all sides as if struck by a malevolent spell.
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always honor these women with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at ceremonies and during festivals. V.3.59.
In that family where the husband is always content with his wife and the wife likewise with her husband, prosperity is indeed certain.
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight the man; and from a lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed. V.3.61.
When a woman is pleasing, the entire family is pleased;
but when she is not pleasing, the whole family is displeased.
Through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas,
and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble lineages fall into the state of being non-noble.
[One becomes a Śūdra] by means of crafts, trade, and solely through the offspring of Śūdra women;
or by [keeping] cattle, horses, and vehicles, by agriculture, or by service to the king. V.3.64.
Families that are deficient in sacred mantras perish quickly through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, through atheism, and through the neglect of ritual duties. V.3.65.
But through the power of mantras, even families with little wealth become prosperous; they attain the status of noble lineages and draw great renown to themselves. (3.66)

The householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules in the nuptial fire, as well as the performance of the five sacrifices and the daily cooking [for the Śrāddha]. (3.57) The section on marriage is concluded. In whichever fire the marriage was performed, in that same fire he should perform the domestic rites (*gṛhya-karma*)—that is, the rites to be accomplished by means of fire, such as the *Aṣṭakā*, the *Pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, and the *Homa*, as taught by the authors of the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*. The "five sacrifices" are those which will be described hereafter; their "performance" (*vidhāna*), meaning their execution, is to be carried out in that very same fire.

Although it has been stated that the performance of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) is prescribed without distinction, nevertheless, the *vaiśvadeva* oblation is accomplished by means of fire, whereas in the case of the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) and so forth, nothing is to be done with fire. How then is there the instruction that "the performance of the five sacrifices is to be carried out in the fire"?

Some say that even a single locative case ending (*saptamī*) is differentiated according to the difference in its objects. Therefore, the term "five sacrifices" is applied to a single part of the five sacrifices.

Alternatively, in the phrase "the performance of the five sacrifices," the word "in the fire" (*agnau*) is not connected [to that specific term], because the fact that the Vaiśvadeva oblation has the fire as its locus is already established by what precedes it. The connection is made thus: "The householder, however, should perform the ritual of the five sacrifices. But regarding the phrase "in the fire," it is required [to refer to] the nuptial fire (*vaivāhika*), for the cooking of the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarman*) and the daily offerings (*anvāhikī*) depend upon that fire.

The word *gṛha* denotes a wife (*dāra*). A "householder" (*gṛhin*), however, is one who has taken a wife; accompanied by his wife, he should perform this or that [rite]. Regarding the marriage ceremony, some authors of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* have stated that the fire should be established by churning the two kindling woods (*araṇi*); others have stated that one should bring a burning fire from anywhere and offer oblations into it. By this statement that [the rite] is "domestic" (*gṛhya*) in that context, the maintenance of the fire is implicitly stated.

On this point, some say: even a Śūdra possesses the maintenance of the nuptial fire (*vaivāhikāgni*), because he too has the entitlement to perform *pākayajña* sacrifices. Furthermore, no specific caste is mentioned here; only the term "householder" (*gṛhī*) is heard. A Śūdra is also a householder, since his taking of a wife has been declared [for him]. This very same point is recited elsewhere: "A householder should perform the Smārta rites daily in the nuptial fire. (YDh 1.96)

To this, it is replied: It is heard in scripture that "the domestic (*gṛhya*) rite is performed in the nuptial fire. Now, there is no such thing as a rite called "domestic" in its own right; rather, in this context, one must understand by "domestic" what is taught in the *Gṛhya-smṛtis* through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the rites have been prescribed for the members of the three higher castes alone by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras*, and not for the Śūdra: "The Vaitānika rites have been stated; we shall now state the Gṛhya rites" (ĀśG 1.1.1). The purpose of this restatement of what has already been mentioned is precisely this: that those who have the entitlement to the Vaitānika rites have the same entitlement to the Gṛhya rites. It is not, however, as explained by others, for the sake of the attainment of those duties (*dharma*). For if that were intended, he would not have said: "Its times for kindling and offering are explained by those of the Agnihotra" (ĀśG 1.9.4). Nor is it logical to define *gṛhya* as "that which exists in the house" (*gṛhe bhavam*). The word *gṛha* either denotes a hall (*śālā*) or a wife (*dāra*). First, no specific rite is traditionally taught as having a hall as its locus such that, by referring to it as "the house," it could be enjoined for the householder. Even that which consecrates the house, such as the examination of the site (*vāstuparīkṣā*), applies only to the three higher castes, not to the Śūdra. If, on the other hand, the word denotes a wife, then since that is already covered by the term "householder" (*gṛhī*) itself, it adds nothing.
Furthermore, another Smṛti states:

"A householder should perform the rites prescribed by the Smṛti every day in the marriage fire, or in the fire obtained at the time of inheritance; however, he should perform the Śrauta rites in the Vaitānika fires. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.97)

Thus, here too, because no specific distinction is made—such as "something is Smārta"—there is indeed a dependence on something else; for it is not possible for every Smārta rite to take place in the fire, nor is there any authoritative evidence that it must have the fire-offering (*homa*) as its object, since a *homa* does not necessarily have the fire as its locus.

Therefore, it must be stated that what is taught by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* is called *gṛhya*. For these two Smṛtis merely restate the rites prescribed by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras*. And thus, how could there be the formal adoption of the sacred fire (*agniparigraha*) for a Śūdra? Furthermore, another rule is recorded there: "Or the *Śrauta* [rites] in the *Vaitānika* fires. In that case, this [rule] must necessarily be understood as referring to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). To claim that the same word refers to all four castes in the former instance and to the three castes in the latter would be to admit a difference in the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of a single term; and when non-difference is possible, a distinction is not logical. *Anvāhikī* means daily. That cooking which is performed every day for the purpose of eating must be done in that very fire. (3.57)
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; by using these, he is bound by sin. (3.58)

This is an instruction regarding the qualification for the performance of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*). "Slaughter-houses" (*sūnā*) are so called because they are like slaughterhouses. Places where animals are killed for the purpose of selling meat—such as markets and the like—are causes of sin because they are practiced for the production of meat. In this way, hearths (*cullyādi*) and other such items are also equal to slaughterhouses through metaphorical attribution (*adhyāropa*), since they too are causes of sin. For there is no direct scriptural prohibition against them, nor is there any general prohibition. Indeed, no one would lack a desire for heat or for the destruction [of pests]. Nor is any action accomplished by means of these [hearths, etc. seen to be prohibited by another scriptural statement. Furthermore, a prohibition cannot be inferred from this very statement, because it is understood to form a single syntactical unit with what follows; if it were intended to convey a prohibition, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Moreover, if one were to accomplish the practical purpose (*arthakriyā*) achieved by these items through other items, then the attainment of those [other items] would result in the [omission of] the five sacrifices. Nor have any defining characteristics been stated by which a prohibition of anything else performing the same function could be expressed. Or, if someone were to consume another's food or perform actions for the sake of water at rivers and the like, for him these sacrifices would be necessary. If the prohibition of the hearths and so forth were intended, then a word for the purpose of prohibition itself should have been recited; why resort to inference? Direct comprehension is more powerful than the literal word. If, however, the purpose were expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then its mention in the eleventh book would be appropriate. Through prohibitions alone, there would simply be non-performance. And since the hearths and so forth are unavoidable, their prohibition is impossible. In the absence of a prohibition, how could there be expiation?

Therefore, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) are not for the purpose of destroying defects. What then? Since [defects] are attributed to the hearth and other such items that are in constant association [with the sacrificer], he states the eternality of the sacrifices as being for the purpose of expiating those falsely imputed defects and as being obligatory.

It is said: *vadhyate*. Or, the initial syllable is read as labio-dental (*dantoṣṭhya*). One is "struck" (*hanyate*) by evil deeds—that is, one is destroyed by means of body, wealth, and so forth—or one is "bound" (*saṃbadhyate*) by sin; for the meaning of the root *badh* is the act of making someone dependent on another.

"Driving" (*vāhayan*): "driving" means engaging them in their respective tasks. When one causes a hearth or similar object to perform its own specific function as is appropriate for it, one is said to be "driving" it by means of those [women]. A "hearth" (*cullī*) is a place for cooking, such as a frying pan and so forth. A "grinding stone" (*peṣaṇī*) is either a large or small millstone. "Household utensils" (*upaskara*) refers to vessels used in the home, such as bowls, cauldrons, and the like. A "threshing tool" (*kaṇḍanī*) is that by which rice and other grains are threshed. A "water-jar" (*kumbha*) is a vessel for holding water. (3.58)
For the sake of expiating all of these in due order, the great seers have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day. (3.59)

For the sake of expiating those slaughter-places, such as the hearth and so forth—in order to purge the defects arising from them—the sequence [of purification] consists of smearing the hearth, scraping the grinding stone, and so on; this is the order established by the great seers (maharṣis) as a duty to be performed. These are the five great sacrifices (pañca mahāyajñāḥ), which must be performed daily by householders (gṛhamedhin). The term *gṛhamedhin* refers to the stage of life of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*). Regarding "daily": since no specific time limit is mentioned, it is understood to mean "as long as one lives. Thus, their obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is established. "Great sacrifices" is the name of these rites. (3.59)

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali-offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men. (3.60)

This is the rule for their essential nature (*svarūpavidhi*). By the word "teaching" (*adhyāpana*), "studying" (*adhyayana*) is also included, since he will state later that "recitation is the *ahuta* offering" (MDh 3.64); and recitation does not require students. Furthermore, it is heard generally in the scriptural passage concerning the announcement of debts (*ṛṇāvedana-śruti*) that "one [repays the debt] to the seers through one's own study" (TS 6.3.10.5). Therefore, both teaching and studying constitute the *brahmayajña* as far as possible. He will state later that "satisfying [the ancestors] is with food and the like, or with water" (MDh 3.72). The *homa* is into the fire for the deities to be mentioned later. The *bali* is what remains, offered in the mortar and other such places; it is called *bhauta*. It is called *bhauta* because its deities are the *bhūtas* and so forth; this is the name of a specific ritual act. For in that context, the offering of the *bali* is prescribed with the word *bhūta*, saying "to the *bhūtas* who roam by day. Due to association (*sāhacarya*), this entire group of rites is designated by the term *bhūtayajña*. Just as among the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, one oblation is the *vaiśvadeva-āmikṣā*, yet the entire festival is said, "one should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*"; the word *bali* refers to an offering into the fire that is not a *homa*. As the tradition records: "The *bali* is the worship of the gods. The honoring and propitiating of guests is the *nṛyajña* (human sacrifice).

But how can the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) be a sacrifice? For in that act, no deities are worshipped, nor are they even mentioned; rather, only the syllables of the Veda are uttered without any intended meaning. And it has been said regarding the repetition of the words of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Some say they are meaningless."

True. In the case of praise, the word *yajña* (sacrifice) is used figuratively, as is the word *mahat* (great). Even in the context of honoring a guest, the word *yajña* is used figuratively; for although it is possible for a guest to function as a deity (*devatā*), nevertheless, in the original injunction (*utpatti*), it is heard that one should "feed" or "honor," and not that one should "sacrifice to guests. This is just as in the expression, "Whatever rite [is performed] for the king of men... [130].

These five sacrifices are not to be performed simultaneously, because they lack a single unified purpose (*ekādhikāra*) and because their purposes are heard of as being distinct. If they were connected by a single purpose, then when three or four have been performed, it would be as if nothing had been done at all, or rather, what was done would be undone. This is just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—the *āgneya*, *agnīṣomīya*, and *upāṃśuyāja*—where the fulfillment of the purpose is not achieved by performing only one or two of them. Likewise, in this very context of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, if there is an interruption regarding any of the deities ending with *Sviṣṭakṛt*, the purpose of the oblation is not accomplished. Furthermore, the purpose for each individual sacrifice is explicitly stated: "One should be constantly engaged in Vedic study" (MDh 3.65) and "One should be constantly engaged in rites for the gods" (MDh 3.65). Thus, due to the connection of these distinct terms of purpose (*adhikārapada*), they are to be performed separately. Moreover, a separate purpose is heard of in the case of hospitality (*ātithya*): "It brings wealth and fame" (MDh 3.96).

Among these, four [rites] are independent; however, hospitality (*ātithya*) depends upon the presence of a guest. Furthermore, a guest is not one who must be invited, because there would be no hospitality [in that case]. For we shall explain later that one becomes a guest only by arriving of one's own accord. Therefore, if one performs any one of the five [daily duties] while the others are not performed, even if he should incur sin [for that omission], what has been done does not become undone. Consequently, for one who is not yet authorized for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice due to not maintaining the sacred fires (*anagnika*), there certainly exists the authority to perform Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), water-libations (*udakatarpaṇa*), and so forth. Moreover, since other Smṛtis mention alternative times for the formal adoption of the sacred fires (*agniparigraha*), the adoption need not necessarily occur only at marriage. For the Smṛti states: "The fire begins with the wife, or it begins with the inheritance" (GDh 5.7).
