But surely, for one who has not yet married, the time for partition will be the occasion for the kindling of the sacred fires?

For this would indeed be the case if the rule for establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) were for one's own sake; however, the establishment of the fires is for the sake of the fires themselves, and the fires are for the sake of ritual acts (*karman*). And ritual acts are prescribed in scripture for one who has a wife as his companion, not for one alone. Even though some authors of *Gṛhya-sūtras* have stated that "one should perform the *śrāddha* after having established the *Parameṣṭhiprāṇa* fire," that too applies only to one who has a wife. That very time [of marriage] is the time for his [the householder’s] establishment of the fires. Nor is there no *śrāddha* for one who does not maintain the fires; for this is prescribed even for one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), according to the rule: "except for the pouring of the *svadhā* offering" (GDh 2.5). Yet, he has no right to establish the fires, because eligibility requires learning (*vidvatva*) and at present he lacks such learning. However, the *śrāddha* must be performed according to one's capacity based on the scriptural injunction, just as in the case of the *Niṣādasthapati*. But when the fires are maintained by an uncle or others, since learned men are available, there is no eligibility for one who is unlearned. If, on the other hand, the establishment of the fires were prescribed specifically within the section on *śrāddha*, then, having established them as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that rite, they would be abandoned once the *śrāddha* is completed.
Some, however, cite another Smṛti: "The Vaiśvadeva oblation must be performed even in a worldly fire"; others say it should be done with dry food. 3.60
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability, even while living constantly in the household, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse. (3.61)

In this context, *nityatva* (obligatoriness) is what is being enjoined; the other [factors] are restated (*anūdya*). Even when these [rites] are deficient in their qualities, they must be performed according to one's capacity. This too is already established by virtue of their obligatoriness; therefore, the phrase is "according to possibility and according to capacity. The suffix *-tasi* is used here because it belongs to the group beginning with *ādi*. In the word *hāpayati*, only the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) is intended, as the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij-artha*) is not intended to be expressed. Alternatively, *hā* means "killing" (*hananam*), formed with the *kvip* suffix from the *saṃpad-ādi* class; then, from that [noun], the suffix *ṇyat* is added in the sense of "causing to reach" (*āpayati*), where *āp* takes the *kvip* suffix in the agentive sense, and from that nominal stem, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of the verbal action itself. Thus, *na hāpayati* means "one should not abandon" or "one should not omit. The praise [of this rule] is that one who dwells in his own home is not bound by the sin of those slaughter-houses (*sūnā*) which are inevitable [for a householder]. 3.61.

"He who does not offer [oblations] to these five—the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—does not truly live, though he breathes. (3.62) This is a praise of the prescribed rule by means of censuring its non-performance. Some read it with the dative case: "to the gods... etc.
"To the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and likewise to oneself—he does not offer to these five. Thus it is said.

In this context, *nirvāpa* means giving (*dāna*), not merely the preparation of materials for that purpose. Because it is primary by virtue of its connection with those [recipients], the use of the dative case is appropriate. He who does not give daily to these—though breathing, though living, though possessing inhalation and exhalation—he does not truly live; he is as good as dead, because the fruit of life is absent. And here, the "dependents" (*bhṛtyāḥ*) should be understood as those specified in the verse: "But when mother and father have grown old" (MDh 11.5, an inserted verse), and not slaves, because the giving to them is based on their performing labor. Alternatively, they may refer to those born as slaves (*garbhadāsa*) and others who, even if incapable of labor due to old age, are still subject to this rule. We shall explain in the section on partition that the maintenance of worn-out cattle and similar animals is mandatory. And Gautama has stated: "He must support those whose livelihood is exhausted" (GDh 6.1). Regarding the deities, *nirvāpa* is the offering into the fire (*agnau homaḥ*), while the *baliharaṇa* on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is for the Vaiśvadeva deities and the deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Or rather, what other *nirvāpa* could there be than that which is connected with the formula: "I offer thee, acceptable to Agni"? Therefore, since they are already included by the mention of "deities," the separate mention of "beings" (*bhūtānām*) is made. The mention of "self" (*ātmanaḥ*) serves as an illustration: just as there is no life for oneself without eating, and thus the consumption of food is inevitable because life aims at desirable objects and because of the injunction, "One should protect oneself from everything" (GDh 9.34), so it is also with respect to the deities and the others. (3.62)
The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the likewise well-offered sacrifice (prahuta),
the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmya-huta), and the consumed sacrifice (prāśita)— these they declare to be the five sacrifices.

The injunction for these [rites] exists in a certain Vedic branch (vedaśākhā) by means of these words. Therefore, in order to demonstrate that the injunction of the five sacrifices (pañcayajña) is rooted in the Śruti, he mentions them again by way of their common renown. The second purpose of mentioning them under different names is that even those duties which have not been explicitly stated as being enjoined in the context of that section—though indicated by such terms as "the offering" (āhuti) and so forth—are also to be included; for example, the Brahmayajña, the Śrāddha, marriage, and the performance of domestic rites, and so on. (3.63)

Recitation is the *ahuta* sacrifice; the fire-oblation is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits is the *prahuta*; the oblation to the elemental beings is the *bhautika bali*; the worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*. (3.64)

That sacrifice which is called *ahuta* should be understood as *japa* (muttered prayer). Because of the scriptural injunction, "One should honor the sages through *svādhyāya*" (MDh 3.71), the study of the Veda is intended for the purpose of *japa*; or else, it refers to recollection during mental activity. The root *jap* is recorded in both senses: in distinct speech and in the mind. *Huta* is the offering into the fire. *Prahuta* is the offering to the spirits (*bhūtabali*). Although this is indeed an offering (*homa*), nevertheless, because offerings are most commonly known to be made into the fire, there might be a doubt that the sacrifice to the spirits is not a *homa*. To address this, it is called *prahuta*, meaning it is a *homa* in a preeminent sense (*prakarṣeṇa*) by way of praise. The honoring of the foremost of the twice-born—the Brāhmaṇas—is the *brāhmya-huta*. The ritual of hospitality (*ātithyakarma*) constitutes the honoring of the foremost of the twice-born. (3.64)
One should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Vedas and in divine rites here on earth;
for it is by being devoted to divine rites that one sustains this world of moving and unmoving beings.

This [verse] clarifies what was stated regarding the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*): that there is a distinct entitlement for each one individually, rather than a single collective entitlement for all together. When, due to defects such as poverty or some other cause, the performance of hospitality and the like cannot somehow be accomplished, then one must remain constantly engaged in *svādhyāya* (Vedic study). Regarding "divine action" (*daive karmaṇi*): the offering (*homa*) into the fire for the deities of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is divine action. Although the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings) and *pitṛyajña* (sacrifice to ancestors) also have deities, by virtue of the context, the offering into the fire alone is here called "divine. On this point, he states an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*): "One who is intent upon—that is, devoted to—divine action supports, meaning sustains, the moving and unmoving, the mobile and the immobile; the meaning is that he becomes the cause of the stability of the entire world. (3.65)
But how does the maintenance of the entire world come about through the oblation poured into the fire? To this he says:
"The oblation duly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain food, and from that, living beings. (3.66)

The oblation (*āhuti*)—consisting of the *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and other offerings—which is cast or thrown into the fire by the sacrificer, reaches the Sun in an invisible form. Since the Sun is the gatherer of all essences (*rasa*), it is said that the essence of the oblation reaches the Sun. Thereupon, that essence, ripened in due time within the rays of the Sun, is born in the form of rain. From that comes food, such as rice and other grains; from that, all creatures, that is, all living beings. Thus, by offering into the fire, the sacrificer acts for the benefit of the entire world. This is a supplement to the preceding injunction, and not one whose purpose is restricted solely to the literal meaning [of the words]. For if it were so, only one desiring rain would have the qualification (*adhikāra*) [to perform this rite]; yet that is not what is heard in the scripture. Since the connection is possible as a supplement to the context under discussion, there is no occasion for such an assumption. (3.66)
Just as all living beings depend upon the wind for their life, so do those in the other stages of life depend upon the householder. 3.67 (V3.77)

By another method, he demonstrates the necessity of performing the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*). Vāyu is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); depending upon that, all live. For there is no life for one who is breathless; the mere maintenance of breath is what constitutes living. The word *jantu* (creature) denotes any living being whatsoever. The inclusion of the term "all" implies that even the gods and sages, though possessed of extraordinary powers, have their lives dependent solely on Vāyu. Thus, the householder is equal to the vital breath for those in all stages of life (*āśrama*). Therefore, the meaning of the injunction is that he must become the means of subsistence for everyone. Although other stages of life are understood from the mention of "others," this is nevertheless not for the purpose of excluding the householder. For the specific duty of giving hospitality and so forth is enjoined especially for the *snātaka*. Therefore, the mention of "others" is intended to show the equality of the householder's stage with the others. Furthermore, it is not heard [in scripture] that they do not subsist by themselves or maintain their own bodies and families; rather, the compound *itarāśramāḥ* means "the other stages of life. (3.67)

Since even the members of the other three stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone through both knowledge and food, therefore the household is the most excellent stage of life. 3.68 (V.78)

Since all three other orders of life (*āśramins*) are supported and benefited by the householder—both through knowledge arising from the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas and through food—therefore the household order is the eldest and the best. In the reading *gṛhī*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; in the reading *gṛham*, it is a descriptive determinative (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "the eldest order is the home. Here too, the phrase "by householders alone" is a restatement based on propriety; it does not constitute a prohibition against forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and others from teaching and so forth. For the forest-dweller, this very duty is prescribed: "He should perform these same great sacrifices" (MDh 6.5). Although for the renunciant (*pravrajita*), favoring [others] is prohibited by the rule, "Being equal toward all beings, he should neither harm nor favor, and should not undertake [worldly activities]" (GDh 3.24–25), nevertheless, the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas is prescribed in the scriptures for mendicants (*bhikṣus*). Furthermore, because those two [orders] are enjoined to focus intensely on the cultivation of knowledge and dispassion, they do not apply themselves excessively to the exposition of Vedic meaning. As for the student (*brahmacārin*), he is not a teacher because his own purpose [in that stage] is lost, and since he is instructed to subsist on alms, how could there be the giving of food? Therefore, since this is generally possible only for householders, it is stated thus: "by householders alone. (3.68)

It should be maintained with effort by one desiring imperishable heaven and absolute happiness in this world—that which is difficult for those of weak faculties to maintain. (3.69) This refers to the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhāśrama*). It must be maintained with effort—that is, it must be practiced—by one who desires imperishable heaven and who desires happiness in this world. "Absolute" (*atyanta*) refers to that happiness which has no end; the word "absolute" implies permanence. That stage of life which is "difficult to maintain"—meaning impossible to sustain—by those of weak faculties.

This is what is meant: since for a householder the enjoyment of women, well-prepared food, and so forth are inevitable, there is a fault in the attachment of the senses to their objects; therefore it is said: [144] "One must maintain [self-restraint] with effort compared to other stages of life (āśrama). Even here, there is great restraint of the senses: one must not approach [one's wife] outside the fertile period, one must not approach the wives of others, and one must eat the remnants of the meal. That discipline which is required when sense-objects are present is difficult to perform."

"An imperishable heaven. By this, it is not meant that all the duties of a householder have heaven as their fruit, because some are obligatory (*nitya*) and others are heard to have different fruits. Even regarding those whose fruits are not explicitly stated and are therefore postulated to have heaven as their fruit, there is no reason for such a qualification when they are merely restated (*anuvāda*). Therefore, this is a restatement of the intended fruits of the prescribed acts. Nor is this a separate qualification (*adhikāra*); it can be said that these very same acts are to be performed throughout one's life by one who desires heaven. Furthermore, from the phrase "by one desiring happiness here," we understand an equivalence with what is not enjoined. For it is not possible here to understand "by one desiring happiness" as a fruit of the ritual act, since no specific [fruit] is indicated. Indeed, all pleasure is perceived as delimited by specific gains such as villages, sons, and so forth. If it were mere pleasure without such delimitation, it would be heaven itself; and that is not something pertaining to this world. Therefore, this is a restatement of one who desires the attainment of visible happiness. For other *āśrama*s are homeless—those dwelling at the roots of trees, those living in the houses of others, and they live in suffering. Thus, this is indeed a restatement. (3.69)
By virtue of its similarity to that [preceding statement], this too is merely a restatement:
"Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests—these expect [support] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty should act toward them. (3.70) V3.80

These [gods and others] solicit from householders—that is, from those living as family-men—and desire to take [wealth]. "Desire" (ākāṅkṣā) here refers to the longing for the instruction [of the scriptures] that seeks one's own benefit. Therefore, one who understands what is established in the scriptures must perform the duty toward those gods and others, such as the prescribed oblations (homa) and so forth. "Family" (kuṭumba) means one's wife. Even by an ordinary person, it is not proper to render fruitless that which has been undertaken with great effort; how much more so the praise of the deities? (3.70)

One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas, the gods with fire offerings according to the rule, the ancestors with śrāddha rites, men with food, and the spirits with the bali offering. (3.71)

The very same meaning as that of the injunction "one should study one's own Veda" (*svādhyāyam adhīyīta*) is expressed by the statement "one should honor the seers (*ṛṣi*) with one's own Veda. That which occurs through devotion at a *śrāddha* ceremony—namely, the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*argha*), garlands, and ointments—is what is called "honor" (*arcā*). Furthermore, this is a statement of praise; it does not mean that both—the study of one's own Veda and the worship of the seers—are to be performed [simultaneously]. The mantras addressed to deities such as Agni praise the seers. Therefore, the phrase "one should honor the seers with one's own Veda" is merely a commendation.

Alternatively, the sages Marīci and others are not intended here; rather, it is the Vedas themselves. Furthermore, the word *svādhyāya* is a term denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*) and does not here refer to the Vedas as such, as in the injunction, "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" (TĀ 2.15). By this, the following is meant: "One should honor the Vedas through study," meaning one should practice them according to the rules, since otherwise honoring would be impossible. Even in this case, "worship" (*arcā*) is merely figurative (*bhākta*). For in the act of oblation (*homa*), the deity is not the primary factor; rather, the deity is a *kāraka* (an instrumental factor).

One should honor the ancestors with the *śrāddha* rite; in this matter, the injunction is exactly as it is heard in the texts, and that will be determined in the section on the rules for *śrāddha*. One should honor men, such as guests, mendicants, and others; the meaning is that one should give food to them preceded by such worship. (3.71)
Day after day, he should offer the Śrāddha with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors. (3.72)

One should give; that is, one should perform. *Aharahaḥ* means every day. *Śrāddham*: this is an extension of the ritual by name. A rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*) prescribed for the new moon day is called *śrāddha*; its specific procedure is extended here by the name *śrāddha*. Regarding the phrase *annādyena*: this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what follows in [Manu Smṛti] 3.257, beginning with "with sesame, rice, and barley," while the intended meaning is explained further below. Regarding *udakena*: *payaḥ* means milk. (3.72)
One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*);

however, one should not feed any twice-born man here with regard to the *vaiśvadeva* offering. (3.73) Since the term "śrāddha" prescribes [the feeding], and thus the entire procedure for that rite would otherwise apply, a certain portion of the ritual requirements is here set aside by the statement: "one should not feed any [Brahmin] here. This means that in this daily (*anvāhika*) śrāddha, there is no feeding of a twice-born man intended for the *viśvedevas*—that is, directed toward the All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*).

Regarding this, some say: the repetition of the phrase "one should feed [the Brahmin] when food is available" indicates that this rite is *apūrva* (unprecedented). Therefore, this *śrāddha* consists merely of feeding a single Brahmin with the ancestors in mind; there is no other procedure (*itikartavyatā*) such as the *arghya* vessel, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth. Furthermore, there is no requirement for celibacy, the prohibition of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), and the like.

"One should feed even a single Brahmin"—because there is no injunction stating that "one [Brahmin] for each of the three [ancestors] at both [the Śrāddha and the daily rite]," and thus [feeding one] is not otherwise established, this one is prescribed. One should feed even one; if possible, many. "For the sake of the ancestors" means for the purpose of satisfying the ancestors. "Pertaining to the five sacrifices" (*pāñcayajñika*): that which arises from the five sacrifices is *pāñcayajñika*; it is included within those [five]. The word *pāñcayajñika* is used here in reference to the Śrāddha. For this is not the libation (*tarpaṇa*) belonging to the five sacrifices. Therefore, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the libation and the feeding. However, there will be an option (*vikalpa*) for this [feeding], as stated: "That very [act] by which he satisfies [the ancestors] with water" (MDh 3.273). 3.73.
A Brāhmaṇa should daily perform the oblation (homa) into the domestic fire from this prepared Vaiśvadeva food, according to the prescribed rule, for these deities. (3.74)

The cooked food (*pāka*) is called *vaiśvadeva* because it is intended for the *Viśvedevas*. Although the word *viśvedeva* means "all," here it serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the recipients of the gift; by this, its purpose for guests and others is also stated. One should perform the *homa* (oblation) of the prepared food for these deities who will be mentioned hereafter. By the word "prepared" (*siddha*), he shows that the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) accompanied by the mantra "devasya tvā... [RV 10.30.1] should not be performed with the deity in mind; rather, the meaning of the injunction is that the *homa* and other rites should be performed simply upon the completion of the cooking for all purposes. In the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, there is an instruction regarding the performance of the *homa* and so forth according to rule. He states the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of sweeping, sprinkling water around the fire, and so on, which is obtained through established custom and preceded by the prescribed rules. The word "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate that the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) have the entitlement. "Every day" (*anvaham*) means constantly. The mention of "deities" is for the purpose of obtaining the use of the *svāhā* exclamation. Because of the use of the genitive case, the formulation would otherwise be "this is for Agni" (*agner idam*). However, by using the word "deity" (*devatā*) or the *svāhā* exclamation, it is understood that the oblation is offered to the gods. Since the *vaṣaṭ* call is prescribed again at the end of the *yājyā* verse, it is absent in the *smārta-homa* (domestic ritual); however, the *svāhā* exclamation is used everywhere. When that is present, the formulation is "to Agni, svāhā" (*agnaye svāhā*). (3.74)
First to Agni and to Soma, and then to those two together;
then to the Viśvedevas and to Dhanvantari.

(3.75) The word "first" (*ādau*) is a reiterative reference (*anuvāda*), since [the offering] to Agni is already established as being first by the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). These are two separate oblations. Then, for those two together, there is the formula "to Agni-Soma," and for the Viśvedevas, the formula "to the Viśvedevas. There is only one oblation for Dhanvantari: *svāhā*. (3.75)
To Kuhū and to Anumati, and to Prajāpati, together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt. (3.76) V3.86

"Together with Heaven and Earth," [and] "To Heaven and Earth, Svāhā! Likewise, at the end, for the Sviṣṭakṛt. "Sviṣṭakṛt" is an attributive term (*guṇapada*), and Agni is the primary subject (*guṇin*) in its own right. This is because another Smṛti states, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," and because it is prescribed in the Śruti for all oblations. Although the word "at the end" (*antataḥ*) would have sufficed by the reading itself, this specific statement is made because other Smṛtis prescribe additional oblations; thus, it is intended to show that when these are combined, the insertion (*āvāpa*) must be performed before the Sviṣṭakṛt.

But surely, because the oblation (*homa*) is one, an option regarding the deity would be appropriate. Why, then, is the oblation one? This very [text] is the origin of the oblations: "Of Agni, of Soma," and so forth (MDh 3.75). And since they are already restricted by specific deities at their very origin, the oblations are understood to be distinct. (3.76)

Having thus properly offered the oblation into the fire, he should present the *bali* offering to Indra, Antaka (Yama), Appati (Varuṇa), and Indu (Soma), along with their followers, moving clockwise through all the directions.

(3.77) "Properly" means being intent on meditation upon the deities with an undistracted mind. Having thus offered [the oblation] into the fire for these deities, he should then proceed clockwise through all the directions in their respective order—first to the east, then to the south; this is the clockwise rotation. Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu are the presiding deities for each direction.

Another says: "The moon is not a recipient of an oblation. If the offering of the *bali* were not made with this word [“indave”], how could the moon possess a share of the oblation? And it has already been explained that the *bali*-offering is indeed a *homa*. Furthermore, for fear of breaking the meter, the specific form of the word is not intended here; rather, the dedication must be performed using the very words prescribed in other traditional authorities (*smṛti*).

[Thus one says: "To those accompanied by their followers" (*sanugebhyaḥ*). "Followers" (*anuga*) means attendants or subordinates (*tatpuruṣa*). Accordingly, the usage is "to the attendants of Indra" (*indrasya puruṣebhyaḥ*), and so forth. (3.77)
One should cast [the offering] at the door with "To the Maruts," and also into the water with "To the Waters";
likewise, one should offer upon the pestle and mortar with "To the Vanaspatis."

Here, the instrumental suffix (*itikaraṇa*) is intended to express the specific form [of the word]. *Ap-su* indicates the locus; *adbhyaḥ* is the designation of the deity. *Vanaspatibhyaḥ* refers to the pestle and mortar. In this case of a dual compound treated as a singular (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*), the two bases are not optional alternatives. By virtue of the function of the subordinate element in the designation, it is logical that the repetition applies to the primary element, which is the oblation (*āhuti*). Furthermore, it is impossible to establish a connection with the oblation for the pestle and mortar taken as a single unit, because their distinctness is perceived even there; for these two cannot be mixed together like milk and water. In that regard, if the offering is made in the mortar, the oblation is not made in the other; likewise, if it is in the mortar, it is not in the pestle. Nor is a partial oblation possible, because the quantity is fixed. Therefore, since they are designated here as a dual compound, it is appropriate that the oblation be made in one of the two joined items. (3.78)
One should place [the vessel] for Śrī at the head and for Bhadrakālī at the feet.

One should offer an oblation to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling. (3.79) The *ucchīrṣaka* is the head-region, the place of refuge for well-known deities; there one should make an offering to Śrī. At the feet—that is, the lower part of the house—one should offer to Bhadrakālī. Her place is also in the eastern part of the door. Others say that the *ucchīrṣaka* is the head-end of the house-bed, and its feet are the lower part. According to this view, this *homa* is performed on a bedstead or the like, or on the ground at the place where the householder sleeps.

"To Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati. Even though they are mentioned as a *dvandva* compound, these two offerings are distinct: one to Brahmā and another to Vāstoṣpati. However, where there is a dual divinity, as in the case of Agni and Soma, one uses either the term "together" (*saha*) or a collective expression, as in "of those two together" (MDh 3.75) and "together with Heaven and Earth" (MDh 3.76), because their association is not otherwise well-known. *Vāstu* means a house; [the offering is made] in its midst. 3.79.

And one should cast an offering into the air for all the gods, as well as for the beings that roam by day and those that roam by night. (3.80) Because of the word "ca" (and), this is a single oblation. For "all the gods," [the offering is made] either in the open space of the house or having gone outside the house. "By day" means for those who roam by day; "by night" means for those who roam by night. The term "beings" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*) is understood to apply to both.
Some say that these two oblations, divided into morning and evening, are for those who wander by day;
however, that is incorrect. For he will later state that there is an oblation in the evening without a mantra.

By this prohibition of a mantra, let it be granted that there is no verbal designation (*śabdoddeśyatā*); but what prevents a mental designation (*mānasas uddeśaḥ*)? And without that, the accomplishment of the oblation is not possible.
But this must be stated: how is this understanding of the distinction arrived at?
If it is argued that it is by the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras themselves, let it be so. (3.80)

One should offer a bali-oblation on the back of the house for the sake of the prosperity of all food; however, one should carry all the remainder of the bali to the south for the ancestors. (3.81) V3.91

This is the remainder of the two previous oblations (*āhuti*). The first half-verse is for the purpose of prescribing the locus (*ādhāra*) [of the offering]. "The site behind the dwelling" (*pṛṣṭhavāstu*) refers to that which is above the dwelling; it includes even the upper portion of a single-roomed house. Therein one should offer the *bali* to those who roam by day and those who roam by night, for the sake of the prosperity of all food (*sarvānnabhūti*). The dative case here is used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*), not in the sense of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Because no specific fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth is mentioned, because the word *bali* is a remainder of what precedes, and because the two previous oblations require a locus, [the meaning is established]. Furthermore, "the prosperity of all food" is nowhere heard of as a deity in another Smṛti within the context of the *vaiśvadeva*. Therefore, this is its meaning: this must be performed for the sake of the successful preparation of all foods; when this *baliharaṇa* is performed, all foods become [prosperous]. Since the understanding of the meaning is possible through the well-known meaning of the individual parts (*avayava*), the postulation of a collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*) has been stated [only as a secondary possibility]. Alternatively, some unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated in relation to a deity. Regarding "the remainder of the *bali*": because of the use of the word "remainder," one should take [the portion] from the vessel and then perform the offering; the *bali* offerings are not to be taken directly from what remains in the cooking pot. "To the south" means in the southern direction—that is, facing toward it. "All" means however much has been taken. (3.81)
One should slowly offer [the food] upon the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms. (3.82) V3.92

Having set aside food in a vessel, one should place it on the ground for the benefit of dogs and other such creatures. "Those with foul diseases" refers to lepers, those suffering from consumption, and the like; "birds" refers to winged creatures. [One should do this] slowly, so that it does not become mixed with the dust raised from the ground. The mention of "the ground" is not intended to exclude the use of a vessel; rather, it means that one should not give it directly into the hands of dog-cookers, outcasts, or lepers. This is a prescription for providing assistance. For this very reason, this verse is recited using the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and not with a word ending in the dative case (*caturthyanta*). As for "birds," it should be placed in such a location where they can eat without fear of dogs and the like. Regarding "worms," it should be placed in a location where they are likely to be found. (3.82)
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by a straight path to the supreme abode, his very form consisting of light.

This is the conclusion of the preceding section. Because of the use of the word "all," one should also assist with food other animals that may be found in the village, such as deer, cocks, cats, and so forth. The root *arc* (in *arcati*) signifies favoring (*anugraha*), not worship (*pūjā*), because that [worship] is impossible for dogs and the like. Furthermore, this term is employed to prohibit contempt; it is not read as "he does not favor. He attains the supreme station, the abode, which is Brahman. By the straight path. He does not wander through the many wombs of transmigratory existence. But what, then, is this injunction regarding the fruit?

We say no. It has been stated that this injunction is obligatory (*nitya*). And in the case of an obligatory injunction, the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). For no injunction is heard here; "he goes" is a statement in the present tense.

"Tejomūrtiḥ" means one whose body consists solely of light; he is not connected with a body composed of the five elements, but rather becomes one whose very nature is consciousness (*bodha*). Alternatively, "stainlessness" (*niṣkalmaṣatā*) is indicated by this term; the meaning is that he possesses a pure nature (*śuddhaprakṛti*). This is also an expression of compassion for living beings (*bhūtānukampana*): since there is no connection with sin when there is no transgression of the scriptures, his purity is logical. Otherwise, because sin is of the nature of impurity, he would not be "one whose body is light. Furthermore, it is entirely reasonable that in the absence of sin, he attains the supreme abode (*paraṃ dhāma*), which is most excellent and free from the nature of suffering. (3.83)
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
and he should give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and to a student of sacred knowledge.

The author will describe the characteristics of a guest (*atithi*). When such a person has arrived, one should first feed him—that is, provide him with food—before all other eaters present in the house. One should also give alms (*bhikṣā*) to a mendicant who asks for them. By the word *bhikṣā*, a gift of food in a very small quantity is meant; for it is said, "A handful (*prasṛti*) is an alms. This is well known in the inner apartments. To a student (*brahmacārin*), however, [the gift] should be given according to rule. It should not be given according to rule to any other mendicant, even one belonging to a heretical sect (*pākhaṇḍin*) or similar group. But for a student, the rule is that the giving of alms must be performed according to the prescribed method, preceded by the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*).

Alternatively, "bhikṣu" refers to a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), while "brahmacārī" refers to one in the first stage of life. The word "ca" (and) is placed out of its logical position for the sake of the meter; it should have been read as "brahmacāriṇe ca" (and to the student). However, if this were the case, there would be no gift for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Therefore, a *bhikṣu* is so called because he "begs" (*bhikṣate*); the mention of the "student" (*brahmacārin*) is merely an epithet of that same person. Thus, the giving of alms to all three types of ascetics is invariably permitted. As for heretics (*pākhaṇḍa*) and the like, they are treated like those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*). By the inclusion of the word "all," the obligation to assist a beggar according to one's ability is indeed established. (3.84)
Whatever merit a twice-born householder obtains by giving a cow to his teacher according to the prescribed rule,
that same merit he obtains by giving alms.

The giving of food to one who asks should always be performed according to one's ability; this, however, is a separate topic. That fruit which one obtains by giving cows to a teacher is obtained by giving alms; it is not distinct from the vow regarding cows (*govrata*). In another *Smṛti*, the gift of cows is heard to yield all fruits and also to serve the purpose of liberation from sin. Regarding those minor benefits for which equality of fruit with great benefits is stated, a distinction in the fruit should be understood in terms of quantity, as is common in the world. That very fruit is obtained, but not for a long duration. For this principle is expressible thus: "What wise man would buy what can be obtained for a *paṇa* with ten *paṇas*? If there were equality of fruit, the great effort [required for the larger gift] would result in futility. Some read "to a teacher according to rule" (*agur yathāvidhi*); in that case, the negative particle (*nañ*) should be seen as signifying "small," i.e., "a small teacher. "Merit" (*puṇya*) means *dharma*; its fruit is [the reward]. (3.85)
One should offer even alms or a vessel of water with respect and according to the prescribed rule to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas. (3.86)

Now, it was said "according to rule" (*vidhivat*); that very rule is now being stated. The mention of the water-pot (*udapātra*), which was not previously under discussion, is intended to show that this applies to all men at all times, and not only to the giving of alms. "Having honored" means having worshipped. That gift for which the rule (*vidhi*) comes first is "preceded by rule" (*vidhipūrvakam*). The word "first" (*pūrva*) signifies the cause; the meaning is that this [gift] is prompted by the scripture (*śāstra*). Alternatively, "rule" (*vidhi*) refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); that must be performed first. And it was stated previously regarding the giving of alms: "he gives, having honored and having worshipped. The "true meaning of the Veda" (*vedasya tattvārthaḥ*) is its ultimate, certain meaning; he who knows that—to such a Brāhmaṇa one should present or give [the gift]. The phrase "to a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya*) is a restriction based on caste (*jāti-niyama*). The phrase "to one who is learned" (*viduṣe*) is a restriction based on quality (*guṇa-niyama*). Therefore, whatever is to be given, that should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, and to him specifically as one who knows the meaning of the Veda, preceded by honor—this is the prescription of three requirements. One gives everything with the intention of wealth; because it is a human composition, there is no prescription of various specific forms of objects. (3.86)
There is a fault in giving when [the recipient] has arrived [uninvited]:
"The offerings to the gods and ancestors of men who lack discernment perish, when they are given out of delusion by donors to Brahmins who have become like ashes" (3.87). V3.97.

The kind of person to whom a gift should be given has been described in the preceding verse; by this [verse], there is a prohibition against giving to one who is unworthy. They "perish," meaning they become fruitless. *Havyas* are those offerings made for the sake of the gods, such as the feeding of Brahmins and other rites; *kavyas* are the other ancestral rites (*śrāddhas*) which constitute the constituent parts of the ritual for the ancestors. [These perish] when [the recipients] have become like ashes—having reached the state of ashes, they are "become-ashes" (*bhasmabhūta*). Alternatively, the word *bhūta* is used in the sense of a comparison, as in "like ashes" (*bhasmānīva*), just as one says "become wood" (*kāṣṭhabhūta*). What, then, is the similarity with ashes? Just as that [ash] is of no use anywhere, being merely refuse to be discarded, so too such a Brahmin is to be excluded from ritual acts; this is the intended meaning. The connection is that [offerings] perish for men who do not understand. "Given out of delusion" refers to those given by donors. The phrase "for those who do not understand, out of delusion" is a restatement of what has already been said: whatever is prohibited by the scripture is done only out of delusion. (3.87)

But what kind of fires are those that have not become ashes? He says: "An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, which are enriched by knowledge and austerity, delivers one from misfortune and indeed from great sin. (3.88)

Those who are enriched by knowledge and austerity are distinct from those who have become mere ashes. "Enrichment" (*samṛddhi*) means preeminent prosperity. Those endowed with extensive learning and great austerity are described in this way. Although knowledge and austerity belong to the whole [the person], they attain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the mouths—which are parts [of the person]—through a connection with that which is connected to them. In the expression "the mouths of the Brahmins are fires," a compound is formed because *vyāghra* and similar terms belong to the class of words known as *ākṛtigaṇa* (cf. Pāṇini 2.1.56). Just as an oblation poured into fire is fruitful, while one poured into ashes is fruitless, so too food placed into the mouth of such a Brahmin is like an oblation; thus, it is the act of eating itself that is praised. Sacrifices, oblations, and the like are well known for their great fruitfulness. Therefore, the unknown is compared to that which is most renowned for its qualities. He "rescues from difficulty. "Difficulty" refers to life-threatening situations such as disease, enemies, or oppression by kings. From that he rescues, meaning he protects him, and he is not touched by it. Furthermore, he saves him from great sin even in the next world, such as falling into hell. This [gift] is not intended only for such worthy recipients regarding rites for worldly prosperity (*ābhyudayika*); it should also be given for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) specifically for the sake of its merit. (3.88)
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water, and food prepared according to one's ability and in accordance with the prescribed rules. (3.89)

To one who has arrived on his own initiative, not one who has been invited; for an invited person does not become a guest. Furthermore, he will state the place where such a guest arrives: "where [the host's] wife or even the sacred fires are present" (MDh 3.93). He should offer a seat and water. First, water for washing the feet, then the seat, and then food. "Having prepared according to his ability" is an adjective qualifying the food; having prepared the food with special care, he should give it—that is, he should feed him—following the prescribed rule (*vidhipūrvakam*). That gift in which the rule (*vidhi*) comes first is described thus. The meaning is that the rule refers to the scripture (*śāstra*), which is the prior cause and the authority (*pramāṇa*). (3.89)
Even for one who constantly gathers grains by gleaning and offers oblations into the five fires, a Brāhmaṇa staying unhonored takes away all his merit. (3.90)

Even for one who is extremely poor, it is not proper to neglect the honoring of a guest. "From stones" means from the remnants left after harvesting the field; "gathering" (uñchataḥ) means picking up [grains]. This is intended to indicate the restriction of one's livelihood. "Even while offering oblations into the five fires"—by this it is meant that if one who is fully accomplished in the performance of the scriptures and yet extremely poor does not honor a guest who has arrived with the gift of food and so forth, then that performance of his and that restraint of his livelihood become fruitless. Consequently, the guest takes away—that is, seizes and renders useless—all of his merit and good deeds (*sukṛta*). "While staying unhonored. Therefore, "one should honor him" is the meaning of the injunction. From the indicative mark of the word "staying" (*vasan*), this rule applies to one who arrives in the evening. The "five fires" are the three sacrificial fires (*tretā*), the domestic fire (*gṛhya*), and the social fire (*sabhya*).

Now, what is this fire called *sabhya*? Thus they say: for one who has gone abroad to another village, where domestic cooking is performed, or that which is carried from the very house of the *gṛhya*-fire among many dwellings of a great sacrificer for the purpose of removing the cold—that is the *sabhya*.
What, then, is the *homa* (oblation) performed there?

To the extent that there is the restrictive rule, "In that [fire] the domestic rites [are performed]" (GDh 5.8), it is on account of this very statement that they consider the Vaiśvadeva oblation to exist for one who is away from home even in a secular fire. They cite the traditional teaching of the Smṛti: "One should offer oblations wherever one sees a well-kindled fire with flickering tongues of flame, [fed] with rice, barley, or dried grains."

In this regard, however, our venerable teachers say: In the *Upaniṣads*, the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) is taught. Therein, the forms of those fires are conceptualized; the meditation upon them in that form and the knowledge thereof are considered to be the *homa*. For that [knowledge] is held to yield a fruit superior to all ritual acts prescribed in the *Śruti*. Indeed, it is thus recorded there: "The stealer of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the violator of the teacher’s bed, and the slayer of a Brahmin—these four fall, as does he who associates with them" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.9). By praising [the guest] with the statement that even the fruit of these five [fires] perishes if the guest is honored and not turned away, it demonstrates the necessity of performing [this rite] through its excellence.

Even though the rule regarding the feeding of guests applies to the morning meal as well, there is a greater expiation for its omission in the evening. As for those who consider the phrase "according to one's ability" in the preceding verse to refer specifically to food, they say that guests should be honored according to one's capacity—whether it be one, two, or many. (3.90)
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—these are never lacking in the house of the virtuous. (3.91) V3.101

If, due to poverty, the giving of food in the evening is not possible, one should not think: "The primary requirement is the feeding of the guest; since I lack that, what is the use of this person who has entered my house? For even for one who is unable [to provide food], the rule for honoring a guest may be fulfilled by the gift of grass and such. Alternatively, this injunction does not terminate solely with the meal; rather, bedding and so forth must be provided for one who will stay overnight. The mention of "grass" is intended to include a straw mat (*srastara*). The ground is the place for sitting, sleeping, and recreation. Pleasant and truthful speech (*sūnṛtā vāk*) consists of words that are agreeable and beneficial, or the introduction of conversation and the like. Even in the absence of food, these things are not withheld from a virtuous guest who has arrived; on the contrary, they are given at all times. (3.91)
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays only temporarily, he is therefore called a guest. 3.92 (V3.102)

Since the meaning of the word *atithi* is not well-known in common worldly usage, he provides its definition: the status of a guest (*atithitva*) belongs to one who stays for a single night in another's house; and that [status] belongs to a Brāhmaṇa, not to another caste. Regarding the ritual of honoring on the second day, there is freedom of choice. One who desires a particular spiritual merit (*abhyudaya-viśeṣa*) has the entitlement to it, but it is not mandatory. Thus Āpastamba says: "By hosting [a guest] for one night, one conquers the earthly worlds; for a second, the intermediate worlds; for a third, the celestial worlds" (ĀpDh 2.7.16). This shows that one who desires such results has the entitlement for the second and subsequent nights. To provide a firm etymological justification for this very point, he says: for his stay is indeed temporary (*anitya*). This word is derived from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *ati*. Its derivation is somehow achieved through the *uṇādi* suffixes. (3.92)

One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin who lives in the same village, as well as one who has arrived from elsewhere, when he has come to the house—whether it be a household where the wife resides or even one where the sacred fires are maintained. (3.93) V3.103

One who dwells in the same village is not a guest, even if he has arrived at the time for the Vaiśvadeva offering; this refers to one who is a companion (*sāṃgatika*), a fellow student (*sahādhyāyī*), or other than a friend (*sakhyuḥ*). For regarding him, a rule will be stated later: "A Vaiśya, a Śūdra, and a friend" (MDh 3.100). Furthermore, even one who associates with everyone through various jests, conversations, and the like—though previously unseen—is included under the term *sāṃgatika* and is intended to be excluded.

Furthermore, for a householder who is away on a journey, even a guest endowed with all auspicious marks does not qualify as such; rather, one should recognize as a guest whoever has arrived at the home—that which is called his "permanent place" or "place of residence. Even when he is away, his wife and the sacred fires constitute his home; therefore, even though the householder is absent, the guest is indeed entitled to hospitality. Consequently, just as he travels after making arrangements for the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and other rites, so too must he make arrangements for the guest.

From the word "or" (*vā*), however, it is understood as follows: when one is traveling abroad together with his wife and the sacred fires, then he indeed remains a guest even while staying in another village, provided that his wife and fires are present in his house even though he himself is not. Consequently, if he should travel abroad with his wife while the fires remain in the house, there is no obligation to perform the hospitable reception of a guest (*atithipūjā*). The word "or" refers to the phrase "one should know [him] to be present in the house," and does not imply a mutual dependence between the wife and the fires. (3.93)
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others go, after death, to the state of cattle belonging to those who gave them that food and other gifts. (3.94)

"Upāsana" means the repeated practice of that. This is a censure directed at a Brāhmaṇa who, with such an intention, attends upon various [offerings] so that he may certainly obtain food, as if he were a guest—namely, one who habitually attends upon the cooked food belonging to another, but not on his own. By that action, after death, he goes to or attains the state of a beast, such as the species of an ox or the like; or he attains the state of an elephant, a donkey, or a horse in the house of the giver of the food and other things. This is the fault of a householder who has prepared the *sthālīpāka* (the sacrificial mess of boiled rice). 3.94.
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating. (3.95)

Evening begins with sunset and ends with the onset of night (*pradoṣa*). At that time, a guest who has arrived is not to be turned away nor refused; he is to be honored with food, a bed, a seat, and so forth. By whom? By the *gṛhamedhin* (householder). *Medha* means sacrifice. *Gṛhamedha* is the name for the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*); one who is entitled to perform them is a *gṛhamedhin*, which is to say, a householder. The phrase "brought by the sun" (*sūryoḍha*) is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*); he is brought or led by the sun. Because he has been brought by fate, he must necessarily be honored. Whether he arrives at the second period—the time for the *vaiśvadeva* offering—or at an improper time even after the evening meal has concluded, he must not stay in the house of this householder without eating. If there is any remnant of food, it should be offered to him; if not, cooking must be done twice. (3.95)
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven. (3.96) V3.106

One should not eat for oneself any superior food—such as soup, ghee, curd, sugar, and so forth—as long as a guest is present and has not been given it. However, that which is prescribed for the sick, such as gruel, meat broth, or bitter herbs, need not be given to one who does not desire it; there is no fault in eating such things if they have not been offered. This teaching is intended to mean that, in every case, one must not eat prepared food alone, nor should a guest be served inferior food. The word *dhanya* means "conducive to wealth" or "for the sake of wealth. The same applies to words such as *yaśasya* and others.

This is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*), because the feeding of guests is an obligatory duty when a guest is present, and because it is a supplement to what precedes it. Since it is possible for it to be construed as a praise, it is not appropriate to postulate a separate injunction (*adhikāra*). [3.96]

One should provide the best [reception] for the most excellent guests regarding their seat, lodging, bed, escorting, and attendance; for those of lower status, a lower reception; and for equals, an equal one. (3.97) When many guests arrive simultaneously—whether they are equal, inferior, or superior—the provision of seats and other comforts must take account of their respective qualities, and not be applied without distinction.

A seat consists of a grass mat (*bṛsī*) and so forth. A dwelling place is a site for rest. A bed consists of a couch (*khaṭvā*) and so forth. Following is following someone as they depart. Attending is remaining in their presence through the introduction of conversation. This [set of services] is the highest among the highest. One who follows for a long distance is the highest; one who follows not very far is the middle; one who follows only a few steps is the lowest. (3.97)

But when the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been completed, if another guest should arrive, one should give him food according to one's ability; however, one need not perform the Bali offering again. (3.98) V3.108

Food intended for all purposes is indeed designated by the term *vaiśvadeva*. When that has been completed—that is, when it is finished, when everyone has eaten, and when no food remains—if another guest should arrive, one should give him freshly cooked food. However, one should not take the *bali* offering from that [remaining] cooking; nor is an oblation (*homa*) into the fire desired, let alone the *bali* offering. This is because the *homa* and the *bali* offering pertain to the morning and evening cookings, and not to those in between. Thus, he will say: "But of the food in the evening... (MDh 3.111). And so, even if one should cook more than once during the day, the *vaiśvadeva* rite does not need to be repeated for every cooking, whether performed according to one's capacity with specific refinements or otherwise. (3.98)
A Brahmin should not proclaim his own family or lineage for the sake of food;
for by praising them for the sake of a meal, he is called by the wise a "vomit-eater. (3.99) V3.109

This instruction regarding a guest is incidental. One who seeks food should not announce or declare, "I am of such-and-such a family, the son of so-and-so. "One's own family and lineage" (*svakulagotra*) refers to one’s own family—meaning one’s paternal ancestry beginning with father and grandfather—and one’s *gotra*, such as Garga, Bhārgava, and so forth, or even one’s personal name. A "slip of the *gotra*" (*gotraskhalita*) refers to the utterance of another name when one intends to state a different name. Study (*adhyayana*) is also prohibited by other Smṛtis; that too must not be announced. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*): for the sake of food, thinking "I shall obtain a meal because of my well-known family and caste," one who praises or declares his family and lineage is called by the wise "one who eats vomit" (*vāntāśī*), meaning he eats or swallows what has been vomited or disgorged. (3.99)

A Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa; nor are a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, a relative, or even a teacher [considered guests in that sense]. (3.100) Even if a Kṣatriya is traveling on the road, he is not a guest when the time for the first meal has arrived. Therefore, food need not necessarily be given to him. The same applies to Vaiśyas and Śūdras. Friends and relatives, being equal to oneself, are not guests. A teacher is to be treated like a lord (*prabhu*); as it has been stated: "Having announced the act of cooking... (GDh 5.26). (3.100)
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may, at his pleasure, feed him once the Brahmins have finished eating. (3.101)

In this regard, the characteristics of a guest (*atithi*) are: having exhausted one's provisions for the journey, residing in another village, and arriving at the time of the meal. If a Kṣatriya comes to the house in such a form, then he too should be fed. By the mention of "feeding," other forms of service are excluded; however, speaking words that are pleasant and beneficial is prescribed without distinction for anyone who has come to the house. And this is the proper time for his feeding: after the Brahmins—who may be non-guests—have eaten, or those who are present in the house and are accustomed to eating first, then he should be fed. The word "if desired" (*kāma*) indicates the absence of a mandatory rule; the meaning is that this injunction is optional (*kāmya*), not obligatory (*nitya*). Since no specific result is mentioned, the reward is heaven (*svarga*). Alternatively, it should be connected here with [the verses] beginning, "It brings wealth and fame" (MDh 3.96). 111.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at the household as one who possesses the status of a guest, he should feed them along with his servants, practicing compassion toward them. (3.102)

The *dharma* of a guest is *atithidharma*. Those two for whom this exists are "possessors of the guest-dharma" (*atithidharmin*). And the duty toward a guest has already been explained previously. The household (*kuṭumba*) is the home; having arrived there, even a Vaiśya or a Śūdra one should feed like a Kṣatriya. However, the time for feeding those two is after the time for the Kṣatriya. For it says: "He should feed those two together with the dependents. Here, "dependents" (*bhṛtya*) refers to slaves. And their time for eating is before all [others]—guests, kinsmen, and relatives—once they have eaten, but prior to the husband and wife. The word "together" (*saha*) indicates merely simultaneity of time. By employing, taking as authoritative, or resorting to "kindness" (*ānṛśaṃsya*), which is compassion or pity—as the meaning goes—he excludes the status of being an object of formal worship (*pūjyatā*). For one who is to be favored is one to be pitied, not one to be worshipped. If a favor can be rendered toward those who are to be pitied, then it is done by one seeking spiritual prosperity; however, the failure to do so does not constitute a transgression against the guest. This is what is meant: the kind of merit that is superior to the feeding of a guest is not matched by a corresponding inferior merit from favoring those who are to be pitied. (3.102)
He should also, together with his wife, feed with affection his friends and others who have come to his house, providing them with food according to his means and their rank. (3.103) V3.113

One should feed those who have come out of friendship—those for whom he is a friend, a companion, or the like. The word "ādi" (and so forth) includes various types of people such as kinsmen, relatives, associates, and fellow students, with the exception of the teacher (*guru*). The inclusion of the term "out of friendship" (*saṃprītyā*) is for the purpose of exclusion, since the duty regarding guests (*atithi-dharma*) is the subject under discussion. One should feed them by preparing food with excellence—that is, having prepared and consecrated it. The word "according to one's ability" (*yathāśakti*) is used as an illustrative term; whatever one's capacity may be, and whatever kind of preparation each person deserves, that very kind of preparation should be made for them. "With his wife": the time for the husband’s meal is the same as that for the wife, because there is no separate time for her meal. For it has been said: "But the husband and wife [eat] what remains" (MDh 3.106). In the *Mahābhārata*, the wife’s eating after the husband is shown in the dialogue between Draupadī and Satyabhāmā (MBh 3.222), where Draupadī, while explaining the duties of women, says: "I eat the remaining food after all my husbands have eaten. Eating the remnants of the husband’s food is the duty of women. Therefore, it is not prescribed here that friends and others should eat at the time of the wife’s meal. Nor does the meaning of "together" (*saha*) imply eating from the same vessel. Rather, they should not be fed alone; instead, the wife should also eat there. Consequently, the rule "but the husband and wife [eat] what remains" (MDh 3.106) is set aside in this case. If some guest of the husband is waiting, or if the husband does not eat due to a lack of appetite, then the wife should eat in his place. In this way, their mutual affection will be manifested. (3.103)
One should feed these—married women, young maidens, the sick, and pregnant women—immediately after the guests, without making any distinction among them. (3.104)

"Suvāsinyah" refers to newly married women, wives, daughters-in-law, and daughters. Others, however, say: "Those whose fathers-in-law and fathers are still living are called *suvāsinyah*, even if they have already given birth. One should feed these [women] immediately after the guests; that is, one should feed them at the same time as the guests are already engaged in eating. Others, however, read the word as "agra" (first). Without hesitation—one should not entertain doubt as to how children can eat while the guests have not yet been fed. (3.104)
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these, while eating, does not realize that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures. (3.105)

If an unwise person—one who does not know the meaning of the scriptures—eats first, before giving food to these [beginning with] guests and ending with dependents, he becomes a ghost (*preta*) and is devoured by dogs and vultures. He does not realize that such "eating" is his own being eaten by them. For the fool thinks, "I alone am eating here," but he does not perceive that such a meal is actually the devouring of his own body by dogs and vultures; it is said so because that is the fruit of his action. (3.105)
When the Brahmins and his own servants have finished eating, the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains. (3.106)

The *vipras* are the guests, and the "one's own" (*sva*) are the kinsmen and so forth. When they have finished eating, the couple—the husband and wife—should eat what remains. The word "afterwards" (*paścāt*) is stated for the purpose of ensuring that the meal occurs only after [the food] has been set aside for them and designated as "leftover" (*śiṣṭa*); otherwise, there might be a meal before that. This [verse] is intended to prescribe the time for the couple's meal; the first half-verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*). (3.106)

"Having honored the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the domestic deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains [of the offerings]. (3.107) This is merely a restatement of the previously mentioned rule for performing the five sacrifices and the time for the householder's meal.

Others, however, describe this as an injunction for a different matter (*arthāntara-vidhāna*). In the preceding [verse], the eating of the remainder at the same time was prescribed for both husband and wife; by this [verse], it is enjoined for the man alone, excluding the woman. Consequently, before the servants, the wife should eat first from the husband’s portion, or having set it aside in that manner, he should feed her. This interpretation will also be consistent. Otherwise, if one were to assume the meaning to be that "the wife should not eat together with them," there would be a violation of the syntactical connection (*padānvaya*) of the word as it is heard. As for the observation found in the *Mahābhārata*, that is merely an illustration (*darśana*) and not an injunction (*vidhāna*); it will be treated as an option (*vikalpa*) within the context of an injunction.

That is incorrect, because this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor is there a contradiction with the singular number in the word *gṛhastha* (householder), since husband and wife have a joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*). And in that case, because the sense of "together" (*saha*) is primary, there is no necessity for a dual number. Just as in the injunction, "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires," the singular number is not contradicted even though the entitlement is shared with his wife. For what reason? Because in that instance, one is the principal (*pradhāna*) and the other is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). A subordinate element cannot impose its own number [upon the principal]. Therefore, because the principal possesses the number one, even though the husband’s purpose is involved, the singular alone is appropriate. The single word *gṛhastha* applies to the wife as well, and that occurs when there is a desire to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*). And that [desire] arises from being the object of a single cognition, whether they are both principals or both subordinates. Consequently, the wife does not eat before the man. Thus, it is established that this is a restatement intended to strengthen the understanding.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *arthavāda*, "one should worship the domestic deities (*gṛhyā devatāḥ*"), some maintain that because the word "deity" (*devatā*) is understood in connection with the injunction "one should worship," this constitutes a figurative injunction for the worship of images. For it is not possible for the primary sense of "deity" to be an object of worship; since being a deity is primarily established only through its connection with sacrifice (*yajña*) and praise (*stuti*). Thus he says, "the domestic ones. Those that exist in the house are the "domestic" (*gṛhya*) ones, and these are indeed the images. For those who have become the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) of a sacrifice cannot be established as having a connection with a house.

For them as well, the term "deities" is used in a secondary sense and does not refer to objects of worship. Why is this so? Because it is logically consistent that those who are to be sacrificed to by a householder are called "domestic deities" (gṛhyāḥ). || 3.107 ||
He who cooks for his own sake alone eats only sin; for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from the sacrifice. 3.108 (V3.118)

He who cooks or causes food to be cooked for his own sake—aiming at himself with the thought, "I am hungry," or "This pleases me; let that very thing be cooked"—he eats only sin; he stores it, takes it into his heart, and does not even take a morsel of the food. Therefore, one who is not ill should not cook food for his own sake. However, for one who is ill, it is proper to resort to whatever means ensures the maintenance of the body, even if it involves transgressing other rules, because of the scriptural injunction: "One should protect oneself by all possible means" (GDh 9.34). Some explain its meaning in this way.
This is incorrect because it contradicts another Smṛti. For they say:

"Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is dear to one in the home—that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that [gift] itself to be inexhaustible. (MBh 13.58.7)
"Beloved" means desired or longed for. And if it were not cooked, how could there be the possibility of giving such a thing?

Therefore, this is its meaning: first of all, there is no such purpose for cooking that is obligatory; the purpose [of cooking] arises when friends, kinsmen, and others have arrived. Otherwise, however, the giving of food to guests and others is prescribed when there is no specific cooking intended for them. By this it is said: this fault applies to one who eats without having given to them. Alternatively, when everyone—including guests and others—has eaten, one should not cook again for one's own sake. And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "The husband and wife should eat the remainder. When everything has been consumed, there is no further cooking. (VaDh 11.11)

"Eating the remnants of the sacrifice" (yajñaśiṣṭāśana) is merely a praise of the aforementioned practice of eating leftovers. "Sacrifice" (yajña) refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites; "remnant" (śiṣṭa) means what remains after being used, and this is the eating thereof. This has a fruit equal to that [of the former], namely, that which is prescribed as the food remaining after guests and others have eaten, belonging to virtuous householders devoted to the performance of the scriptures. (3.108)

One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, a sacrificial priest, a snātaka, a teacher, and one's dear father-in-law and maternal uncle, even if a full year has passed since their last visit. (3.109)

In connection with the worship of guests (*atithipūjā*), a specific form of worship for certain other venerable persons who have arrived at the house is now prescribed. The term "king" refers to one who has been consecrated (*abhiṣikta*), not merely any member of the Kṣatriya caste. For this is an exceedingly great honor; not every Kṣatriya is worthy of it. Indeed, it is not appropriate to mention him alongside the *snātaka* and the teacher (*guru*). Nor is it fitting that his worship be equal to that of the teacher, as is indicated by the scriptural evidence (*liṅga*): "Just as when a king of men arrives here" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 1.15)—this passage from the *Atithyeṣṭi* Brāhmaṇa—and the statement in the rule for the *madhuparka* offering, "the guest is like a cow-slayer," which shows that the subject is a king of men. Therefore, this worship should be performed for a ruler of a realm, whether he be a Kṣatriya or not; however, in the case of a Śūdra, there is no entitlement to the use of mantras.

But is it not the case that the recitation of mantras is forbidden for a Śūdra, whereas it is not forbidden for Brāhmaṇas and others when the rite is intended for a Śūdra recipient? This is not a fault, for even in the case of the *arghya* offerings, there is the recitation of mantras such as "bhūtebhyas tvā. Furthermore, in the Mahābhārata, the performance of the *madhuparka* rite is indeed heard of as being performed by a Śūdra.
He himself duly offered that worthy seat to the Blessed One, as well as the honey-mixture and the cow.

"To the Blessed Vāsudeva, [this is offered by] Vidura. The term *madhuparka* is applied here through devotion to the curd (*dadhi*) which is its constituent part; a word for the whole may be used for its parts, as in "clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is indeed longevity. Furthermore, the word *rājan* refers to the lord of a territory and does not apply to every mere Kṣatriya. They say that a son-in-law is "dear" (*priya*). A *snātaka* is one who has completed both his studies and his vows; otherwise, all officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and teachers (*guru*) are indeed *snātakas*. For those residing in the various stages of life (*āśrama*), the practice of begging alms (*bhaikṣacaryā*) is prescribed, but not eating according to the duty of a guest (*atithidharma*). Alternatively, the *snātaka* is understood here as one who has recently finished his Vedic study. One should honor (*arhayet*) and worship these persons. The word *madhuparka* is the name of the ritual act; its specific nature is to be understood from the *Gṛhya-sūtra*. The phrase "after a year has passed" (*parisaṃvatsarān*) is an adjective qualifying the king and other such venerable persons. It means those for whom a full year has elapsed. If they arrive after a year has passed, then they are worthy of the *madhuparka*; before that time, they are not.
Some explain it thus: if they arrive before a year has passed, then even though the year is not yet completed, they receive another offering for the first worship.
Others, however, say: their worship is annual (*sāṃvatsarikī*), not [to be performed] until their arrival. On this view, arriving early does not obstruct the worship.
There is an alternative reading, *parisaṃvatsarāt*. The meaning is: as long as it is a full year, that is *parisaṃvatsara*; after that, they are to be worshipped again. (3.109)

"A king and a learned brāhmaṇa (śrotriya), when a sacrificial rite is at hand, are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); but not so when there is no sacrifice—this is the settled rule. (3.110) Some maintain that this [rule] is intended for the purpose of obtaining [the guest] even before a year has passed, provided a sacrifice is the occasion.

Others, however, say that the preceding [rule regarding the king and the *śrotriya*] is a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*) specifically to those two. For if there were no such restrictive application, the statement "but not for one who has not performed a sacrifice" would be untenable. Here, the *śrotriya* is either the *snātaka* previously mentioned, or indeed the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) himself; for it is prescribed that the offering of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) is to be made when he is about to begin the sacrificial rite. Even if he should sacrifice with Soma more than once a year, they should officiate for him only after he has been presented with the guest-offering (*arghya*). In this way, this traditional law (*smṛti*) will have its basis firmly established; otherwise, a basis would have to be inferred.

Others, however, maintain that all those beginning with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are indicated by the term *śrotriya*. Accordingly, Gautama has stated without distinction: having said, "The honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) is offered upon the arrival of an officiating priest, a teacher, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle" (GDh 5.27), he then states, "Prior to [the completion of] a sacrifice or a marriage" (GDh 5.29). Therefore, for all those worthy of the guest-offering (*arghya*), there should be eligibility for the offering even before a year has passed when a sacrifice is the occasion; and the prohibition "not when there is no sacrifice" should be understood as applying prior to a year, not after it.

In this second section (*pāda*), there is a manifold understanding of the textual recitation. Some read: "When the sacrifice has been commenced (*tate yajña upasthitau*). For them, the meaning is as follows: "When the sacrifice has been commenced"—that is, if the two arrive having been invited and brought [to the site]—then this *madhuparka* rite is for them; but not when the sacrifice is merely being commenced.

This position is refuted by some: because of the prohibition against all giving on the part of one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*)—to the effect that "the initiated does not give"—the permission to give the *madhuparka* would be in contradiction with that rule. Nor can it be argued: "This is not an act of giving; since there is an injunction to 'honor' (*arhayet*), this prescribes an act of worship. For in the *madhuparka*, there is the giving of curds, the giving of meat, food, and so forth. If it is then said, "That which belongs to another is consumed by oneself," in that case, the fault of theft (*steya*) would ensue. If it is argued, "It is not [theft] because of the scriptural statement," then the sense of "giving" (*dadāti*) certainly exists here, for the root *dā* is enjoined in the rule: "one should give the *madhuparka*. Therefore, there is a contradiction. There would be a contradiction with the rule "the initiated does not give" only if the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) applied exclusively to Soma sacrifices. Since the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and others are also sacrifices, this injunction will apply to them as well.

This is not correct; for if it were so, there would be a contradiction with established custom (*samācāra*). Indeed, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) do not bring the *madhuparka* for an honored guest (*arghya*) on any occasion other than the Soma sacrifices. Custom is based on respect for the Veda; therefore, this reading alone is correct: "when a sacrificial rite has arrived. The learned honor one who has come when a sacrifice is about to begin with the *madhuparka*, but not when the sacrifice is already in progress. Consequently, we do not even consider this [objection]: let there be a cessation of the gift that is obtained generally, but not of that which is specifically prescribed by the revealed text (*śruti*). And "sacrificial rite" (*yajñakarma*) refers to that which is both a sacrifice and an action; "when it has arrived" means when it has been reached. (3.110)
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer the *bali* oblation without reciting mantras;

for this is called the *vaiśvadeva*, which is prescribed for both morning and evening. (3.111) The first [topic] has been explained. Now the second cooking is described. "Evening" refers to the end of the day, the time of *pradoṣa*; there, the entire ritual procedure for the *pākayajña* must be repeated for the food that has been prepared, with the exception of the *brahmayajña* and the *pitṛyajña*.

But is it not the case that only this much is heard: "one should offer the *bali*"? And since the offering of the *bali* is well known as being the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*) alone, how can there be an oblation in the fire or the giving of gifts to guests and others therein?
