If it is argued that this is indeed called the *vaiśvadeva*, and thus the word *vaiśvadeva* establishes its universal application—meaning this is prescribed for all the gods—then for this very purpose, the mention of "morning" is included so that whatever is done in the morning is exactly the same in the evening. Otherwise, since it is already prescribed for the morning, what would be the point of prescribing it for both evening and morning? If that is the case, then the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) and the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) must also be performed.

It is said: because of the statement "of the prepared food" (*siddhasyānnasya*), only that which is accomplished by means of food should be performed; however, the *brahmayajña* (study of the Veda), which is accomplished through recitation, nor the *tarpaṇa* (libation), which is accomplished with water, [are included]. And thus the connection is made: one should offer the *bali* from the prepared food. This rite called *vaiśvadeva* is prescribed for both times of day regarding the prepared food. This is explained in this way on account of both the word *anna* (food) and the word *vaiśvadeva*.

"Without a mantra. By the word *mantra*, what is prohibited is that which is accompanied by sound, addressed to a deity, and ending in *svāhā*, such as "Svāhā to Agni" (*agnaye svāhā*). For no other mantras are prescribed for the *vaiśvadeva* offerings. Furthermore, their status as mantras is asserted by way of praise; however, there is no status as a *mantra* for those things not recited in the *svādhyāya*. A certain portion of the *svādhyāya* consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, or *Sāma* Vedas is conventionally designated as "mantra" by those who study the Veda. And the understanding of the meaning of a thing arises from such conventional usage. Moreover, those words with which the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) and so forth are performed are not recited anywhere [in the Veda]. From the Śruti text, "One should perform the oblation (*homa*) solely for the deities beginning with Agni," and from another statement, "The sacrificial offering (*havis*) is delivered to the deities either with the utterance of *svāhā* or with the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*," the utterance of *svāhā* is enjoined for all *homas*, while the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* is restricted to the end of the *yājyā*: "He utters *vaṣaṭ* at the *yājyā*. When the word *svāhā* is employed, the dative case is prescribed by tradition (*smṛti*). Therefore, since the sacrifice involves the deity as the intended object (*uddeśya*), and since the nature of the deity is understood through words, and because it is appropriate to express this through words alone, the formulation "Svāhā to Agni" (*agnaye svāhā*) and so forth is constructed.

If they are thus prohibited, how then is the completion of the sacrifice achieved? For the essential nature of the sacrifice is not accomplished as long as the dedication has not been performed with the thought, "This is for you, it is not mine. Indeed, a sacrifice is not merely a renunciation devoid of dedication.

True. When the word is prohibited, the wife of the deity will perform the assignment of the deity in the mind, just as a Śūdra utters a salutation (*namaskāra*). Regarding the rule, "For him, the salutation is permitted as a non-mantric substitute" (GDh 10.64), since the mantra is replaced by the salutation for the Śūdra, the salutation is what is permitted for him, not the word for the deity. And in that regard, it has been stated that success is achieved through the application of the deity. However, your honors say here: for the Śūdra, the utterance *svāhā* is replaced by the salutation, but the word for the deity is not prohibited.
Now, regarding the Vaiśvadeva oblation performed in the evening, who is the performer?
It has been stated that the wife herself shall perform it without mantras, due to her proximity, just as in the case of the Bali offering. (3.111)

Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, at the waning of the moon, perform the monthly Śrāddha known as the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka. (3.112)

This other obligatory *śrāddha* is declared distinct from the optional *vaiśvadevika* *śrāddha*. It is to be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), specifically at the time when the moon has waned. Even then, it is not to be done at just any time; rather, it is after having completed the *pitṛyajña*. Having performed that *piṇḍapitṛyajña* which is prescribed by the *Śruti*, the very same time that applies to that sacrifice is obtained for this one as well. Thus it is said: "On the new moon day, in the afternoon, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. For one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is indeed the application of the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). And so he says: "In this manner, one who has not maintained the fires, having cooked [the food] for the daily [rites]" and so forth. One who possesses the fire is either possessed of the marriage fire or of the fire brought at the time of inheritance. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is not intended to be restrictive; it is desired for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well, for it is stated without distinction in other *Smṛtis*. The term *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* is the name of this *śrāddha*. It is called *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* because it is performed (*anu-āhriyate*) subsequent to the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*). It occurs every month and every following month; thus it is "monthly" (*māsānumāsika*). The compound word *māsānumāsa* expresses a repetition (*vīpsā*) regarding the months. This means it is to be performed month after month; hence its status as an obligatory rite is established. Although the sense of repetition is understood from the word *anumāsa*, the word *māsa* is nonetheless redundant; nevertheless, in metrical composition, such prolixity is not considered a fault. *Śrāddha* is also merely a name. *Kuryāt* (he should perform) is the injunction. (3.112)
The wise know the monthly Śrāddha for the ancestors as the Anvāhārya;
that should be performed with effort using excellent meat. (3.113)

The *anvāhārya* is the sacrificial fee for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the two Śrauta rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. This monthly *śrāddha* performed on the new moon day is the *anvāhārya* for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Just as the priests are gratified by the *anvāhārya*, so too are the ancestors gratified by the *śrāddha*. By this, he states that the *śrāddha* has the ancestors as its purpose. It is not the case that the ancestors are the primary deities (*devatā*) of the *śrāddha* in the same way that Agni and other deities are the primary deities of the Darśa and other sacrifices; rather, the *śrāddha* exists solely for their benefit. Accordingly, the genitive case is used in the phrase "of the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*). For if they were merely deities, the use of the genitive would be improper, as the dative case would be required instead.
In this context, there is an alternative reading and a different meaning: "the monthly [offering] for the funeral cakes."

The wise know [this] as the *anvāhārya*. By this, its necessity is stated just like that of the *pitṛyajña*; however, it is not a mere subsidiary (*aṅga*) [of the sacrifice]. This should be performed with *āmiṣa*, that is, meat—preferable, unprohibited, or specifically prescribed, as he will state: "For two months, with the meat of fish" (MDh 3.258). And this is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*). In its absence, curd, ghee, milk, cakes, and so forth will be prescribed. Furthermore, meat is a condiment (*vyañjana*) for the food to be eaten, such as boiled rice; it is not the sole food itself, since he will say: "And side dishes such as soups and vegetables" (MDh 3.216), as well as: "As many [guests] as there are, and with which foods" (MDh 3.114).

Furthermore, are all the rites in a *śrāddha*—such as the fire-oblation (*homa*), the feeding of Brahmins, and the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*)—equally primary and denoted by the term *śrāddha*, or is some part here a subordinate member (*aṅga*) and some part the principal (*pradhāna*)?

It is said: because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such expressions as "one should feed [at] the *śrāddha*" (MDh 3.137) and "the *śrāddha* was eaten by him" (Pāṇini 5.2.85), it is understood that the feeding of the Brahmins is the primary element. (3.113)
And so he said:

"In that regard, I shall describe in their entirety those who are to be fed and those who are to be avoided among the best of the twice-born, as well as how many there are and with what kinds of food. (3.114) V3.124

In that regard, concerning this śrāddha, I shall now explain all of the following: which of the best of the twice-born brāhmaṇas are to be fed and which are to be avoided; how many and of what number they are, according to such rules as "two for the gods" (MDh 3.115); and with which foods they are to be served, according to such rules as "with sesame, rice, and barley" (MDh 3.257). Listen to that.

This is what must be accomplished here primarily; without this, the *śrāddha* is not considered performed. Furthermore, regarding any other constituent part—whether it be an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) or a direct auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)—if that is not accomplished, the *śrāddha* is not performed, and it would lack its full quality (*saguṇa*). Therefore, these are mentioned again for the purpose of declaring their primary importance. (3.114)

One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each of the two; even if he is very wealthy, he should not engage in excessive elaboration. Although it would have been more appropriate to provide a specific explanation of the subject already promised in that same sequence, nevertheless, because there is so little to be said here, this verse sets forth the number [of guests], setting aside what was previously established as "those who are to be fed" (MDh 3.114).

One should feed two Brāhmaṇas for the sake of the gods (*deva*), and three for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Or, in both cases, one may feed one for the gods and one for the ancestors. Although in the term *pitrye*—meaning "this is for the father"—the word *pitṛ* functions as a designation of the deity, nevertheless the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are the intended recipients. In that regard, one should feed one Brāhmaṇa for each individual ancestor, and not just one for all of them, because they are separate deities. And so the author of the Gṛhyasūtra has stated: "But certainly not one for all" (ĀśG 4.7.4), and "This is explained by the [rule regarding] the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*)" (ĀśG 4.7.6). The meaning is that just as a single rice-ball is not offered to all [ancestors], so too a single Brāhmaṇa is not fed for all. Here too, the author will say: "He should invite at least three" (MDh 3.177). That invitation is solely for the purpose of feeding, not for some invisible spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, it should be understood that for the ancestral rite, one should feed three for each [lineage]. Thus he says: "And one should not feed fewer than [three]" (cf. GDh 15.7). Having established this, the statement "even a single learned man" (MDh 3.119) should also be understood in this same way: namely, one for each [ancestor]. Furthermore, the rule "not even one for both" is not an original injunction here; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to prohibit excessive expansion (*vistara*). It is like saying, "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house."

If this is so, then even the rule "two for the gods" would not exist, since that too can be accounted for by having another purpose. If, however, this [latter] rule is a mandatory injunction because it was not otherwise established, then why should the rule "one for each" not also be a mandatory injunction?
To this he replies: Let there be no mandatory injunction for either of the two.
From what, then, is the understanding of the number derived?
"One should invite at least three," so says Manu (MDh 3.177).
But surely there is no mention of the gods (*daiva*) there.
In that case, the number is understood from another *smṛti*: "An odd number, or according to one's ability" (GDh 15.7–8), and "An even number for the gods" (YDh 1.226).

If this were a rule regarding a specific number, then since there would be no possibility of exceeding that limit, the prohibition would be meaningless. Therefore, as many Brahmins as must be fed so that the faults associated with an extensive feast (*vistara*) do not occur—so many should be fed. At a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), they should be odd in number; at a rite for the gods (*daiva*), however, there should be only two. Even if one is extremely prosperous or exceedingly wealthy, one should not engage in an extensive feast. Furthermore, this prohibition against extensiveness is not for the sake of some invisible spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). (3.115)
What then? Hospitality, the proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five things elaborate ritual destroys; therefore, one should not seek elaboration. (3.116)

These faults arise [from excessive elaboration]. No further detail is pursued here. However, if it is possible to provide hospitality and the other requirements, then one may proceed according to one's enthusiasm. Hospitality (*satkriyā*) refers to a special preparation of food. Place refers to ground sloping toward the south and so forth, as will be stated later: "in clean open spaces" (MDh 3.197). Time refers to the afternoon, as in: "when the sun has moved past midday. Purity pertains to oneself, the Brahmins, and the servants. The excellence of the Brahmins refers to the acquisition of virtuous Brahmins. These qualities must necessarily be secured; yet they are lost through elaboration. Elaboration leads to deficiency. And this [deficiency] occurs when there is a great multitude of Brahmins. Therefore, one should not seek [excessive elaboration]; one should not perform it. (3.116)
This well-known performance for the deceased, called the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), occurs at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that [practice], it is always merely a worldly performance for the dead.

This rite called *pitrya* (ancestral) is not like divine rites which have no purpose for the deities; rather, it is the celebrated and well-known performance of funeral rites (*pretakṛtyā*), the service rendered to the deceased, at the waning of the moon. "Waning of the moon" (*vidhukṣaye*) means the disappearance of the moon, i.e., the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). There is an alternative reading, "at the waning of the lunar day" (*tithikṣaye*). However, the reading "at the waning of the rule" (*vidhikṣaye*) is faultless. For the interpretation there is as follows: the rite called *pitrya* is an action enjoined by rule (*vidhi*) performed in the house (*kṣaye gṛhe*). For one who is engaged in—that is, devoted to—that ancestral rite, [the result] always attends the performer. It is indeed the funeral rite itself; even for that deceased person, a service (*upakāra*) such as the *śrāddha* and so forth is performed by the sons. In this manner, the non-interruption of the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth is established as the fruit of the *śrāddha*. And this is not an entitlement for one desiring that fruit, because its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) has already been established.
Others, however, maintain that this is a separate entitlement for one who desires the non-interruption of the lineage;
the meaning is that this duty is worldly, that is to say, it is based on the Smṛti. || 3.117 ||
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit. (3.118)

A *śrotriya* is one who has studied an entire recension (*śākhā*) consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa texts according to the Vedic tradition. To such a person should be given the *havyas*—the offerings of food prescribed as part of the *śrāddha* rite intended for the Viśvedevas—and the *kavyas*—the foods intended for the ancestors. "To the most worthy" (*arhattamāya*): worthiness (*arhattā*) consists of being venerable and qualified. One born of a noble family is venerable; one born into a great lineage and endowed with learning and virtuous conduct is [most worthy]. What is given to him, whether other than a *śrāddha* or even the *śrāddha* itself, yields great fruit. Thus: [225] a gift to one who is not a *śrotriya* is fruitless; [226] a gift to a *śrotriya* who lacks qualities such as noble birth and learning yields little fruit; [but] to the most worthy, it yields great fruit. (3.128)
By feeding even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors, one obtains abundant fruit; but not even many who are ignorant of the mantras.

He demonstrates what was stated [in verse 3.118], namely, "for the sake of the highest arhatship": by feeding even a single learned man, one obtains abundant fruit. And "learnedness" has been explained as the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas; for it is said: "Not even many who do not know the mantras. The mention of "mantras" is intended to indicate the Vedas generally. The meaning of the injunction is that, in the absence of five who are knowers of the Vedas, one should feed even a single learned man. "Abundant" (puṣkala) means nourishing or extensive. (3.119)
One should examine from afar a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas; he is the proper recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is considered a guest. 3.120 (V3.130)

One should not be fed simply because he has mastered the Vedas. Rather, one should examine him from afar with skill, seeking to know the purity of both his maternal and paternal lineages. As it is said: "Those for whom one may determine the *brāhmaṇya* on both sides—ten generations back from mother and father—through their established learning and austerity, and through meritorious deeds"; this is examination from afar. Likewise, there is the knowledge of the reality of his study, understanding, and performance of rites. "The end of the Veda" (*vedasya pāraḥ*) means its completion; one who has gone to that is "one who has mastered the Veda" (*vedaparaga*). One does not become worthy [of offerings] merely by reciting the Vedic *saṃhitā* or the *Brāhmaṇa*. From this very perspective, it is understood that by the word *śrotriya*, even one who studies only a portion of the Veda is designated. He is a "ford" (*tīrtha*) for the offerings to gods and ancestors (*havyakavya*). Like a ford (*tīrtha*), he is a ford; just as those seeking water obtain it when they descend by such a path, so too do the offerings to gods and ancestors reach the ancestors through such a Brāhmaṇa—this is a praise. Regarding another Brāhmaṇa, whether through sacrifices, charitable works, or gifts: just as one gives without hesitation to a guest who has arrived of his own accord, and what is given yields great fruit, so too should offerings to gods and ancestors be given without hesitation to such a Brāhmaṇa; they yield great fruit. (3.120)

For where a thousand times a thousand who are ignorant of the *Ṛgveda* eat, a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, is worth all of them according to the Dharma. (3.121) "Those ignorant of the *Ṛgveda*" (*anṛcām*) means those who do not know the meaning of the *Ṛgveda*. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), because for those who are truly ignorant of the *Ṛgveda*, there is no possibility [of being invited] at all, due to the restrictive rule that [the guest] must be a *śrotriya*. The suffix forming the compound is not applied because of the archaic nature of the text (*chāndasatva*) and to conform to the meter (*vṛttānurodha*). For they recite it thus.

"One may even turn a *māṣa* into a *maṣa*, but one must not disturb the meter. Alternatively, "anṛcāḥ" is the nominative plural. The connection is: "Just as a thousand non-Vedic ones (*anṛcāḥ*) eat," as in the expression "a thousand cows. One who knows the mantras, one who knows the meaning of the Veda—being pleased, satiated, and fed—deserves all those non-Vedic ones; he takes them unto himself, he assimilates them, and attains non-difference from them. And when there is this non-difference, the understanding arises that whatever fruit is obtained when those thousands have been fed is obtained in the single [mantra-knower].

This censure of the ignorant is intended for the sake of enjoining the learned; it does not, however, state that those numbered in the thousands and the one [the learned] possess equal results. Since the learned are being enjoined, there is no possibility at all of the ignorant being included. Even if, in the absence of a learned person, one might suspect the possibility of the ignorant being included by the phrase "to a *śrotriya* alone," nevertheless, so that there might be no prohibition against the extensive [distribution], the literal meaning of the text remains possible. (3.121)
Offerings for the ancestors (*kavya*) and offerings to the gods (*haviṣ*) should be given to one who is preeminent in knowledge.

For hands smeared with blood are not cleansed by blood alone. (3.122) One who is "preeminent" (*utkṛṣṭa*)—meaning superior or distinguished—by virtue of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) or sacred learning (*vidyā*): to him the *kavyas* should be given. This is the meaning of the simile regarding hands smeared with blood. Hands smeared with blood, when wiped with blood, become even more stained; they do not become clean. In the same way, an ignorant Brāhmaṇa, when fed, leads the ancestors even further downward. (3.122)

As many mouthfuls as one who is ignorant of the mantras consumes at offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya), for that many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls does the deceased (preta) consume.
[Note: Although this occurs within the section on *śrāddha* rites, this is a restatement of the fault pertaining to the eater, based on the statement of the text. And so it has been said:
"Therefore, an ignorant man should fear from whatever gift he accepts" (MDh 4.191).

*Śūla* and *ṛṣṭi* are specific types of weapons; *ayoguḍa* is an iron ball. For the sake of which the *śrāddha* was commenced, that person is made to eat those glowing, heated iron balls by the messengers of Yama.

However, according to Vyāsa’s view, this fault belongs to the one who feeds [the guest], not to the eater; nor does it belong to the ancestors. For it is not logical that those who have died should incur a connection with guilt due to another's transgression of a prohibition, as that would entail the fallacy of "the acquisition of what was not done" (*kṛtābhyāgama*) and other such faults. If indeed such a Brahmin has been fed by the son, what offense is there on the part of the deceased?

But surely, by this same logic, the benefit rendered to the ancestors by their son would not be attained? It would not be attained if the *śrāddha* and other rites were not enjoined for that purpose. However, in this case there is no such injunction stating, "One desiring to benefit the father should act in this manner," as is the case with the *śyena* sacrifice. As for the statement, "The deceased consumes as much as that," it is applicable even when the connection is with the one who feeds [the Brahmins]. The proper connection is: "He whose Brahmin eats such a *śrāddha* obtains this fruit. Furthermore, this prohibition against feeding the ignorant is contextual (*prākaraṇika*). If it is transgressed, there is a deficiency in the rite; and if there is a deficiency in the rite, the fault is simply the cessation of the qualification for the *śrāddha*. The ancestors obtain benefit from the assistance of the *śrāddha*. Even so, if there is a transgression of the rule, it is logical that the son incurs demerit (*pratyavāya*). What then of that statement of the venerable Vyāsa?
Whatever morsels of sacrificial oblation one ignorant of the ritual consumes,
for that many spikes shall he swallow upon reaching the abode of Vaivasvata.

There is an alternative reading, "pretya. It is for the enjoyer alone that there is the state of having departed [from this life]. One who lacks knowledge should not partake in offerings made to the gods or the ancestors. (3.123)
Some twice-born ones are devoted to knowledge, and others likewise to austerity; some are devoted to austerity and self-study, and others likewise to ritual action. (3.124)

The classification of qualities is stated in order to praise knowledge (*vidyā*) above all other qualities, and this praise is intended to encourage giving to the learned. Those for whom there is "steadfastness" (*niṣṭhā*)—meaning excellence—in knowledge, that is, in learning, are called "steadfast in knowledge" (*jñānaniṣṭhāḥ*); they are those qualified for knowledge. Although the members of the compound belong to different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is permissible because the meaning is clear. Those who have intensely studied the meaning of the Vedas and are devoted to them are described in this way. This should be understood to apply to all terms ending in *niṣṭhā*. *Tapaḥ-svādhyāya-niṣṭhāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*: "austerity" (*tapaḥ*) refers to practices such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*, and "Vedic study" (*svādhyāyaḥ*) refers to the recitation of the Vedas. "Ritual acts" (*karmāṇi*) refer to the *agnihotra* and other such rites. It should be understood that all these qualities are to be combined in all [categories of recipients]. For the presence of only one quality does not make someone a worthy recipient if they lack the others; rather, the excellence of a particular quality in a certain person is being expressed. Just as the word *niṣṭhā*, while denoting completion, indicates excellence (*prakarṣa*), so too one who is "steadfast" in that is said to be "devoted" to it. Even when all qualities are present, if there is excellence in only one and the other qualities are mediocre, one is still indeed a worthy recipient. However, if even one quality lacks excellence, they do not attain the status of a worthy recipient, even if all other qualities are present.
And the compendium is also explained, by which it was stated in the second [chapter] that there is the actual performance of ritual action for one who is devoid of knowledge.

Others, however, explain that the one established in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭha*) is the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). For him, the practice of self-knowledge is specifically ordained through the renunciation of ritual action (*karmanyāsa*). The one established in austerity (*taponiṣṭha*) is the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); for he is called an ascetic (*tāpasa*), as it is said: "In the summer, he should perform the 'five-fire' penance" (MDh 6.23). Those established in austerity and Vedic study (*tapas-svādhyāya*) are the religious students (*brahmacārins*). Those established in ritual action (*karmaniṣṭha*) are the householders (*gṛhasthas*). Consequently, those who do not belong to any of the stages of life (*anāśramin*) are excluded. Thus, the authors of the Purāṇas state: "One should never offer a *śrāddha* to those who stand outside the four stages of life. (3.124)
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be established with effort among those devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) should be given according to the rule to all four [classes] alike.

He states the purpose for the classification of qualities: *kavya* is that which is given in honor of the ancestors; the meaning is that these [offerings] are to be established in, or bestowed upon, those devoted to knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭha*). Because of the mention of "effort," in their absence, [the gift] goes to the [next four], just as with *havya*. In rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), those devoted to knowledge are the most worthy recipients. For it has been said: "Of all worthy recipients, he is the most worthy recipient" (VaDh 6.26). The meaning of the verse is that the gift of food is to be given without distinction to all four. *Nyāya* refers to the scriptural injunction. 3.125.

He whose father is unlearned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) but his son has mastered the Vedas; or he whose son is unlearned in the Vedas but his father has mastered the Vedas. (3.126) This verse is intended to introduce a doubt. (3.126) V3.136
One should know the elder of these two to be the one whose father is a learned scholar of the Vedas (*śrotriya*);

however, the other deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras. (3.127) Having raised the doubt as to which of the two is superior—between one whose father is unlearned but who himself has mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-vedādhyāyī*), and another whose father has mastered the Vedas but who himself is ignorant—the author states the established conclusion.

Between these two—the one whose father is a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) while he himself is ignorant, and the one who is himself ignorant but whose father is a learned Vedic scholar—one should know that the latter, whose father is a *śrotriya*, is superior, praiseworthy, and fit for the *śrāddha* rite, provided his father is indeed a *śrotriya*. The other is not [fit] by virtue of being considered a Brahmin for the purpose of honoring the mantras; rather, it is the mantras studied by him that are honored therein. Since the honoring of mantras is not prescribed in the *śrāddha*, therefore he should not be fed.

By means of two verses, through the presentation of a doubt and its resolution in the form of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), it is stated that both the father’s status as a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) and one’s own status as a learned Vedic scholar are grounds for being invited to a *śrāddha* feast, and not one’s own status alone. However, this does not prescribe that one who is himself unlearned may be fed on the basis of his father’s status as a *śrotriya*. As it has been said: "One should examine [the guest] from afar" (MDh 3.120). Here, the examination of Vedic study is restricted by this rule to the scope of two persons. But the examination of caste and qualities pertains to more than those two persons. Therefore, because these [two verses] serve to specify that very [examination], there is no tautology. (3.127)
One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
One should feed at a śrāddha that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend. (3.128)

This prohibition applies even when there is a full possession of prior qualities such as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), on account of [pre-existing] friendship and the like. One should not feed at a *śrāddha* a friend—one whose joys and sorrows are shared and who is indistinguishable from oneself. "Making a friend" (*maitrīkaraṇa*) means winning over this friend by means of wealth; or rather, "friendship" (*maitrya*) is continuity, which is to say, assistance. Not only should one not feed a friend, but even an enemy (*ari*, a foe). "Neither an enemy nor a friend"—one whom one knows to be neither. This refers to one in whom there is neither passion nor hatred, nor any other relationship, where one might suspect that affection is motivated by some ulterior purpose; for the mention of "enemy and friend" is intended to be illustrative. Likewise, it is precisely because of the suspicion of such a relationship that the maternal grandfather and others are mentioned in the section on secondary options (*anukalpa*).

If there is the possibility of performing acts of giving for the sake of cultivating friendliness even toward an enemy, then "cultivating friendliness" constitutes the means of integration; thus, one need not separately mention the "integration of enemies.
This will be for the sake of clarity. (3.128)

"For one whose *śrāddha* rites and sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) have friendship as their primary motive, there is no fruit after death from those *śrāddhas* or those offerings. (3.129) This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding prohibition. This word "friend" (*mitra*) emphasizes the state [of being]; "having friendship as their primary motive" means having benevolence (*maitrī*) as their primary motive. Therefore, it refers to the case where both parties are friends. By "sacrificial offerings" (*havīṃṣi*), one understands either a gift given with reference to a deity for the sake of transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), or simply the feeding of Brahmins. There is no fruit after death [for such acts].

But surely, because there is no common agent [for the two verbs], the effect cannot arise? For the agent of the prefix *pra-* is the person who performs the *śrāddha*, whereas the fruit belongs to "existence" (*astitā*) as qualified by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Some say that the word *pretya* is a different term signifying the next world and is designated as a particle (*nipāta*).

Now, if the agent of the prefix *pra-* is also the recipient of the fruit, then its fruit—having come very near after departing (*pretya*)—does not exist; it does not become something to be enjoyed. (3.129)
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships with those devoted to ancestral rites, falls from the heavenly world—being a friend to such śrāddhas. (3.130)

He who, out of delusion and ignorant of the meaning of the scriptures, forms friendships with those devoted to *śrāddha* rites, falls from heaven; the meaning is that he does not attain heaven. He is said to "fall" because of a lack of connection (*asaṃbandha-sāmānya*). Just as one who has reached heaven and then fallen from it is no longer connected with heaven, so too is this man. By this, it is stated that he simply fails to obtain the fruit of the *śrāddha*. For such is the case when [the rule] applies to all remaining instances. A "friend of *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhamitra*) is one for whom *śrāddha* is the friend; since *śrāddha* itself is the cause of obtaining a friend, it is called "friend," and thus the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed. He is the lowest among the twice-born. The mention of the "twice-born" is for the sake of illustration; even a *śūdra* should not entertain friends at a *śrāddha* meal.

But surely, because he is not a Brāhmaṇa, a Śūdra cannot attain the status of a friend [to a Brāhmaṇa]. Who has made this rule: that a Śūdra must not have Brāhmaṇas as friends? If you argue that the practice of friendship exists only among those of the same caste, and not between those of higher castes and those of lower castes— [The response follows: This is not so. For it is observed in the world that even when there is a difference in caste, friendship arises from mutual affection. And since the Śūdra is included within the category of "human beings" (*manuṣya*), he is indeed entitled to friendship with those of other castes. Furthermore, there is no prohibition against a Śūdra having Brāhmaṇas as friends. Therefore, the Śūdra may indeed be a friend to the Brāhmaṇas. This also is not so; for thus it is said: "Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi, [said], 'I have a Kṣatriya friend among the Pañcālas. Furthermore, the prohibition regarding a friend has been explained as being for the purpose of indicating a general relationship. And there are Brāhmaṇas who are related to a Śūdra through financial interests, as well as even the kinsmen of a Pāraśava. (3.130)
That which is called a communal feast is declared by the twice-born to be a Piśāca-like sacrificial gift;
it remains in this very world like a blind cow in a single house.

The prefix *sam-* signifies "together. That by which one eats together is called *saṃbhojanī*. For it is through friendship that communal eating (*sahabhojana*) proceeds; or rather, *saṃbhojana* is understood as a feast held in a social gathering (*goṣṭhī*). This is the custom of the *piśācas*: that at a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), friends are gathered. These men of the streets are like *piśācas*; such a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) remains only in this world and is not capable of yielding fruit in the next. Just as a cow remains in a single house where she is blind, so too does this gift remain only here; it serves only the purpose of the circle of friends. It is not effective for the benefit of the ancestors. Giving is the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*). (3.131)

Just as one who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain a fruit, so too the giver does not obtain a fruit after having offered an oblation to one who is devoid of the *ṛc* verses. (3.132) *Irīṇa* means saline or barren soil. That field in which seed, when sown, does not sprout due to a defect in the earth is called *irīṇa*. In such a place, the sower—the farmer—does not obtain a fruit. Likewise, having offered an oblation—whether for the gods or the ancestors—to one who is "devoid of the *ṛc*" (*anṛca*), that is, one who lacks the study of the Vedas, the giver does not obtain a fruit. The term *anṛce* ends in the locative case; the word *ṛc* is used here as an indicator for the Vedas in general. (3.132)

By giving a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to the rule to one who is learned, one makes both the givers and the recipients partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death (3.133). It is logical that the sacrificial fee given to a learned person makes the givers partakers of the fruit; however, what fruit do the recipients enjoy? If it were an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) result, that would be incorrect, because the act of receiving has not been enjoined [as a duty] and because people engage in it for the sake of obtaining a visible reward. If, on the other hand, it is a visible result, then that is seen even for one who is unlearned.

True; this is a praise. Such is the gift to a learned man that even the recipient becomes a partaker of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaphala*). How much more so, then, the giver, even with respect to visible results? "In the next world, heaven; in this world, fame": people offer words of praise, saying, "He practices according to the scriptures. The phrase "in accordance with the rule" is a restatement [of what was said previously], as in the verse: "And he who gives thus in matters of dharma... (3.133).
One may, if one wishes, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*, even if he is not highly qualified, rather than someone else;
for an oblation consumed by an enemy becomes fruitless after death. (3.134) One should, with great effort, feed at a *śrāddha* a reciter of the Ṛgveda who has mastered the Veda. (V.3.144)
Then [he should approach] the Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his branch, and the Chandoga who has completed [his recitation]. || 3.135 || V3.145

Words such as *vedapāraga*, *śākhāntaga*, and *samāptika* denote those who have studied an entire branch (*śākhā*) together with its *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions; they do not refer to one who has studied only the *mantra-saṃhitā*, nor the *brāhmaṇa*, nor even a single portion thereof. Furthermore, those who study only a single branch of the Veda are also called *śrotriyas*. Therefore, in order to exclude them, it is stated that "it should be given to a *śrotriya*. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda, and the word "Veda" denotes a branch consisting of both *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa*. This [definition] is intended so that one who studies only a portion of it might not be included among those who have studied the entire branch.

But has it not been stated that those belonging to the stages of life (*āśramin*) are to be fed? In that case, for those who have not studied their entire *svādhyāya*, the possibility of entering the stage of the householder (*gārhasthya*) and so forth does not exist at all. For it has been said: "The entire Veda is to be mastered" (MDh 2.165).

In that case, could it apply even to a student (*brahmacārin*) who has begun the study of the Veda but has not yet completed it? For the words "one who has reached the end of the Veda," "one who has gone through the various branches (*śākhāntaga*)," and "one who has completed [the study]" are synonymous, and all of them express the sense of totality (*kārtsnya*).

Since the purpose is accomplished by a single word alone, the utterance of multiple words with various forms but a single meaning is for the sake of following the meter. "He goes to the further shore of the Vedas" (*vedānāṃ pāraṃ gacchati*). "One who has reached the end" (*samāptikaḥ*) means one for whom there is a completion at the end of a branch (*śākhā*). An *adhvaryu* is a student of a branch of the Yajurveda; this word *adhvaryu* does not denote a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). What is called the *pravacana* (traditional recension) of the Adhvaryus is the [text]; because of his connection to the study of that, a person is called an *adhvaryu*. A *chandoga* is a student of the Sāmaveda. In another Smṛti, it is stated that a *trisāhasravidya* is one who has reached the end (*samāptika*). Therein, the word *sahasra* refers to the Sāmaveda because of its connection to a thousand songs (*gīti*); he whose three branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) consist of these three thousand [verses] is a *trisāhasravidya*. These three branches of the Sāmaveda—which has a thousand paths (*sahasravartman*)—are the *Tāṇḍava*, the *Aukthikya*, and the *Sāmagāna*. The *Daśatayī*, the *Catuḥṣaṣṭi*, and the Brāhmaṇa constitute the *Bāhvṛcya* (the Rigveda).
Others, however, consider this verse to be for the purpose of excluding the followers of the Atharvaveda. If the intention were to speak of [the Vedas] in their entirety, he would have said simply:
"One should feed that twice-born man who has studied an entire branch of the Veda.

Now, one might object that this is equally true even regarding the exclusion of the Atharvavedins; for in that case as well, it would have been possible to say that, had there been an intention to exclude them, he would likely have stated it exactly thus: "An Atharvavedin is not to be fed," since expressing the prohibition by its own specific term would be more concise.

This is not so. Is the negation of one thing understood through the prescription of another, or is there a negation by its own specific word? Manu’s composition of the instruction on dharma is manifold. (3.135)
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at his *śrāddha*, the satisfaction of his ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations.

(3.136) Someone might think: "It has been stated [in verse 3.115] that 'three [should be fed] for the ancestral rite,' and in the preceding verse, those who study various *śākhās* were mentioned. In that case, there is no possibility for fellow students (*sabrahmacārin*) to be included. To remove this doubt, this [verse] is provided.

Any one of these three types of those learned in the three Vedas (*traividyas*) is worthy of being fed. This is what is meant: those who study the same Vedic branch (*śākhā*) or those who study different branches are worthy of being fed. "Honored" means worshipped and requested with offerings of water for the feet (*argha*) and so forth. "Satisfaction extending to seven generations": it pervades seven persons. Because the *anuśatikādi* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), there is vowel lengthening in both parts of the compound. This is intended to indicate the greatness of time; the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes long-lasting. As long as seven future generations—sons, grandsons, and so on—have been born or will be born, the ancestors remain satisfied by such a gift to Brāhmaṇas. "Eternal" means that it does not cease in the interim and arise again; rather, it remains established forever. (3.136)
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;

however, this following alternative should be understood as that which is always practiced by the virtuous. (3.137) Starting from the verse "The sacrifice to the ancestors" (3.112), twenty-five verses have been passed; therein this much has been stated: the *śrāddha* must be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). A learned man who has studied the Vedas, whose conduct is virtuous, who is of noble lineage, and who is the son of a Vedic scholar—provided he is not a relative—should be fed. All that remains is for the purpose of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

This first method just described is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*), namely that which is given at a *śrāddha* to one who is not a relative. However, this one which is about to be described should be known as the secondary rule (*anukalpa*). That which is performed in the absence of the primary rule, according to the logic of a substitute (*pratinidhi*), is called a secondary rule. The words "always" (*sadā*) and so forth are for the purpose of praise. (3.137)

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the son-in-law, a kinsman, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices. (3.138) The term *svasrīya* means the son of one's sister. The term *viṭpati* means the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*), because the word *viṭ* signifies progeny. Others say it refers to the guest; for he is the lord of all people (*viś*), and even in common worldly usage, one who has arrived at the house is called by the word *viṭ*. The term *bandhu* refers to a relative by marriage (*śāla*) or one of the same lineage (*sagotra*), and so forth. (3.138)
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa for a rite dedicated to the gods;
but when a rite dedicated to the ancestors is at hand, he should examine him with great care. (3.139)

This is not a prohibition against examining Brāhmaṇas for rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*); rather, its purpose is to permit those who are one-eyed, afflicted with elephantiasis, and so forth, to be invited occasionally at such rites. When the time for the ancestral rite (*pitrya*)—the *śrāddha*—has arrived, one should examine [the guests] with great care, but not so for the rites to the gods. One may, on occasion, feed even those who will be mentioned later. We shall point out those who are permitted [to be invited]. Others, however, maintain that this verse is merely an introductory statement intended to ensure the diligent avoidance of those to be prohibited in the upcoming section; it does not serve to permit the one-eyed and others for rites to the gods. (3.139)
Those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or those who follow the lifestyle of nihilists—Manu has declared that such Brahmins are unworthy of offerings to the gods and the ancestors. 3.140 (V3.150)

A thief is a robber. An outcast (*patita*) is one who has committed any one of the five great sins (*mahāpātaka*). A eunuch (*klība*) is a neuter, one possessing both sexual organs, one whose semen is wind, or a *ṣaṇḍha*. Atheists (*nāstika*) are the Lokāyatikas and others; those whose settled conviction is that "there is no gift, there is no oblation, there is no other world," their conduct or behavior is characterized by lack of faith. This is "the conduct of atheists" (*nāstikavṛtti*). [This is a compound with the loss of the middle term. Since the meaning "atheists" alone would suffice, the inclusion of the word "conduct" is for the purpose of completing the meter. Alternatively, they are so called because their livelihood or means of subsistence (*vṛtti*) depends upon atheists. Manu has declared them unworthy of offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). The mention of Manu is for the sake of showing respect for the prohibition, since all duties have been proclaimed by Manu. (3.140)

One should not feed at a *śrāddha* those who officiate as priests for a *jaṭila* who does not study, nor for one with matted hair (*durvāla*), nor for a gambler, nor for those who perform sacrifices for groups [of people].

(3.141) A *jaṭila* is a religious student (*brahmacārin*), for this particular style of hair is prescribed for him optionally by the rule: "He should either be shaven-headed or have matted hair" (MDh 2.219). Furthermore, the matted hair is merely an indicative mark of the student; therefore, even the shaven-headed student is prohibited. And the prohibition applies specifically to that student who does not study.

But surely, according to the rule "gifts are to be given only to a *śrotriya*" (MDh 3.118), there is no possibility at all for one who has not studied; for if one who has begun his studies but has neither mastered nor grasped the Veda were to qualify, [how could that be?
Indeed, because of the statement "one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas" (MDh 3.135), how can there be any possibility for one who has merely begun his studies?

In that case, even one who has studied the Veda but has not mastered it is intended here as a non-student. Or, someone might think that by the rule, "Even a daughter's son who is observing his vows" (MDh 3.224), the status of being a daughter's son (*dauhitrata*) alone is what is required here and not the act of studying; for that reason, this [present rule] is stated. Since there is a prohibition against one who does not study, it is understood that a learned person (*vidvas*) has the entitlement [to perform the rite].

One who has coarse hair, whose hair is reddish-brown, or whose sense organs are impaired. Regarding him, they provide this etymological explanation: "Even with *dūrvā* grass or green turf, his dwelling is sufficient. For he is indeed covered by *dūrvā* grass alone; and out of shame, in the absence of clothes, he covers his private parts with that much alone. A gambler is one who plays at dice. And those who officiate for groups or assemblies—for it is prescribed that a sacrifice is to be performed for Vrātyas who have gathered together by means of the *Vrātyastoma* and other rites—and yet officiating for them is forbidden, as in: "Having performed a sacrifice for Vrātyas... (MDh 11.196). We say: even one who officiates for many individuals one after another, or performs the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) many times, is not one whose food may be eaten. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "And he who is a sacrificer for many, and he who initiates many [into the sacred thread]" (VaDh 14.17).
Some say: "Because of the mention of *śrāddha*, this prohibition applies only to the ancestral rites (*pitrya*) and not to the divine rites (*daiva*).
That is incorrect; for even that [ancestral rite] is indeed a constituent part of the *śrāddha*, and it is therefore proper to speak of it using the word *śrāddha*. (3.141)
Physicians, temple-priests (devalakas), meat-sellers, and those who live by trade—these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors. 3.142 (V3.152)

Physicians are those who practice medicine; temple-attendants (*devalaka*) are those who serve idols. These two are prohibited because of their connection to making a livelihood; however, there is no fault in being a physician or a temple-attendant when it is for the sake of dharma. Meat-sellers are butchers. In the reading with the accusative case-ending, the verb from the preceding verse is to be supplied. Those who live by trade—that is, by forbidden trade—are prohibited. The forbidden trades will be described in the tenth chapter; therefore, those who live by them are to be avoided in both cases. But meat-sellers are prohibited even when acting for the sake of dharma. For instance, if someone has brought meat and another person has need of it, while the one who brought the meat needs clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for use in a fire-oblation (*homa*), and he exchanges the meat for that butter—this constitutes an exchange for the sake of dharma. Since the term "selling" (*vikraya*) applies to such an exchange as well, even those who sell meat for the sake of dharma are prohibited. (3.142)
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; 3.143. V3.153.

A *preṣya* is a servant who carries out orders; one who is sent by a village for some task anywhere is likewise called a *rājapreṣya*. A *kunakhī* is one with deformed nails; a *śyāvadantaka* is one with black teeth. A *pratiroddhā* is one who opposes his teacher in verbal discourse and otherwise acts as an obstacle or behaves with hostility toward him. One who has abandoned the sacred fires is one who has given up either the *tretā* or the *āvasathya* fire. A *vārdhuṣi* is one who lives on interest when other means of livelihood exist; however, it is said that lending grain at interest is specifically termed usury (*vārdhuṣitva*).

Thus, that which is a traditional recollection (smaraṇa) applies only to its own specific context. For grammarians are those who live by interest and remember the word *vārdhuṣika* even for things other than grain; and they are more authoritative regarding the recollection of word-meanings due to their specialized application (*abhiyoga*). 3.143.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who has been expelled from his caste, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a communal group (of heretics).

3.144 V3.154: "Afflicted with consumption" means diseased; others say it refers to one seized by *rājayakṣman* (tuberculosis). "Cattle-herder" means one who holds a staff in his hand and lives by that occupation.

A *nirākṛti* is one who, despite possessing the entitlement [to perform rites], is devoid of the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*). Even in the present day, one who is not to be depended upon is called a *nirākṛti*; for thus it is stated in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: "He who does not worship the gods, nor the ancestors, nor men" (ŚB 6.3.1.24). As for those who recite: "One who is destitute of Vedic study, sacred learning, and wealth is designated as a *nirākṛti*," they do not understand the relationship between words and their meanings. For such a person, there is simply no eligibility here [for eating at a Śrāddha], due to the restriction concerning those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). There is a conformity with the root-meaning in the sense that a *nirākṛti* is "one who rejects" the gods and so forth; and when the identity of the attribute and the possessor of the attribute is intended, the use of the suffix *-ktin* is also justified. This root preceded by the prefix *ni-* functions in the sense of "rejecting" (*apavarjana*). Those who are rejected are called *nirākṛta*, as in "rejected from a meal" or "rejected from an entitlement. Furthermore, *ākṛti* means "exclusion"; since it has departed from him, he is a *nirākṛti*. Alternatively, *ākṛti* means "form" (*saṃsthāna*); thus, in the sense of contempt, the prefix *nis-* should be seen as applying to "one of bad form," who is thereby prohibited. And it says: "One endowed with speech, appearance, age, and character" (GDh 15.9). "Endowed with speech" means eloquent and having a sharp faculty of speech; one who is double-tongued is not to be fed. "Endowed with appearance" means having a pleasing arrangement of limbs. "Endowed with age": "Giving first to the young, according to some, then to those of middle age" (GDh 15.10–11). Or rather, this is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) ending in the suffix *-ktic*.

A *brahmadviṭ* is one who hates Brāhmaṇas or the Veda, because the word *brahman* has both meanings—as seen in the statement, "One who knows the *brahman* is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa. A *gaṇa* is a group or assembly; those who live together by means of a single activity are denoted by the word *gaṇa*, and this includes the Brāhmaṇas belonging to the four branches of knowledge (*cāturvidya*). The *parivettṛ* and *parivitti* are of the nature that will be described later. (3.144)

An actor, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, a son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour [of his wife]. (3.145) *Kuśīlava*s are actors, dancers, performers, singers, and the like. An *avakīrṇin* is one whose student-vow (*brahmacarya*) has been violated. A *vṛṣalī* is a *śūdrā*; some authorities maintain that this term applies only when there is no other [wife], while others hold it refers specifically to one who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* alone, meaning he has no wife belonging to the twice-born classes.

Whence is this [known]? In another context, there is heard a summary of censurable conduct: "these censurable practices" (MDh 3.157). Furthermore, marriage with a Śūdra woman is not censurable, since it is permitted for all; moreover, that [marriage] is permitted for one who has already performed a marriage with a woman of his own caste. Therefore, it is here that a man who possesses no woman of his own caste is prohibited from taking a Vṛṣalī as a wife.

"One who has been remarried" (*paunarbhava*) refers to a woman who has married again (*punarbhū*), one who has been wedded a second time; as he will state in the ninth chapter: "Or one abandoned by her husband" (MDh 9.175). "One-eyed" (*kāṇa*) means one who is defective in one eye. And [he is so called] when there is a paramour (*upapati*)—the wife's lover—while his wife remains present. He is censured for such negligence; as it is said: "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the eater of the food, and the unfaithful wife transfers hers to the husband" (MDh 8.317). 3.145.
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught for a fee, one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one who is a teacher of a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka. (3.146)

A *bhṛtakādhyāpaka* is one who stands as a teacher while being a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*). Regarding the term *bhṛtaka*: he who proceeds by means of a contract, saying, "If you give me so much, I shall teach you the Veda," is a *bhṛtakādhyāpaka*. For this is the well-known form of hire among porters and the like. However, one who does not determine beforehand by a verbal agreement, "With such an amount of wealth I shall teach this much," but first teaches and subsequently receives payment for the purpose of teaching, is not a *bhṛtakādhyāpaka*. Teaching performed when the giving of wealth has not been previously determined as to its measure is what is prescribed [as permissible].

Thus is one described as "taught for hire. This refers to one who, possessing a developed intellect, studies by himself after paying a fee, like Satyakāma. However, there is no reprehensibility of conduct for one who is taught by his father or others after they have paid the fee due to the absence of another teacher; for a child must indeed be turned away from prohibited things by his father. This has been stated: "The pupil and the sacrificer [must act] toward the teacher" (MDh 8.317).

A Śūdra may be a pupil in the sciences such as grammar, and a Śūdra alone may be his teacher. Even though [the word "Śūdra"] is a subordinate member of a compound, its connection [to the preceding term] is established because this is a Smṛti treatise, and because the status of having a reprehensible practice applies to all [the categories mentioned]. Furthermore, having a Śūdra as a teacher is reprehensible, but not the others. One who is corrupt in speech is one who speaks harshly or untruthfully; others say it means one who has been formally accused (abhiśasta). The Kuṇḍa and Golaka will be described later. (3.146)
One who abandons his mother, father, or teacher without cause;

and one who enters into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections. (3.147) [V.3.157] He who, when there is no valid reason, abandons his mother, father, or teacher—the term *guru* being a general term that applies to the *upādhyāya* as well.

As for the argument that, such being the case, the mention of "mother and father" would be unnecessary since [the status of] a teacher is established by virtue of [their] very greatness, and therefore they explain that "the teacher alone is the *guru* here"—that is incorrect. For if the mention of "mother and father" were absent, the word *guru* would apply only to the father according to the maxim of the artificial and the natural (*kṛtrimākṛtrimanyāya*). But when they are mentioned separately, it is established—as in other treatises—that "the teacher is the best among *gurus*," whereby the word retains its general sense.

And the grounds for abandonment are stated in such passages as: "One should abandon a father who is a regicide" (GDh 20.1). Abandonment of mother and father consists in the failure to perform service, such as attending to their feet, and a lack of devotion toward their propitiation. The same applies to the teacher (*guru*). Likewise, if the teacher is capable of teaching but fails to do so, one may study elsewhere by abandoning him.

"Having entered into association with outcasts" means having established a connection through *brāhma* relations—namely officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), or receiving gifts (*pratigraha*)—or through *yauṇa* relations, such as giving a daughter in marriage and so forth.
But surely, he [the outcast] is already to be avoided simply because of his status as an outcast?

Some say: "By associating with one who has fallen [from his caste] for a year, one falls" (MDh 11.179). This prohibition does not apply to a period shorter than that. Now, what is the meaning of the expression "having entered into a connection"? Here, the word *saṃbandha* (connection) does not denote a physical conjunction such as *saṃyoga* (conjunction) as it is understood by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; rather, it is the very act itself that is called "connection" because it is the cause of the relationship. Furthermore, in the context of officiating at sacrifices and so forth, the word *saṃyoga* indicates the mere fact of a relationship. (3.147)
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats food from a sacrificial vessel, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; 3.148. V3.158.

One who burns a house or a dwelling; one who gives *gara* (poison)—the mention of *gara* being for the sake of illustration and including other poisons such as *viṣa*; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* (the son of an adulteress); likewise, the son of a *golaka* (the son of an unmarried woman), since the mention of the *kuṇḍa* is illustrative; one who sells *soma*—*soma* here meaning the medicinal herb, which he sells either for the purpose of sacrifice or for medicine; others, however, say it refers to the sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* which have *soma* as their means. Although the sale of these [sacrifices] is impossible because an action is formless, nevertheless this prohibition exists because such conduct is observed among the ignorant, who say: "Whatever merit has been performed by me, let that be yours. "Merit" (*sukṛta*) refers to *dharma* accomplished through good deeds. And thus: "Between the night you were born and the night you shall die, whatever *iṣṭāpūrta*, world, merit, life, or offspring belongs to you, I shall seize it if you would deceive me. Just as with oaths, so too one who performs giving or selling by word of mouth is to be avoided. From this very fact, the impropriety of such acts as oaths, gifts, and sales when performed merely by speech is inferred. One who goes to the ocean; a *bandin*, a reciter of praises; a *tailika*, a crusher of sesame seeds and other grains; a *kūṭakāraka*, one who speaks falsely in witness-depositions. (3.148)
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard, one afflicted with a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (V.3.149).

He who quarrels with his father speaks harshly to him, litigating in the royal court by means of the sequence of plaintiff and defendant for the sake of a share of the inheritance and so forth. And thus says Gautama: "Those who have separated from their father against his will" (GDh 15.19).

Regarding the phrase "one who opposes the teacher," how is this not a redundancy? It is said that opposition (*pratirodha*) is one thing, while dispute (*vivāda*) is another. When there is some matter intended by the teacher, such as "How might this be accomplished?", explaining the connection to that is opposition. Opposition, moreover, is the obstruction of the teacher's will even regarding a matter that is reasonable. There is an alternative reading, *pratirāddhā*. In that case, one who has physically harmed the teacher with hands and so forth by giving a slap and the like is an opponent. In this interpretation, the distinction from dispute remains established.

A *kitava* is one who causes gambling to take place, namely the master of the gaming house (*sabhika*). He who is himself a participant has already been excluded previously. Others read "one with squinting eyes" (*kekara*), meaning a drunkard; he is one whose gaze is turned aside, looking with a half-closed eye. Others read "timid" (*kātarah*); he is one whose pupils are like those of a parrot. A drunkard (*madyapa*) is one who drinks liquor other than *surā*, such as *ariṣṭa* and the like; a drinker of *surā* (*surāpa*) is excluded by the very fact of his being fallen from caste.

A "pāparogī" is one afflicted with leprosy (*kuṣṭhī*). For he is extremely despised in the world, and it is appropriate to designate him as such. Precisely because of this prohibition, in the term *yakṣmī*, not every person seized by disease is included; who then? One suffering from consumption (*kṣayī*). For if everyone were included, since the purpose would already be accomplished by that [term alone], the author would not have mentioned "pāparogī.
An *abhiśasta* is one renowned in the world as a perpetrator of either a mortal sin (*pātaka*) or a minor offense (*upapātaka*), even in the absence of certainty regarding his having committed them.
The hypocrite practices dharma through deception for the sake of gaining popularity in the world; he performs his actions not out of a sense of duty, but because he thinks, "it must be done.

The seller of *rasa* is a dealer in poison; for this is its designation: "the secret sower of discord is a *rasada*," and "the *rasada* is a spy" (*sattrin*), and so forth; one who gives poison is called a *rasada*. (3.149)

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, one who betrays a friend, one who subsists by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; 3.150, 3.160.

He who, like an artisan, makes bows and arrows; and he who is the husband of an *agredidhiṣū*. The word *didhiṣū* is connected with both [terms], like the eye of a crow (*kākākṣivat*). Since this is a legal treatise (*smṛti-śāstra*), such a connection is permissible; for even signs such as lines on the ground or clods of earth are conventionally established for the purpose of legal tradition and serve to convey meaning. Therefore, one should not ask: "How can a single word contained within a compound be connected with two distinct referents? For Gautama has prohibited both [types of persons] (GDh 15.16). Here too, there is an indication for this distinction in the relationship: it is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. Indeed, there is no such person as a "husband of an *agredidhiṣū*"; rather, these two are defined by the characteristics that will be stated below.

A betrayer of friends (*mitradhruk*): one who acts treacherously toward a friend; one who persists in obstructing the interests of a friend. [289] One whose livelihood is gambling (*dyūtavṛtti*): one for whom gambling is the means of subsistence.
But has this not already been stated here: "A gambler is a drinker of intoxicants"? [290]

It is not necessarily the case that only one whose livelihood is gambling (*dyūtavṛtti*) is the one who causes gambling; rather, it refers to one who does not know how to gamble himself or does not gamble out of fear of his elders. But a man addicted to vice, being cursed by the gods, causes another to gamble. For this purpose, there is a second sense of the word *kitava*. Alternatively, those who stand as pillars in the gambling hall, speaking untruths, are "those whose livelihood is gambling. [The compound *putrācārya* means] one for whom the son is the teacher (*ācārya*) or the instructor (*adhyāpaka*). Primary teacherhood is not possible in a son. (3.150)

One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas—these are to be avoided. 3.151 (V3.161)

These [terms] refer to specific types of diseases: *bhrāmarī* is epilepsy; *gaṇḍamālī* is one on whose cheeks or throat eruptions arise in the form of a garland; *śvitrī* is one afflicted with white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*); *piśuna* is a backbiter who reveals the secrets of others and whispers into the ear; *unmatta* is one whose mind is unstable due to a disturbance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), possessed by a *piśāca*, speaking or acting recklessly; *andha* is one deficient in sight; and *vedanindaka* is a reviler of the Vedas. [Objection: But surely the reviler of the Vedas is already included by the term "hater of Brahman" (*brahmadviṭ*), since the word "Brahman" has multiple meanings?
It is not so; blame is one thing and hatred is another. Hatred is a mental state (*cittadharma*), whereas blame is the disparagement of that [state] by means of the word "displeasure. (3.151)

One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); one who is a breeder of birds; and likewise one who is a teacher of combat (3.152). A trainer of elephants and so forth is a *damaka*, one who teaches their gait. "One who lives by means of the lunar mansions": by the word *nakṣatra*, the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is indicated; one who lives by that is an astrologer. A breeder of birds such as hawks for the purpose of hunting. An instructor of combat is a teacher of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*).
One who diverts watercourses, one who delights in obstructing them, a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees; 3.153 V3.163.

"Srotāṃsi" refers to water-channels; he is one who breaks them. Having broken a dam, he leads [the water] to another place for the purpose of irrigating rice and other crops. And he delights in the obstruction of those very channels; "obstruction" means covering over. He conceals that spot from which the water emerges. He is a teacher of the layout of houses, one who lives by the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), such as a master builder (*sthapati*) or a carpenter (*sūtradhāra*); however, he is not one who constructs his own houses. A messenger is a servant of a king, to be employed like a slave; yet a messenger is sent specifically for matters such as peace or war. He plants trees for a price. But there is no fault if it is for the sake of Dharma, because such conduct is irreproachable. The planting of trees is enjoined: "One who plants ten mango trees does not go to hell. (3.153)

One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, one who is cruel, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for groups (of people). 3.154 (V3.164)

A *śvakrīḍī* is one who plays with dogs; that is, one who keeps dogs for the purpose of playing. One who lives by means of hawks through buying, selling, and so forth, is a hawk-trainer. As previously mentioned [in verse 295], a *pakṣipoṣaka* is a keeper of birds, one who maintains them in cages and the like. A *kanyādūṣaka* is one who defiles a maiden—that is, one who makes her no longer a maiden (*akanyā*). A *hiṃsra* is one who is cruel by nature and delights in killing. One of *vṛṣalavṛtti* is one who lives by serving Śūdras and so forth. There is an alternative reading, *vṛṣalaputra*, meaning one whose sons are exclusively Śūdras. This refers to one of censurable conduct, as stated in Manu Smṛti 3.64: "and by those who have only Śūdra offspring. A *gaṇānāṃ yājaka* is a priest for groups; such sacrifices for groups (*gaṇayāga*) are well known. (3.154)

One who is devoid of proper conduct, one who is impotent, a constant beggar, one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous—[these are not to be invited]. (3.155) V3.165

*Ācāra* refers to worldly custom, consisting of the application of honor and other rites toward those who have arrived at one's home; he is devoid of that. A *klība* is one of little strength, whose enthusiasm is broken regarding what ought to be done. A *yācanaka* is one who always begs, and who causes distress to others by his begging. This is the very nature of things: that one being begged from is distressed by the begging. [The suffix] *yu* is applied after *nandi* and others [according to Pāṇini 3.1.134], and the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). One who lives by agriculture (*kṛṣijīvī*) lives by agriculture performed by himself, or even by that not performed by himself when other means exist. A *ślīpadī* is one whose one foot is large. One censured by the virtuous is *durbhaga*; he is hateful to the good even in the absence of any fault. (3.155)
A sheep-butcher, a buffalo-herder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and a carrier of the dead—these must be avoided with great effort. (3.156)

One who deals with goats and rams—meaning he trades with them through buying, selling, and so forth, or whose wealth primarily consists of them—or likewise one who keeps buffaloes; one who is the husband of a woman who had another before her—that is, the husband of a woman who was previously given to or married by another, whom he marries again, becoming her husband once more according to the scriptural rule that such a man is a *paunarbhava*; and one who carries out or conducts the funeral rites for the deceased: these should be avoided with great care. (3.156)
A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid both these lowest of the twice-born, whose conduct is censurable and who are unworthy of sitting in the row at a meal. (3.157)

Those whose conduct—that is, their performance of actions—is censured and condemned; such as those who are one-eyed and the like, by virtue of the signs of previous faults; and those such as thieves and the like, whose faults are directly perceived through perception and other means—one should avoid them in both rites for the gods and the ancestors. One should exclude them; they are "unfit for the row" (*apāṅkteya*), meaning they do not deserve a place in the row. The suffix *ḍhak* should be understood here in the sense of "belonging to. Their very unfitness is indicated by their exclusion from the row. They do not deserve to eat together with other Brāhmaṇas; for this very reason, they are called "defilers of the row. Others who sit together with them also become defiled. (3.157)
For a Brahmin who has not studied [the Vedas] is extinguished like a fire of grass;

one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes. (3.158) Just as these [others], such as thieves and so forth, are defilers of the row (*paṅktidūṣaka*), so too is one who has not studied [the Vedas], possessing an equal fault. It is for this purpose that there is a restatement.

Others, however, explain it thus: [the mention of] *havya* (oblations to the gods) is for the sake of occasional inclusion when those who study, such as the followers of Kaṇāda and others, do not possess reprehensible conduct in the present. A Brāhmaṇa who does not study is to be avoided; however, that which is to be offered to the gods (*havya*) or to the ancestors (*kavya*) is not given to one who studies—this is precisely the purpose of mentioning *havya* here. Regarding *havya*, only one who does not study is to be avoided, as well as those whose reprehensible conduct is visible. Therefore, those who are prohibited by specific scriptural statement in both cases are to be avoided at rites for the gods and the ancestors, while others are to be avoided only at rites for the ancestors. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"But if he is a knower of mantras and free from bodily defects that defile the company, Yama has declared him to be undefiled; indeed, he is a purifier of the company. (VaDh 11.20)

"It is extinguished like a grass-fire. Just as a grass-fire is unable to cook the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*), but is extinguished by the mere offering of the oblation and flares up again—being a fire in which what is offered does not turn to ash, and from which no fruit comes of that sacrifice—so it is heard in scripture: "One must not offer into a fire that is not well-kindled; Agni is indeed all the deities. In this way, a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied is equal to a grass-fire. This very point is stated: "For an offering is not made into ashes. Just as a grass-fire first turns to ash and nothing is offered therein, so such a Brāhmaṇa is not to be fed. 3.158.

I shall now declare in its entirety the fruit that arises for the giver after death from giving to those unworthy of the company at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors. He states the result of this rule of prohibition: "Those who deserve the company" are *paṅktyas*; those who do not deserve the company are *apaṅktyas*. The formation of the word is established by analogy with words such as *daṇḍya* (one deserving punishment). Whatever arising of fruit—that is, whatever production of fruit—occurs for the giver from giving to them, all of that I shall now speak; therefore, be attentive. (3.159)

Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not kept their vows, as well as by those such as a younger brother who marries before his elder, and by others excluded from the company at meals—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.160)

Those who are without vows, unrestrained, and devoid of scriptural conduct—such as those who marry before their elder brothers (*parivettṛ*) and others—though they are outside the pale of the scriptures, are mentioned separately either for the sake of specific enumeration or to indicate the gravity of their transgression. Others who are unworthy of the company at a meal (*apaṅkteya*), such as the one-eyed (*kāṇa*) or the club-footed (*ślīpadin*), are also included. Whatever food has been eaten by them at a *śrāddha* is consumed by the *rakṣas*, the enemies of the gods, and not by the ancestors. Thus it is said that such a *śrāddha* becomes fruitless. The mention of the *rakṣas* is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). (3.160)

"He who enters into marriage and the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*. The term *agraja* refers to a uterine brother born first—that is, at the beginning. For it is recited thus:"

"There is no fault in marrying [another] if one marries the sons of a paternal uncle, the sons of a co-wife, or the sons of another's wife, provided there is union with a wife and the *agnihotra*. (PSm 4.28). Here, "elder brother" refers to a uterine brother.
