While he remains unmarried and has not entered into union with the *agnihotra*, the younger brother is enjoined to act when the elder’s natural duty has ceased. Although the word *agnihotra* denotes the ritual itself, it is used here in the sense of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) for that purpose. A specific distinction is recited in another *smṛti*:
One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, one who has fallen from his caste,
a eunuch, and one afflicted with consumption— such a person is not fit to be waited upon.

This [period] is also intended as an indication of lack of eligibility; therefore, even one who is excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkteya*) is included. A specific period of time is additionally required. And so says the *Smṛti*: "One should wait for eight years, or six, according to some" (GDh 18.19). This number of years is to be understood as starting from the time when the younger brother has reached the age for marriage. And the time for marriage is the cessation of the rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).

But is it not the case that this was recited under the section concerning those who have gone abroad? For, having introduced the period of exile for women when their husband has gone abroad, the text beginning with "to her brother," and so forth, was recited.

True. In another sentence, the direct connection of the word *proṣita* (absent) has been understood. However, in this other case, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the connection must be stated; and that does not exist, as in the rule "the governing force [is indicated] by the circumflex accent" (*svaritenādhikāraḥ*, cf. Pāṇini 1.3.11). Nor is there the word *tat* (that) here. Furthermore, it is not on account of that [word *tat*] that the sentence would remain incomplete in its absence. Moreover, Vasiṣṭha has included even the fire prescribed in the Smṛtis by using the term *agni* without qualification.

Some maintain that this rule applies even when the father has not performed the *ādheya* rite, on the grounds that the term *agraja* (elder brother) is etymological and thus the father is also an elder brother.

Even if this were so, it would follow that the same would apply to any other elder brother; however, this conventional usage of "elder" and "younger" does not exist between father and son. Furthermore, another *smṛti* reads: "and [the sin of] marrying before an elder brother (*parivedana*) occurs when the brother is senior" (GDh 18.18). Thus, the *parivitti* is the elder, the first-born.

The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him, she who is thus married by the younger, the giver, and the officiating priest as the fifth—all these go to hell. (3.162)

In this context, he prohibits others related to the act of supersession (*parivedana*) by pointing out their faults as well. One who is superseded (*parivitti*) is one who is abandoned or treated with contempt because of the supersession. One who performs the supersession by passing over the elder brother is the *parīvettṛ*. And the girl by whom the supersession is performed—*all these go to hell*, including the giver and the officiating priest (*yājaka*), who is the fifth among those destined for hell. The "giver" is, in this context, the father or other relative of the girl. The "officiating priest" is he who performs the *homa* at the wedding, or whoever provides instruction therein. Alternatively, the term refers to the sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*) even for sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* belonging to those very individuals—the superseder, the superseded, and the giver of the girl. Therefore, the elder brother must act in such a way that he does not become an obstacle to the marriage of his younger brother. The younger brother, too, must observe a waiting period of twelve, eight, or six years, etc. The girl, likewise, must not be given to such a person. The compound "those of whom the giver and the officiating priest are the fifth" is a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*. (3.162)
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—even though she has been appointed according to dharma—is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. (3.163)

One who, having proceeded according to the law of *niyoga*, should feel passion—that is, cultivate affection—upon approaching the wife of his deceased brother; that is, out of lust. By transgressing the law of *niyoga*—that is, by abandoning the injunction that "it shall be once at each season" (*sakṛt sakṛd ṛtau*)—if he should engage in intense embracing, kissing, and so forth, or act repeatedly out of desire for pleasure, or if his mind should be transformed, being revealed as impassioned through signs such as loving glances toward the woman, embraces, and affectionate words, he is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. However, the definition of an *agredidhiṣūpati* is to be understood from another Smṛti text: "The husband of an *agredidhiṣū* [is so called] while [the elder sister] is still living."

Some, however, say that this verse does not exist at all in the traditional recension (*samāmnāya*), and they argue that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [of its existence] is incomplete. For when the definitions of two types of men were to be given, it would not be appropriate for only one of them to be mentioned by those who perform their duties. Furthermore, both of these are observed in another Smṛti: "The wise call him an *apatit* whose wife was previously married to another; he is called an *agredidhiṣū*, O Brahmin, whose wife is the younger sister of his deceased elder brother."
But that is not possible here, because the husband of a woman who has had another prior husband is prohibited separately. Therefore, the *didhiṣūpati* is someone else. (3.163)
Two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from another man’s wife.

While the husband is alive, he is a *kuṇḍa*; when the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*. (3.164) When the husband is alive and his wife remains in his house, a son who is born secretly, either through a paramour or by the husband’s own consent, is called a *kuṇḍa* because he was born of another. But when [the husband] is dead, he is a *golaka*.
Some say that these two are the sons of an unauthorized union (*aniyuktāsuta*);

that is incorrect, because they do not attain [the status of] Brāhmaṇa-hood precisely because they are not Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are those born from an authorized union (*niyoga*).
But how is it that the sons of an unauthorized union lack Brāhmaṇa-hood, while the other two possess it?

Because the term *patnī* (wife) is employed in the definition of caste [in the rule], as in: "among wives of equal status from all castes" (MDh 10.5). Furthermore, the word *patnī* is a relative term, just like the word *bhartṛ* (husband). And the word *patnī* is derived in connection with the sacrifice; nor does one have the right to perform a sacrifice together with the wife of another.
If this is so, then even for those born through *niyoga*, there is no Brahminhood, since the same principle applies;
we shall resolve this in the tenth chapter.

Or, let there be no Brāhmaṇahood for either the son of an appointed woman (*niyuktā*) or the son of an unappointed woman (*aniyuktā*). But has it not been said that, in the absence of Brāhmaṇahood, since there is no possibility of its occurrence, a prohibition is untenable? This will follow precisely from the prohibition against those who have fallen (*patita*). Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is what constitutes "falling. Since eating at a *śrāddha* is a duty of the twice-born, how could there be any possibility of its performance by one who has fallen? Furthermore, the prohibition is recorded in the scripture: "Those who are thieves or fallen... (MDh 3.140). 3.164.
But those beings born in the field of another cause the destruction, both after death and in this world,
of the offerings of sacrificial oblations (havya) and ancestral gifts (kavya) given by their donors.

Regarding the rule *jātyākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.58), the plural form is used for "living beings. These living beings disregard the designations such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth; they are worthy of being designated simply as "living beings" and do not deserve any other designation. Therefore, they destroy the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, rendering them fruitless for the donors, that is, the givers. Since persons such as the *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother) are not well-known in the world and are not remembered by their specific names, this definition is formulated for the sake of establishing a clear distinction. (3.165)
As many members of a worthy company as one who is unworthy to sit in their company beholds while they are eating, for so many of them the foolish donor receives no fruit therefrom. (3.166)

Those who are worthy of the *paṅkti* (the row) are called *paṅktyas*. Being worthy of sitting, eating, and so forth together with the virtuous constitutes *paṅktyatva*; the absence of that quality makes one *apaṅktya*. As many learned, ascetic, and Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) as he sees eating in the row, for that many there is no fruit known as the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛtṛpti*). Therefore, thieves and the like must be removed from that place by one performing a *śrāddha*. A *bāliśa* is a fool. (3.166)

Having looked [at the gift], a blind man destroys the fruit of ninety [gifts], a one-eyed man that of sixty, a leper that of a hundred, and one afflicted by a foul disease that of a thousand of the donor. (3.167) But surely, how can there be seeing for a blind man, such that it is said here: "having looked, a blind man [destroys the fruit] of ninety"?

True. By this, proximity to that place is indicated. As much space as falls within the range of vision of one with sight—that much unobstructed space from which the blind man should be excluded; the one-eyed man, from sixty. The meaning here is not that he is to be fed beyond that point; rather, it is merely made known that by the reduction in number, there is a lightening of the fault, for the purpose of specifying the penance. One afflicted with *śvitra* is called a leper (*kuṣṭhī*); one with a "sinful disease" (*pāparogī*) is well known [as a leper]. (3.167)

As many Brāhmaṇas as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs, for that many [Brāhmaṇas] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the *paurtika* gift. (3.168) As many Brāhmaṇas as he touches with his limbs while seated in the row, even here the touching of the limbs is not intended; rather, as before, it refers to proximity to that place. *Paurtika* means the fruit arising from *pūrta*. That fruit which arises from giving outside the sacrificial altar is *paurtika*. (3.168)
Even a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, having accepted a gift from him out of greed, quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water. (3.169)

By way of incidental discussion, the unacceptability of gifts from one who officiates for a Śūdra is stated here. Even if a knower of the Veda accepts wealth belonging to that Śūdra-officiant—this being a restatement on the grounds of greed—he too goes to destruction; he is deprived of the desired object, such as wealth, sons, cattle, his own body, and so forth. How much more so, then, one who is ignorant of the Veda? For it will be stated later that there is indeed no great fault in a knower of the Veda accepting gifts. An *āmapātra* is an unbaked vessel, such as a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) or the like; it is cast into the water. (3.169)
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood;
what is given to a temple-attendant is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation. (3.170)

He is born into that species where excrement becomes his food. The same applies to a physician. "Lost" (*naṣṭa*) means fruitless or causing distress; for lost wealth produces anxiety. That which lacks a foundation or stability is "unfounded" (*apratiṣṭha*). Through various expressions, the fruitlessness of such a gift and the connection with fault on the part of the giver are established. One should not suspect that there is no difference in meaning between "lost" (*naṣṭa*) and "unfounded" (*apratiṣṭha*), because their respective effects differ. (3.170)
That which is given to a trader brings no fruit either in this world or the next;
it is like an oblation poured into ashes, so too is that given to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.

This verse also is to be explained as before. Eating at the house of a trader is forbidden, but proximity to his place is not. For there is no such basis here as there was previously, where the word "having seen" (*vīkṣya*) indicated proximity by metaphorical extension to the place within the range of vision. A man born of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*) will be described in the ninth chapter (MDh 9.175).
But regarding other unworthy persons who have been specified as those unfit for the company (apaṅktyas), the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone. (3.172)

Those such as the blind and others mentioned in this section on demonstrating the fruit of giving to those unworthy of the company (apaṅkti), and others such as thieves who are specified in their respective categories—when these are fed, the following things accrue to the giver: fat, blood, flesh, and so forth. He is born into a species where these constitute food, namely among the species of worms, carnivorous beasts, vultures, and the like; so say the wise who know the Vedas.

This is the meaning of it all: if those unworthy of the company are fed, the duty (*adhikāra*) regarding the *śrāddha* has not been fulfilled; and since this rule is obligatory (*nitya*), the fault of transgressing the injunction (*vidhyatikrama-doṣa*) is inevitable if it is not performed. (3.172)
Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify the assembly (paṅktipāvana), by whom a row defiled by one unworthy of the company is purified. (3.173)

Listen to those Brāhmaṇas by whom a *paṅkti*—an assembly defiled or corrupted by the previously mentioned persons unworthy of the company (*apaṅktya*)—is purified, that is, rendered free from fault. I shall speak of them in their entirety, without omission; the other words are merely explanatory (*arthavāda*). The meaning is this: just as one who eats in a company, if he is corrupt, defiles even those who are not corrupt, so too a purifier of the company (*paṅktipāvana*), by virtue of his superior qualities, removes the defects of others. Nor does this authorize the feeding of those unworthy of the company; rather, a purifier of the company must necessarily be sought. And when such a person is found—even if the others have not been scrutinized with extreme care for three generations—if they are nonetheless free from observable defects, they should be fed even if [the rest are otherwise imperfect]; such is the purpose of the instruction regarding the purifier of the company. (3.173)
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the Vedas], and who are born into a lineage of *śrotriya*s, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).

"Foremost" means excellent, having mastered the Vedas through the thorough removal of all doubts. Likewise, they are "foremost in all the expositions. Those by whom [the meaning] is proclaimed and explained—these are the "expositions," namely the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) of the Vedic meaning. They are those by whom the Veda with its six auxiliaries has been studied and is being studied. Furthermore, they are "born into a lineage of *śrotriya*s," meaning those whose fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, were likewise such [learned men].

But surely, such persons alone are prescribed as those to be fed; what excellence, then, is there by virtue of which they are now said to be "purifiers of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*)? Giving to the learned is prescribed only when they possess Vedic learning (*śrotriyatva*). And here, being learned is not specifically mentioned. Nor is the status of being a purifier of the row established by mere learning. For the status of being a purifier of the row depends upon specific qualities; it is not appropriate when those qualities are diminished. Therefore, this [text] is intended for the purpose of giving to a mere *śrotriya* in the absence of a learned man. What is meant is that, when no learned man is available, giving to a *śrotriya* is indeed primary, not secondary.
The plural number is used with reference to individual instances. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of conjunction. (3.174)

One who has performed the *triṇāciketa* sacrifice, one who maintains the five sacred fires (*pañcāgni*), one who knows the *trisuparṇa* hymns, one who is learned in the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one born from a lineage where the gift of a Brahman’s daughter was made, and likewise one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*.

The *triṇāciketa* is a specific division of the Vedas belonging to the *adhvaryu* priests, beginning with the words: “Their water drunk, their grass eaten” (cf. Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3). Because of his connection to the study of that text, a person is here called *triṇāciketa*. Furthermore, a specific vow is prescribed for those studying the *triṇāciketa*; he by whom that vow has been observed is a *triṇāciketa*. In this context as well, the term refers to the person only through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

One should not think that mere [knowledge] constitutes the quality of purifying the assembly (*paṅktipāvanatva*); rather, this quality should be seen as superior when it is conjoined with qualities such as being a *śrotriya*, serving as a cause for purifying the assembly.

The knowledge called the "Five-Fire Doctrine" (*pañcāgnividyā*) is taught in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (ChU 5.3–10), the fruit of which is stated in "the thief of gold," etc. (ChU 5.10.9). By virtue of the connection with the study of that [doctrine], a person also becomes a "five-fire" individual, as previously described.

Others, however, define one who possesses five fires as a *pañcāgni*: namely, the three sacrificial fires of the *tretā*—the *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, and *dakṣiṇāgni*—along with two others, the *sabhyāgni* and the *āvasathyāgni*. Among these, the so-called *sabhyāgni* is that which is employed in many regions specifically for dispelling the cold during great ritual performances.

The mantra named *Trisuparṇa* is found in both the *Taittirīyaka* and the *Bāhvṛcya*: "Those Brāhmaṇas who recite the *Trisuparṇa*," and so forth. One who knows the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is called a *ṣaḍaṅgavit*. One who is born from the lineage of a woman given in marriage according to the *brāhma* rite of dharma is [also so designated]. Furthermore, one who sings the *Jyeṣṭhasāman* is called such; the *Jyeṣṭhadoha* chants are Sāmans in the *Āraṇyaka*, and he who sings them is thus addressed. Here too, by virtue of singing the Sāmans or performing their specific vows, a person is so called. (3.175)
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder [of the sacred texts], a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), one who bestows a thousand [cows],
and one who has reached a hundred years of age— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). (3.176) [He] knows the meaning of the Veda.
But has it not already been stated that one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is [an authority]?

True; however, the person intended here as a knower of the meaning of the Veda is one who, even without the auxiliaries, deduces [the meaning] by himself through his own wisdom. Alternatively, this is a restatement of that very same point, made again and again: for without knowledge of the meaning of the Veda, people are not worthy of receiving offerings (*śrāddha*), even if they possess other qualities.

A reciter is one who explains the very meaning of the Veda. A *brahmacārī* is a student of sacred knowledge. "A giver of a thousand" means one who has given a thousand cows, since no specific distinction is mentioned; this is appropriate because the word "thousand" is a synonym for "many," thus meaning one who gives much or is liberal. For there is no authority for taking the number of cows as fixed. It is even stated in the Veda: "Cows are indeed the mothers of sacrifice. When there is an injunction without specification, cows are understood [as the intended object]. "One whose life is a hundred" (*śatāyu*) means one who is advanced in age; for he attains purity through the ripening of his impurities (*kaṣāya*). "One whose life is a hundred" (*śatāyu*) means one whose lifespan is a hundred. Years are the things to be counted, according to common usage. Alternatively, the word "hundred" has the sense of "many," meaning one who has a long life. And it is advanced age that is intended here. For it is said in the Gautama Dharma Sūtra: "Some say that giving to the young comes first, like [the offering] to the ancestors" (GDh 15.10–11). It is precisely for this purpose that they explain the mention of the *brahmacārī* here; for he is of early age. (3.176)
On the day before or on the very day when the Śrāddha rite is to take place, he should properly invite at least three Brahmins of the kind previously described. (3.177)

The types of Brāhmaṇas who are to be fed have been described. Now, the remaining procedure is stated. On the day before—that is, on the fourteenth or twelfth day prior to the day when the Śrāddha is to be performed, whether on the new moon (amāvāsyā) or the thirteenth day—one should invite the Brāhmaṇas if the Śrāddha is to take place on the following day; or one may do so on the very same day. Here, the option depends on the observance of rules: he who is able to maintain the rules should invite them on the previous day, while one who is unable may do so on that very day. Moreover, there is great fruit from observing the additional rules. When the invitation is to be made, it consists of a formal request, the engagement, and the acceptance. "Tryavarāḥ" means those of whom three is the minimum; if they are extremely few, then there should be three. However, it has been stated that if possible, an odd number should be used according to one's capacity. The remainder of the verse is for the purpose of completing the meter. "Upasthite" means when [the time] has arrived. "Yathoditān" means as previously described. (3.177)
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedas while that śrāddha lasts. (3.178)

One invited to a *śrāddha* for the ancestors should remain self-controlled; with a restrained mind, he should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and practice other restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*), such as the vows of a *snātaka*. It is ordained that among the "vows of men," the prohibitions against dancing, singing, and the like, constitute an integral part of the ritual act. The performer of the *śrāddha* must act in such a way that the invited Brāhmaṇa remains one whose senses are restrained from the moment of invitation; otherwise, the *śrāddha* would be defiled. Furthermore, he should not study the Vedas (*chandāṃsi*). What is prohibited here is the formal recitation (*adhyayana*) consisting of the pronunciation of Vedic syllables; however, silent repetition (*japa*) during the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and similar rites is not forbidden. The construction of the words is as follows: "He who has that *śrāddha* to perform should be self-controlled, just like one invited to a *śrāddha* for the ancestors. Thus, from the moment of invitation, the rule of non-study and the requirement of restraint apply equally to both the eater and the performer. (3.178)
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit.

"One must remain self-controlled when invited"—this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for this injunction. For the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) attend upon the invited Brahmins in an invisible form and enter their bodies, just as one possessed by a spirit or a demon (*bhūtagraha*). They follow them like the wind; just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is like the wind, follows a man as he walks and does not abandon him when he stops, so too the ancestors become like the wind. Thus they wait upon the seated Brahmins; they follow them when they walk and sit down when they have sat down. The meaning is that the invited twice-born (*dvija*) become possessed of the form of the ancestors. Therefore, those who have been invited must not act independently. (3.179)
But when the best of the twice-born has been duly invited for the offerings to the gods or the ancestors, that sinner who somehow neglects them shall go to the state of a pig. (3.180)

"Ketita" means invited to offerings for the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*). Having accepted the invitation—that is, having agreed to partake in the *śrāddha* meal—if he somehow transgresses it, failing to present himself at the time of the meal, or does not maintain celibacy, then that Brāhmaṇa goes to the state of a pig. "Somehow" means either out of desire or through forgetfulness. The phrase "according to rule" (*yathānyāyam*) is used merely to complete the meter.

Others, however, say: "The transgression consists precisely in not accepting what is being requested. And thus it is stated in the *Śrāddhakalpa*: "One who is invited by an irreproachable person should not refuse. But this is incorrect; for engagement in the *śrāddha* rite proceeds from desire (*lipsā*), and not from scriptural injunction. In that case, if there is no desire and one does not accept, what fault could there be? (3.180)
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, takes pleasure with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), incurs all whatever evil deed has been committed by the giver. (3.181)

The term *vṛṣalī* is intended as an indicator for women in general, because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is prescribed universally. Therefore, even a Brāhmaṇī woman is indeed a *vṛṣalī*. He demonstrates the etymological derivation: she "desires the male" (*vṛṣasyati*), that is, she agitates her husband. Thus is the meaning: having accepted the meal, he who on that day rejoices—that is, takes pleasure—with a woman, and who even produces conversation, embraces, and so forth with her out of a desire for sexual union; upon him falls this fault. Whatever evil or sin belongs to the giver, that is, the performer of the *śrāddha*, all of that transfers to him. By this, merely the connection with an undesirable result is indicated. Otherwise, where the giver is a performer of meritorious deeds, there would be no fault at all. "Rejoicing" (*modana*) means the arising of delight. Consequently, even conversation, embracing, and the like should not be performed [with such a woman]. (3.181)
Free from anger, devoted to purity, always practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons, the highly fortunate ancestors are the deities of the past.

Free from anger means devoid of wrath. Devoted to purity (*śauca*): purity is cleanliness, whether through earth and water, through expiation, or through internal purification. This is a qualification of "constantly" (*satatam*). Therefore, in cases such as spitting, one must perform *ācamana* (sipping water) and so forth at that very moment. A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) avoids sexual intercourse with women. Having laid down weapons (*nyasta-śastra*): those by whom weapons have been laid down or abandoned. The mention of "weapons" is intended to indicate physical violence in general. Of great fortune (*mahābhāga*): the possession of qualities such as magnanimity and wealth constitutes "great fortune. Since the ancestors possess such a form and they enter into the Brāhmaṇas, the meaning is that one should become like them by assuming that form; this matter is enjoined by way of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). The ancestors are called "former deities" (*pūrva-devatā*); the praise is that even in another *kalpa*, these are indeed deities. The term "former" (*pūrva*) is used because the ancestors were worthy of worship in former times. (3.182)
Since the origin of all these [impurities] occurs entirely without exception, learn now those rules by which they are to be treated. 3.183 (V3.193)

Learn now, understand in its entirety, all that has been stated regarding the origin of these ancestors, who they are, and by whom they are to be honored—such as that the *Somapās* are to be honored by a Brāhmaṇa and the *Haviṣmants* by a Kṣatriya, and so forth. The phrase "with observances" (*niyamaiḥ*) is a restatement, since it was already enjoined previously in the rule, "one should be self-restrained" (MDh 3.178). The plural number is used because there are many such observances. 3.183.
The sons of all those sages, such as Marīci and others, who were the sons of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha, are remembered as the groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇāḥ).

Hiraṇyagarbha is Prajāpati; his son is Manu Hairaṇyagarbha. As it was stated in the first chapter: "Having thus created all this, including me... (MDh 1.51). Those sons of that Manu, such as Marīci and others, namely Atri, Aṅgiras, and so forth—who are the sons of those sages—they are these very groups of ancestors.

But surely, one's father and the rest are the fathers of everyone; for it has been enjoined thus: "One should offer rice-balls to the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather. Likewise: "Beyond these three, the sons should give [the offerings]. In that case, why is this said: "The sons of the Ṛṣis are the fathers named Somapas, belonging to the Brahmins"? Nor can an option be admitted, such as: "One should give to the Somapas, or to the father and grandfather. Furthermore, regarding its origin, it is heard in scripture: "It must be performed by a son. And the word "son" is a relative term. Likewise: "He whose father has passed away... (MDh 3.211). Therefore, the meaning of this section must be explained.
It is said: this is a praise that serves as a supplement to the preceding injunction. Here, their status as recipients (*saṃpradāna*) is not explicitly heard in the text.
But surely there is the injunction: "they are to be honored" (MDh 3.183)?

This term *carati* cannot be the subject of an injunction (*vidhi*) as a form of ordinary action. A specific ritual called *upacāra* (service/attendance) is not recognized in the Veda in the same way as *dāna* (giving) or *yāga* (sacrifice). For this term is generally used, like the verb *karoti* (to do), with reference to an action proximate [to the speaker]; and what is proximate here is the *śrāddha*. Since that [śrāddha] has already been enjoined as having specific recipients (*saṃpradāna*), it cannot be enjoined again; furthermore, there is no proximity for it in its capacity as something to be enjoined. The term *carati* would thus sublate what is proximate. Even regarding the worldly usage "the gurus are to be attended upon" (*gurava upacaryāḥ*), there too the meaning understood is service characterized by washing the feet and so forth. That too is not possible in the case of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) as described above. Moreover, since the meaningfulness [of the passage] is established through syntactic unity with the root [text], there is no possibility of postulating another meaning. And if the Somapas and others were intended as deities in the *śrāddha* according to their respective castes (*varṇa*), then the description of their lineage (*abhijana*) would be useful. But if [the passage] functions as a praise (*stāvaka*), then everything is consistent.

This [work] is commenced for the sake of engaging anyone whose intellect might be impaired and who would be disrespectful toward ancestral rites (*pitrya-karman*) due to hatred of their ancestors. Do not think thus: "The ancestors are merely deceased human beings; what harm will they do if they are not gratified at the *śrāddha*, or what benefit will they provide if they are gratified? For these [ancestors] possess great power. Hiraṇyagarbha is the lord of the entire world; Manu is his son, and these [ancestors] are his grandsons. It is for this very reason that they are called the "grandsons of the sages" (*ṛṣi-pautra*). They are not just any other sons of Manu; rather, they are the sages of renowned power, such as Marīci and others. Their sons are the ancestors. Furthermore, there are many kinds of practitioners who are especially inclined to act upon such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Furthermore, those who assert that "the view of Soma and others should be applied to the ancestors" are to be disregarded due to a lack of authoritative evidence; for there is no such statement here as there is when the view of Brahman is taught in relation to the sun.

As for those who say, "Having taken the lineage (*gotra*) and the name, one should offer them to the ancestors," this lineage—such as "Somapas" and so forth—is distinguished by the [four] castes (*varṇa*). That too is incorrect; for this is a designation of names, not a designation of lineages, since we hear the expression "of the Somapas. If it is argued that even if it were a name for a lineage, the word "name" (*nāma*) would still be appropriate, then in that case, there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the designation of the lineage: it would have to be "the lineage of the ancestors is the Somapas," rather than "the ancestors are the Somapas."

Now, if it is argued that the designation of a "continuum" (saṃtāna) is seen to occur by means of the lineage (gotra) through a metaphorical identification with it—as in the case of saying "Babhru is Mandu"—[we reply:]...

To this it is replied: Here it must be determined what this so-called *gotra* is. Is it the original progenitor, the most renowned founder of a name through his possession of qualities such as learning, wealth, heroism, and generosity, by whom the family is designated? If that were the case, then there would indeed be internal subdivisions of *gotras* for all classes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. Furthermore, people born in that lineage remember such a person, thinking, "We are born in the family of so-and-so"; therefore, designation by him alone is appropriate. For no one remembers "Somapās" as a *gotra*, in the way that they remember Bhṛgu, Garga, or Gālava. And for Brāhmaṇas, designation by those [original sages] alone is proper, for those are the primary *gotras*. The word *gotra* does not apply to them in its conventional sense. For these *gotras*—unlike the castes of Brāhmaṇas and so forth—are beginningless; thus the definition "the original progenitor who establishes the name is the *gotra*" does not apply to them. Indeed, the designation "Pārāśara" is not applied to certain Brāhmaṇas only from the birth of Parāśara onwards. If that were the case, it would follow that the Veda has a beginning. Therefore, because this designation of *gotra* is eternal, that very *gotra* must be relied upon in rites such as the libation of water (*udakatarpaṇa*). Those who establish names, however, are not eternal; they are of the present day. And when an eternal [designation] is available, it is not proper to employ a non-eternal one, such as "Somapā," in a Vedic rite. Therefore, Brāhmaṇas, having made the dedication with words such as "May this *svadhā* and this water be for Gārgya" or "for one of the Garga *gotra*," and then having uttered the [individual's] name, they should perform the offering of water and other rites.

Among Kṣatriyas and others, such a practice regarding lineage (*gotra*) does not exist. For Kṣatriyas and the like do not remember their lineage as fixedly as a Brāhmaṇa does. Therefore, their lineage is merely worldly; it consists of a most famous founder who established a name. Consequently, they are designated in rites such as the *śrāddha* by that very name, even though it has a beginning. However, those Kṣatriyas do not deserve to be designated in the *śrāddha* and other rites by means of lineages such as "Havirbhuj" and so forth.

As for those who say that for those whose names—such as those of their fathers and so forth—are unknown, the *śrāddha* and other rites are enjoined by these words: "I summon the Somapās; to the Somapās, svadhā!"—this too is not correct. For it has been stated: "If one does not know the names, then [one says] 'grandfather,' 'great-grandfather,' and so on. Furthermore, if the meaningfulness [of the specific names] could not be obtained as a supplement to the subject matter (*prakṛtaśeṣatva*) because they are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), then indeed such ritual options (*kalpa*) might be resorted to. But when a connection as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) is possible, it is not logical to derive meaning by assuming a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). (3.184)
The sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are the ancestors of the gods, being the offspring of Marīci.

These verses are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) regarding the *śrāddha* rite, for they form a single syntactical unit as a whole. For the Sādhyas are not taught to be the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) of the *śrāddha*, because the Sādhyas are deities (*devatā*). And deities have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to ritual acts, because they lack the status of being those to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*). Indeed, a deity cannot be enjoined, as that would entail the loss of their status as a deity. If there were such an entitlement, there would have to be agency (*kartṛtva*) to be assumed; and if there is agency, how could there be the status of being a recipient? Nor is there any other form of "deity. The sons of Virāj are the Soma-sitting ones (*somasaḍ*), by name; they are the ancestors of the Sādhyas. Such a constant rite must necessarily be performed, since even the Sādhyas—the ancient gods who have already accomplished all that was to be done—worship the ancestors. Those who relish what is cooked in the fire, such as the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the cake (*puroḍāśa*), are the Agniṣvāttas, the ancestors of the gods beginning with Indra and Agni. Born of Marīci are the Mārīcas; they are world-renowned and well-established. (3.185)
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are remembered as the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras. (3.186) V3.196

All these beings, beginning with the Daityas, who are not entitled to the study of the scriptures, are mentioned here for the sake of explanatory praise (arthavāda). Their true nature is well-known from the Itihāsas. The Suparṇas are a particular kind of bird; the Kinnaras are horse-faced animals. Such is this ancestral rite (pitrya karma) that even the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas—who are destroyers of sacrifices—do not bypass it, nor do even animals who lack consciousness and memory. Those born of Atri are named Barhiṣads. (3.186)
Among the Brahmins they are named Somapas; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaiśyas, Ājyapas; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins. (3.187) V3.197

The meaning of this verse has already been explained. Indra and the other deities [348] drink the *soma*; the *havirbhujas* are the deities who consume the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth; the *ājyapas* are the deities of the *āghāra*, *ājyabhāga*, *prayāja*, and other offerings; and the *sukālins*. They are called *sukālins* because they "bring to a conclusion" (*kālayanti*), that is, they bring the ritual action to its end. These are the deities of the concluding oblations (*apavarga-homa*) prescribed by such mantras as "O Agni, thou who art *ayās* and free from imprecation... (MS 1.4.3). 3.187.
The Somapas are the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmants are the sons of Aṅgiras;

the Ājyapas are the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins are the sons of Vasiṣṭha. (3.188) The Haviṣmants are indeed the Havirbhujas. Kavi is Bhṛgu; for they remember that the descendant of Bhṛgu is called Kāvya, as in the saying, "They call Uśanas Kāvya. Just as these deities are the sons of the sages, so too are your ancestors of the very nature of deities; do not hold them in contempt. (3.188)
One should designate the *anagnidagdhas*, the *agnidagdhas*, the *kāvyas*, the *barhiṣads*, as well as the *agniṣvāttas* and the *saumyas*, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins. (3.189) V3.199

*Soma* is not burnt by fire, for there is no cooking of it by fire. Therefore, those deities who are worshipped with that [soma] are also said to be "not burnt by fire" (*anagnidagdha*) and "prosperous" (*samṛddha*) because of that quality. In this way, the sacrificial oblations such as *caru* and *puroḍāśa* are cooked by fire; the deities who are worshipped with them are "burnt by fire" (*agnidagdha*). This connection is made just as before: one should designate those who are called "burnt by fire" as *agnidagdha*, and those who are "not burnt by fire" as *somapa* (drinkers of Soma). The same applies to the *kāvyas* and the *barhiṣadas*. The *kāvyas* are the sons of Kavi, and they are described as "the sons of Kavi are the drinkers of Soma" (MDh 3.188). The *barhiṣadas* are said to be the sons of Atri. This particle *eva* ("only") should not be understood as restricting the scope according to the specific location [of the word]; for if it were so, the meaning would be that the ancestors belong only to Brahmins and not to Kṣatriyas and others, which would contradict what was stated previously. Furthermore, these are not mentioned as ancestors according to a distinction of caste, such that their connection to Brahmins and others could be asserted by detaching them from that [general category]. Therefore, the particle *eva* should be drawn back and connected thus: "one should designate only the *agniṣvāttas* as [the *somapas*]" and so forth. The mention of "Brahmins" (*vipra*) is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to indicate the Kṣatriyas and others as well. These ancestors are heard of in the Veda by these names: "The *agniṣvāttas* are the ancestors who are burnt by fire, and those who are not burnt. Having cited these mantras, he explains them.

Alternatively, the connection may be made in this way: one should designate as one's own ancestors those very Pitṛs who are denoted by these words [in the verse], and they belong exclusively to the Brahmins. Nor should one entertain the doubt that a difference in meaning follows from a difference in words. The mention of the "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*), because of his preeminence. For an indication is made by means of the principal, as in the expression, "The King is going. (3.189)
Moreover, regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed, it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite. (3.190) V3.200

These, however, are the principal classes of ancestors (*pitṛs*), beginning with the *Somapas*. They too have sons and grandsons who exist in infinite numbers; they also are indeed ancestors. From this statement of restriction, it is understood that the *Somapas* and the others are not the ones to be designated as the objects of the rite. For if their sons and grandsons—who are the actual ancestors—were to be the objects of the rite, then no name for them would have been handed down in the tradition. Therefore, it is determined that this is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Because it begins with "cattle and horses" (*gavāśva-prabhṛti*), the term "sons and grandsons" (*putrapautram*) is treated as a singular collective compound. *Anantakam* means "unlimited"; the suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (without changing the meaning). [3.190]
From the sages the ancestors were born; from the ancestors, gods and humans;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—arose in due succession. (3.191)

The ancestral rite (pitrya-karma) should not be regarded as inferior to the divine rite (daiva-karma); rather, it is the most preeminent. For the ancestors are the eldest-born of the gods. Indeed, the sequence of creation is this: from the sages (ṛṣis) the ancestors were born, and from the ancestors the gods. From the gods, the rest of the entire world—both the moving (jaṅgama) and the stationary (sthāvara)—arose in due order, according to the sequence stated in the first chapter. The discussion of explanatory passages (arthavāda) has now concluded. 3.191.
Even water, when given with faith using silver vessels or those adorned with silver, serves for their inexhaustible benefit. (3.192) V3.202

The vessels should be made of silver, that is, of silver material; in its absence, they should be made of wood, copper, gold, or even materials mixed with silver in one part. This vessel to be offered is the one intended for the satisfaction resulting from the consumption of ghee, honey, and other condiments; it is in this context that the requirement for the vessel to be made of silver is prescribed. Furthermore, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so forth must be performed with the hands alone. Even the pouring of water upon the rice-balls and the washing (*avanejana*) and so forth must likewise be done with the hands, according to the scriptural injunction: "with the hand [having the sacred thread] over the right shoulder" (*apasavyena hastena*). As for the daily libation of water (*udakatarpaṇa*), that too may be performed with either the hand having the sacred thread over the right shoulder or with the left hand.
For this has been recited in the section on the *śrāddha* ceremony.
That is not so; for even a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of a rite that is not part of the current context may be taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*).
There is indeed a statement to that effect.

Let it be; this is a restatement [of what has been said]. "Even water": the word "even" (api) indicates praise for the vessel. Let alone the giving of refined food—if even mere water is given with a silver vessel, it becomes inexhaustible due to its connection with the quality of the silver; it serves as a means for the inexhaustible. The meaning is that it becomes the cause of inexhaustible satisfaction. "With faith" is a restatement because it is prescribed for all acts of giving. (3.192)

For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (devakārya); indeed, it is traditionally taught that the rite for the gods is the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors. (3.193) V3.203

That which is performed for the sake of the gods is the rite dedicated to the gods (*daiva*). After that, the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*) is distinguished; it is specifically designated as that which must be performed. By this, he states the preeminence of the ancestral rite. It is thereby stated that the rite for the gods is merely an ancillary act (*aṅga*) therein. He clarifies its status as an ancillary act: for the feeding of Brahmins, which constitutes the rite for the gods, serves to nourish and increase the rite for the ancestors; it is not itself a primary act, but rather a sustainer of the ancestral rite alone. (3.193)
One should first appoint a deity as their protector;
for the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection. (3.194)

"Guard" (*rakṣā*) means protection (*ārakṣa*); that which has been obtained is "protective," meaning it serves for the purpose of protection—this is what is intended. Alternatively, the word *bhūta* is used in the sense of a comparison: "as if for the purpose of protection. When, however, it is for the sake of protection, one should first appoint—that is, invite—a divine Brāhmaṇa and seat him upon a seat. This is another explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). According to the Itihāsas, there are certain invisible beings called *rakṣas* who plunder—that is, snatch away—the *śrāddha* from the ancestors. But which deities are to be designated? First, according to the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the Viśvedevas are understood from the application of the mantra: "We invoke the Viśvedevas. It is also stated in the Purāṇa: "The Śruti says, 'the Viśvedevas'. (3.194)
That [rite] which begins and ends with the divine (daiva) would not have the ancestors (pitr) at its beginning and end;

however, one who performs it beginning and ending with the ancestors perishes quickly along with his lineage. (3.195) "Beginning and end" means the initial and the final parts. "Beginning and end with the divine" means that which has the divine as its beginning and end. By means of the divine rite, the commencement (*ādi*)—that is, the undertaking—of the *śrāddha* must be performed. Therefore, the invitation of the gods must first be carried out. "End" means the conclusion. When the Brahmins associated with the ancestors have been dismissed, the dismissal of the gods must subsequently be performed.
Even regarding the giving of perfumes and other such items, they consider it to be initiated by destiny.

However, for those constituent acts (*padārtha*), it is not possible for both the commencement and the conclusion to be performed by the gods (*daiva*), because that would entail the consequence of repetition. This property of beginning and ending with the gods is a property of the ritual performance (*prayoga-dharma*), not a property of each individual act. Regarding the constituent acts such as the offering of perfumes and garlands, it is specified that they must be performed with the specific distinction of beginning with the gods; this is accomplished simply through the sequence in which they are undertaken. First, the invitation must be performed beginning with the gods. Since one particular act was commenced first, it is logical that the commencement of the others follows from that very point. For one constituent act determines the commencement of the next constituent act. As it has been said: "Because of the commencement of those qualities whose time is fixed by their nature."

One should strive—that is, one should perform—that *śrāddha* rite. The remainder is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). It should not begin and end with rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*); since it has been prescribed that it must begin and end with rites for the gods (*daiva*), the prohibition against beginning and ending with ancestral rites is to be understood as an explanatory praise, like a common worldly statement. For in the world, having enjoined something, one prohibits its opposite even if it is not otherwise established; for action disciplines the substance, not the non-substance. "He perishes quickly along with his lineage"—this is an explanatory praise of censure (*nindārthavāda*) intended to show the lack of fruitfulness of one's progeny. Therefore, everything, including the serving of food and so forth, must be performed beginning with the rites for the gods.

As for the serving of food and the like in between, or the giving of drinks and so forth to those who are thirsty, that should be offered to whichever person first develops the desire. If one were to serve it to someone who does not desire it merely out of compliance with another, there would be a subversion of the primary injunction: "one should gladden the Brahmins. Likewise, suppose one person prefers sweet flavors while another has a natural affinity (*sātmya*) for sour flavors; in that case, when there are many kinds of drinks available according to the rule, "various kinds of food and drink, and fragrant [substances]" (MDh 3.217), if one were to fail to provide the flavor-accordance to the other out of deference to the first, then illness might be produced in him. Therefore, the commencement and completion [of the meal] should be done only according to [the individual's preference], even if by chance (*daiva*) or other circumstances [it differs]. (3.195)
One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung and, with great care, ensure that it slopes toward the south. (3.196) V3.206

"Pure" means not defiled by ashes, bones, skulls, and so forth. "Secluded" means spacious and not crowded with many people. "Sloping toward the south" means inclined in the southern direction. One should prepare such a place with effort. If such a site is not found by its very nature, one should act in such a way that it is prepared through one's own exertion. And one should smear it with cow dung; clay and other materials are excluded because of the rule of smearing specifically with cow dung. (3.196)
The ancestors are always satisfied by what is given in open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and in secluded places. (3.197)

*Avakāśa* means an open space. *Cokṣāḥ* refers to places such as forests that are pure by nature, which produce clarity of mind. *Jalatīrāṇi* refers to riverbanks, sandy shores near streams, and the like. [The phrase] "in secluded and solitary sacred spots (*tīrtha*)" constitutes another rule. Consequently, there is no mandatory requirement for smearing with cow-dung, because of the statement "one should prepare [the place]. That rule applies where purity must be achieved through effort; in places that are pure by nature, fitness is attained merely by what is seen [as naturally clean], according to the rule: "that which has been washed with water" (MDh 5.125). By performing a *śrāddha* in these locations, the ancestors become exceedingly satisfied. (3.197)
When separate seats provided with sacred grass have been prepared, he should cause those Brahmins, who have duly sipped water, to sit down upon them. (3.198)

He should provide separate seats for each of them, individually and according to their respective divisions—such as long-washed wooden planks or other types of seats—and not give them all a single seat. The mention of "separate" implies that they should be seated in such a way that they do not touch one another. These seats should be provided with *barhis* grass, meaning they are strewn with mats of *darbha* grass. He should cause those previously invited to sit down after they have touched water—that is, after they have bathed and performed the ritual of sipping water (*ācamana*). (3.198)
Having seated those irreproachable Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the gods.

After they have been seated, one should honor them with perfumes and garlands. One should offer perfumes such as saffron (*kukkuṃkuma*), camphor (*karpūra*), and so forth; garlands are strings of flowers. The inclusion of the word "fragrant" (*surabhi*) is an epithet of the garlands: one should not offer flowers that lack fragrance. This epithet is also appropriately applied to the perfumes themselves, for there are perfumes that are unpleasant, and its purpose is to exclude those. Alternatively, it may mean "with fragrant incenses. The term "fragrant" is used independently [as well]. Having first given to the Brahmins representing the gods (*daiva*), one should then give to those representing the ancestors (*pitrya*).

However, they say that this mention of "beginning with the divine" (*daiva-pūrva*) is for the purpose of establishing the rule that the items [of the meal] must begin with that [divine portion] prior to the commencement of eating; but for those who have already commenced eating, there is no such restriction regarding drinks, condiments, and so forth. Otherwise, what would be the point of stating it again?

"Brahmins who are not to be despised and are blameless"—this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). It is an injunction specifically for such individuals. Alternatively, even though there is an indication of the past tense (*bhūtapratyaya*), this is merely a prohibition against the duty [to despise] implied by the verbal root. What is meant is that one should not, in the future, feel contempt or revile them. Scholars hold that it is better to abandon only the meaning of the suffix than to abandon the meaning of the entire word; for in a restatement, the entire word would otherwise be purposeless. (3.199)
Having brought water for them, along with sesame seeds and *pavitra* blades, the Brāhmaṇa, permitted by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the oblation in the fire (3.200).

Water for the *argha* offering should be presented to those who have been anointed, are wearing garlands, and are inhaling fragrant incense; with that same water, he should also offer the sesame seeds together with the *pavitra* blades. The word *pavitra* refers to *darbha* grass. Having brought and given water to those Brāhmaṇas, and being permitted by them, he should perform the *homa* in the fire. The connection is that he should act "having been permitted by the Brāhmaṇas"; all of them should give permission simultaneously.

The sentence for requesting permission is also obtained by implication; for they would not grant permission unless requested. Consequently, interrogative sentences such as "I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa*," or "I will perform it," are understood. The sentence of granting permission is likewise obtained through implication. And all of this must be performed with correct words (*sādhu-śabda*). This has been demonstrated by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras*: "He should request permission, saying, 'I shall perform [the *agnaukaraṇa*]' or 'I will perform it'; they should say, 'Om, do so. (3.200)
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama according to the rule by means of the offering of oblations, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors.

That which is to be performed in the fire is now stated. The genitive case for *agni* is used in the sense of the dative; thus, Agni is one deity. The dual compound *somayamābhyām* functions as a single deity, just like *agnīṣoma*. Having first performed the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of these two deities by means of the offering of the oblation (*havirdāna*), he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors. The meaning is that he should perform the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*) and the feeding of the Brahmins. However, other deities are enumerated in the *Gṛhyasūtras*; this statement regarding the deities is intended for those who do not possess a *Gṛhyasūtra*. Nourishment (*āpyāyana*) means providing sustenance. "The deities are nourished by the oblation"—this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). (3.201)
But in the absence of fire, one should place [the offering] directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras (3.202).

This rule is stated for the case when there is no fire—whether it be the one established according to the Smṛti, the nuptial fire, or the ancestral fire. However, regarding the ordinary (laukika) fire, its presence or absence need not be considered, because of the prohibition against performing the ancestral sacrifice (*paitṛyajña*) in such a fire. As he will state: "The oblation pertaining to the ancestral sacrifice is not to be offered in the ordinary fire" (MDh 3.272).
How, then, can there be an absence of that fire?

It has been stated that the time for a *śrāddha* occurs when one who is away from home is without fire, yet possesses the requisite materials, a worthy Brahmin, and the proper location; it is not restricted solely to the new moon day (*amāvāsya*). In that regard, this rule is prescribed for when one who is away from home encounters a person who purifies the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*), or when materials such as the *kālaśāka* vegetable are available.

But how can one who is away on a journey have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform a *śrāddha*? If the wife is traveling abroad, the sacred fire (*agni*) must also be present right there; for it is not desired that either the wife or the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) be separated from the fire. Thus it is heard in scripture: "The fire must not be left behind by those who travel. If, however, the householder were to travel alone, then there would indeed be an absence of the fire. But because he acts as a mediator and because the entitlement belongs to them jointly, when the wife is not present, how can there be an application of the common property in the *śrāddha*, given the absence of her consent? For in the case of property held in common, if one of the two parties does not consent, the act of renunciation (*tyāga*) cannot take place at all.
Now it is argued: by this same logic, the performance of *śrāddha* at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) would not be established either. In that case, the following scriptural statements would be contradicted:
"At Puṣkara, the *śrāddha* is inexhaustible, and asceticism yields great fruit;
one should know that it is exactly the same at Mahodadhi and Prabhāsa. Thus it is said.

This is not a fault. For one who possesses the sacred fire (*sāgnika*) and goes on a pilgrimage with his wife, [the performance of the rites] will be possible. In this case, however, there is travel abroad with the wife; therefore, there is no absence of the fire. If, on the other hand, he were alone, then there would be no entitlement because the wife’s consent would be unknown. It is said in reply: while traveling abroad, he asks permission of his wife, saying, "I shall employ the wealth for the sake of dharma. Having obtained her permission, he shall be entitled [to perform the rites].

And prior to initiation (*upanayana*), since there is no maintaining of the sacred fire (*agniparigraha*), this rule shall apply. Furthermore, one who has not been initiated possesses the entitlement to perform ancestral rites (*śrāddha*); this is demonstrated by the statement, "from the offering of the *svadhā*" (MDh 2.172). Moreover, for one who has completed his Vedic studies (*snāta*) but before marriage, there is an absence of the sacred fire in cases such as the death of a parent.
But is it not the case that the maintenance of the sacred fire upon the death of the father is taught in the *Kāṭhaka*?

This [observance] is to be observed by one who has taken a wife, not merely by a *snātaka* (one who has completed his Vedic studies). For two times are prescribed for the maintenance of the *smārta* fire: "The beginning with marriage (*bhāryādi*) or the beginning with inheritance (*dāyādi*)" (GDh 5.7). In that regard, for one by whom the fire was not maintained at the time of marriage—either because he remained undivided from his father or because he lived together with his elder brother according to the rule, "For brothers who are undivided, a single religious duty prevails" (NSm 13.37)—this is his second opportunity, as stated in the rule, "Or [at] the time of inheritance. This very "time of inheritance" occurs when the father dies; it is with reference to this that [the texts state]: "Having become pure, he should offer to the ancestors," and "Having brought the fire from the frying pan, he should maintain it. If the establishment of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) were not an integral part of the *śrāddha*, then its production would not occur prior to that, nor would the *śrāddha* take place. Furthermore, there is no abandonment [of the fire], for it is recited: "This is the *aupāsada* fire; in it, the *pākayajña* [is performed]. Nor is one who lacks a wife entitled to perform even a *pākayajña*. For in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "The clarified butter (*ājya*) is to be inspected by the wife," and "The wife should undertake the vow. It cannot be reasonably maintained that these acts—the undertaking of the vow and the inspection of the butter—will occur with the wife as the agent only when she is present, because they are enjoined as permanent (obligatory) duties. Thus, the injunction necessarily follows that the fire must be offered.
But is it not the case that the father's death alone is not the time for inheritance? For it is recited thus: "Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the sons should then divide [the estate].

This is the time for partition (*vibhāga*), not for the inheritance itself (*dāya*). Furthermore, there is no such restrictive rule even regarding partition, since it is recited: "Separation is lawful" (MDh 9.111). And its lawfulness consists in the fact that those who have been separated perform the *śrāddha* rites individually and honor guests and others separately.

Furthermore, sentences such as "nine [brothers] should give the bride-price together" do not pertain to one who has completed his studies. Rather, they refer to one who—having acquired some knowledge and fearing that he might transgress the restriction of being faithful to his own wife due to an excess of passion—marries and applies himself to the study of the Veda; for him, when his studies are completed in just one year, this is said: "Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, they should divide [the inheritance]. At that time, for one whose wife has died and who wishes to take another wife, there is an absence of the sacred fire until he obtains a wife. Since there is a scriptural statement that one must sacrifice with a wife in every respect, one who has not married does not undertake the maintenance of the sacred fires.

This being the case, in the absence of fire, one should cast the oblations into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa. Of which Brāhmaṇa? Into the hand of any one of those who have been invited—either of that one seated for the rite to the gods (*daiva*), or of another invited guest. This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*): "For he is indeed the fire," as is agreed upon by the seers of mantras and those who understand the meaning. (3.202)
"The ancients say that these best of the twice-born are gods at the *śrāddha*, free from anger, easily propitiated, and intent upon the nourishment of the world.

(3.203) This is indeed an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise); it establishes the divine nature of the Brahmins. Fire is a deity; when an offering is made therein, the deities eat through its mouth. A Brahmin is also of such a form; when food is placed even in his hand, the deities truly eat it as well.

Furthermore, what is the form of the deities by virtue of which even a Brahmin is said to have the form of a deity? To this he says: "those who are free from anger. How do they speak? He shows that for this purpose: oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) should be cast into the hands of those Brahmins who possess such a nature.

However, others say: previously, by the words "free from anger" and so forth, the qualities of being free from anger and so on were prescribed for the praiseworthy ones invited on behalf of the ancestors (pitṛs). By this [present verse], the distinction is made for those invited on behalf of the deities.

And so he says: "The gods at the *śrāddha*. The ancient sages speak thus. Or rather, the accusative case ending should be read [for *devān*]. These ancient gods, the *sādhyadevas*, who have arisen in this *kalpa* and are engaged in nourishing the world—thus they partake of the *śrāddha*. In this regard, one should not think: "Seeking visible pleasure, they act for their own sake out of greed; therefore, why is worship offered to them? Since they nourish the world—the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens—one must not treat them with contempt. (3.203)

Having performed the entire circumambulation around the fire in the *apasavya* manner, he should pour water upon the ground with his left hand (*apasavya*). (3.204) Regarding the action to be performed in the fire—namely, the rite characterized by the casting of oblations with the formula "To Agni, *svadhā*, obeisance"—that must be done in the *apasavya* manner. It should be performed with the right hand, not with the left, nor with both, because of the prohibition: "released from both hands" (MDh 3.215).
Some say that when there is a doubt as to whether the action should be performed with both hands joined, it is specified that it should be done with the *apasavya* (left) hand;

however, this is incorrect. What is prescribed here is the *apasavya* nature of the *āvṛt*—the circumambulation—that accompanies those oblations which are offered into the fire. One should perform the oblations ending toward the south, not ending toward the north, as is done in rites for the gods (*daiva*). Or rather, one should have the offerings made with a ladle facing south, not toward the north; instead, they should be performed facing south, just as water is poured in ancestral rites (*pitrya*) by means of the *tīrtha* sacred to the ancestors.

Because of the inclusion of the word "all," other acts such as serving food and so forth must also be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). One should pour out the water with the hand that is *apasavya*. Alternatively, there is a reading "slowly" (*śanaiḥ*); this is the meaning here. Otherwise, the rule regarding the left hand would be for the purpose of obtaining silver vessels, in accordance with the statement "with silver vessels" (MDh 3.192). *Āvṛt* means a turning around. 3.204.

Then, having formed three balls from that remainder of the sacrificial food, he should, with a concentrated mind, offer them facing south according to the very same rite prescribed for the water libation. (3.205)

Having formed three *piṇḍas* from that food which was taken in the vessel for the purpose of the *homa*—the remains of what was offered—one should offer them while facing the southern direction. One should cast them upon *darbha* grass, intending them for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). A solid mass of substance is denoted by the word *piṇḍa*; therefore, the food should not be given as loose grains. This is done with the "water-rite" (*audaka*), which is the procedure just mentioned beginning with "with the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*apasavyena*) and so forth (MDh 3.204).

In this regard, a doubt arises: should the preparation of the oblation (*havis*) be performed by taking a portion from that very food prepared for feeding the Brāhmaṇas, or should a separate *caru* be prepared? And what is the quantity of that oblation? For in this case, a measurement such as "four handfuls" and so forth is not possible.

This has been deliberated upon. Since no specific rule is heard, there is freedom of action. The quantity [of the offering] is that by which the purpose is accomplished. And because of the extension of the rules for water-offerings, the presentation of the *piṇḍas* is performed with one's own hand and in the counter-clockwise direction (*apasavya*), not with silver vessels. The inclusion of the word "concentrated" (*samāhita*) is for the sake of completing the meter. (3.205)

Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) there, being self-restrained and according to the prescribed rule, he should wipe that hand upon those Darbha grasses for the sake of those entitled to the scrapings (lepabhāginaḥ).

Having offered—that is, having given—those rice-balls upon the Darbha grasses, he should wipe that hand upon those very Darbha grasses upon which the offering of the rice-balls was performed; however, according to the observation of another Smṛti, the wiping is to be done at the roots of the Darbha grasses.

Furthermore, others maintain that there is no wiping of food or water adhering to the hand onto the *darbha* grasses. Even if nothing at all were adhering to the hand, one should nevertheless wipe the hand on the *darbha* grasses. For this is not merely a ritual act of disposal (*pratipatti-karman*), such that it would not be performed in the absence of a specific scriptural injunction. Here, it is not heard that "one should wipe what is adhering to the hand," but rather simply "the hand."

But is it not heard in the scripture: "for those who partake of the smearings"? Since there would be no smearings in that case, [the rite] would not apply. Therefore, why is it said: "Even if nothing at all adheres to the hand, it must still be performed"?

It is replied: tangible food itself may sometimes not adhere; however, while the rice balls (*piṇḍas*) are being rolled, the essence of the food transfers to the hand due to contact with heat. That very thing is called the "smearing."

The genitive case in the phrase "of those entitled to the smearings" (*lepabhāginām*) expresses the relationship of the act of smearing to them. Furthermore, there are no "smearers" who are perceptibly visible, to whom a relationship such as that of owner and owned could be attributed regarding the smearings. Therefore, one should either meditate in the mind, "May this portion belong to those entitled to the smearings," or designate them by means of words.

Others, however, say that those ancestors prior to the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) are the ones entitled to the smearings. According to this view, when their individual names are not known, the designation should be made using such expressions as "to the father of the great-grandfather" (*prapitāmahapitre*), "to the grandfather of the great-grandfather" (*prapitāmahapitāmahāya*), and so forth.

By the use of the singular number in the word *hastaṃ* ("with the hand"), he indicates that the offering of the *piṇḍas* is to be performed with one hand, specifically the right hand (*apasavya*). The term *prayataḥ* ("purified") is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since [the state of being purified] has already been enjoined. By the phrase *vidhipūrvakam* ("according to the prescribed rule"), he incorporates the rule observed in other scriptures (*śāstra*). Śaṅkha states: "One should offer the *piṇḍa* with perfumes, garlands, incense, clothing, and prepared offerings. If the rule heard here were stated solely according to his own opinion, then the expression *vidhipūrvakam* would be redundant. Therefore, the statement *vidhipūrvakam* is intended to include the rules from other scriptures. (3.206)
Having sipped water, turned away from the water, and slowly restrained his breath three times, he should pay homage with mantras to the six seasons and to the ancestors. [3.207] V3.217

Having offered the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) upon *darbha* grass, he should turn toward the northern direction by way of the left (*savyāvṛt*). For in another Smṛti it is read: "Turning to the north, having turned back by way of the left. Standing facing north, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Having sipped water, he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*). This means restraining and completely holding back the vital breaths (*asūn prāṇān*). And in this context, the rule beginning with "the *Gāyatrī* together with its head" (YDh 1.23) does not apply. [He should do so] slowly, so that there is no excessive distress. Thus it is said: "Having held the breaths according to the instruction," he should offer salutation once while facing that very direction, saying "Salutation to Spring," and so forth. He should also offer salutation to the ancestors with the mantra, "Salutation to you, O ancestors," and so on. The salutation to the ancestors must be performed facing the rice-balls. For another Smṛti states: "By turning around in succession. (3.207)
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the rice balls;
then, with a concentrated mind, he should smell those rice balls in the order they were placed. (3.208)

From the very same vessel from which the water was poured onto the *darbha* grass prior to the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*), one must pour water again near the rice balls, that is, in their vicinity. The mention of the word “remainder” (*śeṣa*) is for the purpose of disposing of that water; thus, the use of the word “remainder” is appropriate. Consequently, if by some chance that [water] is absent, there is no further pouring. However, in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, it is stated: “The pouring is obligatory. And one should smell those rice balls. Smelling (*avaghrāṇa*) is the perception of fragrance. In the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, however, it is stated: “One should consume the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) as a breath-sacrifice (*prāṇabhakṣa*”). “In the order they were offered,” meaning in the sequence they were set out: for the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather. The word “concentrated” (*samāhita*) is for the purpose of completing the verse. (3.208)

Having taken very small portions from the *piṇḍas* in due order, he should first cause those same Brahmins who are seated to eat according to the rule. (3.209) The term *atyantālpikā* means a minute portion or part. That Brahmin who has been seated for the sake of the father—him alone one should cause to eat a certain amount from that [father’s] *piṇḍa*. The phrase *anupūrvaśaḥ* has already been explained. Here, because the word *tat* refers back to what is under discussion, there is no mention of the subject in the expression *agnyabhāve* (in the absence of fire). *Pūrvam* means before any other food. (3.209)
While his father is still living, he should perform the offering for his ancestors alone;
or else, like a *vipra*, he should cause his own father to partake in that *śrāddha*. (3.210) V3.220

It has been stated: "One should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Who, then, are these so-called ancestors? For the word *pitṛ* has multiple meanings; it refers to a progenitor. It is observed as a relative term meaning "one who begets" (*janaka*). Furthermore, those previously deceased, such as fathers and others, as well as other deceased relatives, are called ancestors. Thus, the mantras beginning with "Homage to you, O ancestors" (*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*), which end in the plural number, are appropriate as recitations (*nigada*). For this very reason, they are not modified in a Śrāddha for women. One does not perform [the modification] by saying, "Homage to you, O mother," or "Homage to you, O grandmother," and so forth. Therefore, in the *ekoddiṣṭa* (rite for a single individual), a modification of the number is made, but not a modification of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). And so says the author of the Sūtra: "One should modify the mantras into the singular," and so on. Thus, the modification is made as "Homage to you, O father" (*namas te pitar*). When one performs the *ekoddiṣṭa* for a brother, a grandfather, or others, he modifies it thus: "Homage to you, O brother," "Homage to you, O grandfather," "Homage to you, O paternal uncle," and so forth. The performance of Śrāddha for paternal uncles and others who are childless is prescribed: "Whoever receives from someone, he should give to him. There is also the word *pitṛ* used to denote specific deities, referring to the eternally immutable state. For the authors of the *Nirukta* enumerate the Pitṛs among the middle deities: "The Maruts, wearing Rudrākṣa beads, are the Pitṛs."

Thus, since the word *pitṛ* has multiple meanings, he speaks in order to specify the particular sense: while the father is still living—that is, while the father exists—one should offer [the oblation] to the ancestors, namely the grandfather, the great-grandfather, and that father’s father; it is for three, as indicated by the use of the plural number. And so it is stated in the Gṛhyasūtra: "To those whom the father gives, the son should give; if both father and son are maintainers of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
