Now, it is said: "The funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) does not go to a fourth. True; in this case, no fourth cake is offered at all.

He states another alternative: "Or like the Brāhmaṇas. Just as Brāhmaṇas who are celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and observant of vows are honored after being invited, in the same way, a father should be fed by one whose father is still living. *Śrāddha* refers to the food intended for the *śrāddha* rite. And in this case, the status of being a father alone is the criterion for being fed; neither caste nor specific qualities need be considered. For thus they say: "The *śrāddha* is for the sake of pleasing the father. Since it is the deceased who must be pleased, what disrespect could there be toward a living father that one would not feed him?
"One's own" is a restatement (anuvāda), since it is already established by the very fact that [the term] is a relative word.

In this context, eating is prescribed for the father as being beneficial; however, there is a contradiction regarding the offering of the *piṇḍas* (rice balls) on *darbha* grass, as it is said, "this must be done for the ancestors. For if the *darbhas* were in the place of the vessels [for the ancestors], then it would not be logical to feed even a small portion while the father is still living and thus possesses ownership over the gift, since that which belongs to one who is alive may be employed according to his own will. Furthermore, the application of collyrium and other items to that *piṇḍa* is not appropriate, as it would lead to the fallacy of the "half-old woman" principle (*ardhajaratīya*). Indeed, there is no purpose for the father here in being consecrated with collyrium and such. Therefore, the giving of collyrium and so forth is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). However, a *piṇḍa* devoid of collyrium and the like might sometimes be fit for the eating of oneself, one's father, or another; thus, it would be half-old. Consequently, under this view, the offering of the *piṇḍas* is for the two ancestors, the grandfather and the great-grandfather. But the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* record: "For one whose father is living, there is neither the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* nor the *Śrāddha*; rather, there is simply the non-commencement of that rite, or its conclusion at the *Homa*. (3.210)

But he whose father is deceased while his grandfather is still living should, having pronounced the name of his father, pronounce the name of his great-grandfather. (3.211) By the mention of the father’s name, his invitation (*āvāhana*), the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), and the feeding of the Brahmins are indicated. He should pronounce the name of the great-grandfather. He should not offer [the oblation] to the living grandfather; rather, they record in the Smṛti that one should present it to those prior to him, according to the rule: “One should offer to the ancestors of the father” (*pituḥ pitṛbhyo nipṛṇīyāt*). (3.211)
"Or the grandfather may eat that *śrāddha*," so Manu has declared;

"or, being duly authorized, he may perform it himself at will. (3.212) Just as [the offering] is eaten by one whose father is living, so too is it for the grandfather. Having obtained permission from the grandfather, he may perform it himself. Beyond those two, he should give to the great-grandfather, or to only one. This is the meaning of the two phrases "at will" and "himself. (3.212)
Having placed the water with sesame seeds and the *pavitra* grass into their hands, he should offer them the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for these. (3.213)

Regarding what was stated, “He should cause [the recipient] to eat a very small portion from the balls” (MDh 3.209), this is the rule for the time and the place for that act. A portion of the ball is to be taken from its front part. Having offered *darbha* grass and water with sesame seeds, he should thereafter present a portion of the ball while saying, “May there be *svadhā* for them. By the pronoun “for them” (*eṣām*), the specific names are intended. The connection is made thus: having uttered whichever names belong to those [ancestors], he should say, “May there be *svadhā*. Therefore, when joined with the word *svadhā*, the name must be indicated in the dative case: “May there be *svadhā* for Devadatta,” “May there be *svadhā* for Yajñadatta. In this interpretation, there is no contradiction with other scriptures. (3.213)

Having personally taken hold of the vessel filled with food with both hands, while meditating upon the ancestors in the presence of the Brahmins, he should slowly set it down near them. (3.214) Having himself grasped with both hands the *vardhita*—the vessel full of food—from the kitchen or similar place, he should set it down in that location where the Brahmins are being fed; he should place it in the vicinity of the Brahmins.

Others, however, explain that "increased" refers to food that has been rounded up; one should place it near the Brahmins while meditating on the ancestors, thinking "this is for you," just like the scattered offerings (*vikiro*). That is incorrect, because the author will later state, "Having brought everything, he should serve it" (MDh 3.218). Therefore, this is the placing of the food after it has been brought from another location for the purpose of serving. 3.214.

The Asuras, who are evil-minded, suddenly snatch away that food which is being brought while released from both hands. (3.215) Food should be brought and served with both hands, and not with one alone. "Bringing" (*upanayana*) is indeed the same as "serving" (*pariveṣaṇa*). Therefore, in that case as well, this very rule previously stated applies. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding it.

When food is brought for the purpose of serving that has been released—that is, set down—by both hands, being unheld and not grasped, the Asuras, who are evil-minded and wicked-natured enemies of the gods, suddenly and by force plunder it, that is, destroy it. The word "ubhābhyām" (by both) is used in the locative case to indicate the locus of the action; "muktam" means released, not drawn back, and not held. And indeed, case endings denoting the factors of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*) occur even in proximity to a negation: e.g., "he does not come from the village," "he does not sit on the seat," or "he does not fast for three nights. (3.215)

With a restrained mind and full concentration, he should first place upon the ground itself the various side dishes—such as soups and vegetables—as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey. (3.216) "Side dishes" (*guṇa*) refers to condiments. The subsequent detailed explanation is for the purpose of illustrating these very items. He should place the soups, vegetables, and so forth directly on the ground; he should not set them down on wooden vessels, platters, or similar objects. (3.215)

Various kinds of solid food (*bhakṣya*) and soft food (*bhojya*), as well as roots and fruits, savory meats, and fragrant drinks; [3.217] parched grains, cakes, and the like are *bhakṣya*; for that which is to be swallowed and is hard and distinct is called *bhakṣya*, while *bhojya* refers to items such as *ghṛtapūra* (butter-filled cakes). [3.217] V3.227.
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great composure, being self-restrained and extolling all its qualities. (3.218)

Having brought [the food] near and having presented all of this in the presence of the Brahmins, he should then serve it. "Bringing near" (*āvarjanam*) refers to taking hold of the vessel for eating. Although serving while they are eating requires being in close proximity, nevertheless, it should be placed near them so that it does not come into contact with the leftovers of those who are eating. "Proclaiming the qualities" means pointing out the qualities of the substances to be eaten or consumed, such as their sourness and so forth—informing them by saying, "This is sour," "This is sweet," "This is sugary"—and then giving whatever they prefer; this is the connection with what follows. The phrase beginning with "gently" (*śanakair*) is a restatement for the purpose of completing the verse. (3.218)
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it. (3.219)

*Asram* means tears or weeping; one should not shed them, nor should one perform it. Generally, the shedding of tears occurs during funeral rites (*preta-śrāddha*) and the like due to the recollection of suffering born from separation from what is beloved; this is prohibited. However, there is no fault in the spontaneous shedding of tears of joy. One should never, at any time, release tears. One should not become angry—that is, one should not harbor wrath. This prohibition regarding untruthful speech—which is already forbidden for the sake of human conduct—is here stated specifically for the purpose of the ritual act. One should not touch food with the foot, whether it be the remains of a meal (*ucchiṣṭa*) or not. Nor should one shake or cause this food to tremble; having lifted it with the hand or other means, one should not toss it about again.
Others, however, explain: that shaking which is performed with a cloth for the purpose of removing dust and the like should not be done over food. 3.219.
Tears cause the *preta*s to go away; anger, the enemies; falsehood, the dogs;
the touch of one's feet, the *rakṣas*es; and shaking [the head], the evildoers. (3.220)

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). The shedding of tears causes the *śrāddha* to go to, that is, reach, the *pretas*; it does not benefit the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Here, the term *preta* refers to a specific class of beings similar to *piśācas*, and not to those who have recently died before their *sapindīkaraṇa* rite has been performed. *Rākṣasas* are to be understood as being like *bhūtas* and *pretas*. *Aris* (enemies) are well known. Likewise, *duṣkṛtins* are those who have committed evil deeds, the perpetrators of sins. (3.220)
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without avarice; and he should engage in discourses on the Vedas, for this is what is desired by the ancestors. (3.221)

Whatever food, condiment, or drink they may desire, one should give that very thing without stinginess—that is, without greed; for *matsara* is a name for greed. It should be pleasing, meaning it should generate delight. *Brahmodyāḥ*: those which are uttered or spoken regarding the *brahman*, namely the Veda—such as the battle between the gods and the asuras, the slaying of Vṛtra, the deeds of Saramā, and so forth; or alternatively, such passages as "Who indeed wanders alone? (VS 23.9). Or there is the reading "and stories concerning Brahmā and others," referring to discourses and conversations in worldly language that determine the meaning of the principal mantras and so on. This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) stating that this is what is desired and longed for by the ancestors. 3.221.

At a rite for the ancestors (pitrya), one should indeed cause [the officiant] to recite his own Vedic study (svādhyāya), as well as the treatises on Dharma (dharmaśāstra), narratives (ākhyāna), histories (itihāsa), Purāṇas, and supplementary texts (khila).

[Note: *Svādhyāya* refers to the Veda. The *Dharmaśāstras* are the works of Manu and others. *Ākhyānas* are those such as the Sauparṇa and Maitrāvaruṇa which are recited in the Ṛgveda; *itihāsas* are the Mahābhārata and similar works; *Purāṇas* are those composed by Vyāsa and others, consisting of descriptions of creation and so forth; and *khilas* are the Śrīsūkta, Mahānāmnikā, and other such texts.
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and praise for their virtues. (3.223)

Even when there is a cause for distress, one should not manifest one's own suffering in any way, such as by long sighs and the like; rather, one should appear as if joyful. One should gladden the brahmins with song and so forth prompted by others, or with harmless, contextually appropriate jesting. If someone becomes weary while the *svādhyāya* is being recited, then one should desist from that and delight them with narratives, song, and the like. One should feed them slowly. Taking a few morsels, one should feed them with pleasant words such as, "This is excellent," or "This is a perfect meal. One should speak slowly and not with agitation. With food and drink, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and various flavorful side dishes prepared for the purpose of giving, one should encourage them to eat by emphasizing their deliciousness. Standing before them, one should repeatedly say things such as, "These cakes are savory," or "This milk-pudding is delicious," while holding the items in one's hand even though they are already placed in the bowl. This is the method of encouragement. (3.223)
One should carefully feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.

In the case of a secondary option (*anukalpa*), it is stated with effort that the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) is to be fed. A *kutapa* is a cloth in the form of a blanket made from goat-hair thread; it is well known as a *kambala* among those in the North. One should give that as a seat. This does not apply only in the case of the daughter’s son, but rather at other times as well, because he will later state: “Three things are purifiers at a *śrāddha*” (MDh 3.225), since this refers to the *śrāddha* in general. And one should scatter sesame seeds upon the earth; that is, one should cast sesame seeds upon the ground. (3.224)
Three things are purifying at a *śrāddha*: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds.

And in this regard, they praise three other qualities: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste. (3.225) The term *pavitrāṇi* means purifying, that is, effecting goodness. The first half-verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while the latter half contains the injunction (*vidheya*). "Purity" (*śauca*) consists in avoiding contact with impure things; or, it is the cleansing according to the scriptures by means of earth, water, and so forth, of any impurity that has arisen through negligence. "Lack of haste" (*atvarā*) is the performance of eating and other rites with confidence and composure. (3.225)
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent.
And the twice-born should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering when asked by the giver.

(3.226) The term *uṣṇam eva atyuṣṇam* means "extremely hot," having passed beyond mere heat, just as *praparṇa* means "one from which the leaves have fallen. This applies to all food and its qualities. This injunction regarding heat pertains only to that food for which eating hot is appropriate; it does not apply to curd-rice (*dadhyodana*) and the like, which would become unpleasant or cause disease if eaten hot. In such cases, it would contradict the rule: "He should gladden the Brahmins" (MDh 3.223).

Furthermore, because of the rule regarding the serving of warm food, not all the rice should be served at once; for in that way, the food would become cold for those who eat much. Therefore, one should give more after they have eaten. Nor should it be said that giving while they are eating is improper because it constitutes the offering of leftovers; such is indeed the nature of the ritual of feeding. The duty of the host lasts until the guest is satisfied. For in this context, the rice and other foods are not connected as objects to be received [in a formal gift]; for this very reason, the mantra for receiving a gift (*pratigraha-mantra*) is not employed there in relation to the rice and other items.

*vāgyatāḥ* means those by whom speech (*vāk*) is *yatā*, i.e., restrained; the reversal of the word order is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, it is a compound formed with an instrumental (*sādhana*) and a past passive participle (*kṛt*), meaning "restrained by speech. In this case, the word *yata* expresses the agent; restraint (*niyamanam*) is the prohibition of activity, and the activity of speech is the utterance of sounds. Thus, a prohibition is made against that: one must not utter distinct or indistinct sounds, nor should the qualities of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) be mentioned. As they record in the traditional law (*smṛti*): "When [the guests] are eating with their loved ones and virtuous companions, there is no desire to speak on the part of the giver. But is this not already established simply by the restraint of speech?

True. It should not be performed even by means of gestures and the like. The root *brū* functions in the sense of "communicating"; thus, "they should speak" (*brūyuḥ*) does not refer merely to the utterance of sounds. (3.226)

As long as there is steam from the food, as long as they eat while restrained in speech, for so long do the ancestors eat—until the qualities of the sacrificial offering have been described. (3.227) This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning the preceding injunction. "Steam" (*uṣmā*) means heat (*auṣṇya*). (3.227)
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats while wearing shoes—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.228)

"Enveloped" means by a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) and so forth; for in the north, they wrap the head with pieces of cloth. As for those who explain it thus: "He has his head enveloped even by hair arranged in the form of a topknot (*cūḍā*)," they do not speak according to reason. It is the hair that is being wrapped, not the head; and the hair itself is not the head, for it resides upon the head. However, there is no prohibition regarding thread and the like, for in common worldly usage, the term "enveloping" is not applied to them.

Because of the mention of a fault regarding one facing south, he permits eating even while facing a direction other than the south in a small space; otherwise, since facing north is prescribed [for others], how could facing south ever be obtained? [409] *Upānahau* refers to leather footwear for protecting the feet. Others, however, explain that *upānahau* refers to leather sandals. The statement "the Rākṣasas eat them, not the ancestors" is a censure. 3.228.
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog, a woman in her menses, and a eunuch—these must not look at twice-born men while they are eating. (3.229)

The *varāha* is the boar (*śūkara*), and that is the domestic variety. Although it is heard in the scripture that "they should not look [at the food] because of the proximity of a dog," nevertheless, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) do not approve of even its mere proximity to that place. And thus, another action is heard as a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*): "The boar [is defiled] by smelling" (MDh 3.231), and so forth. For one who is not looking, smelling is not possible; however, this is a restatement of the nature of things for those who are in close proximity: "the boar sniffs," "the cock flaps its wings. "Therefore, one should give [the food] in an enclosed space" (GDh 15.25) is the injunction. The purpose of this is that in the absence of such defects, one may give it even in an unenclosed space. A *ṣaṇḍha* is a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*). (3.229)
Whatever is looked upon by these [outcastes] at the giving of a house, at a meal, or at an offering to the gods or the ancestors, that goes to ruin. (3.230)

In the domestic *agnihotra* and other rites, or in oblations for pacification (*śānti*) and the like; in giving, that is, regarding gifts such as cows, gold, and other materials; for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*); in feeding, where Brahmins are fed for the sake of dharma; in the sacrificial offering (*havis*) to the gods, such as the *darśa* and *paurṇamāsa* sacrifices; and in the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), the *śrāddha*: whatever action is performed while being looked upon [by such a person], that goes astray from its proper nature. It brings about the opposite of that for which it was intended. Although this occurs within the context of the *śrāddha*, nevertheless, by virtue of the statement, this prohibition applies elsewhere as well, such as in the *homa* and other rites. (3.230)

The pig destroys [the merit] by its smell; the cock, by the wind from its wings; the dog, by the casting of its gaze; and one born of the lowest caste, by touch. (3.231) The cock destroys [the merit] by the wind produced by its wings; this has already been explained. Their presence must be excluded from such a distance as far as they can see while standing there. And "one born of the lowest caste" refers to the *caṇḍāla*, because that is his natural state.

It has already been explained that *sparśa* (touching) and the other terms refer to the specific actions under discussion, rather than their literal etymological forms. Therefore, this objection is not tenable: "Since there is a general prohibition against touching a *caṇḍāla*, and thus no possibility [of such contact] arising, the prohibition would be redundant. Consequently, the term *śūdra* refers to one born of a lower caste (*avaravarṇaja*), and the prohibition against touching him applies only during a *dvija*'s *śrāddha* rite, not in ordinary circumstances."

Even though this is the intended meaning, it is not this defect of contact with food, drink, and so forth that is being stated; rather, it is the contact with a location such as a riverbank that has been appropriated but is not enclosed. For the purification of such a place by means of wind, the sun, and so forth has been taught. Therefore, since the possibility of contact exists, the prohibition is appropriate. (3.231)

Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the donor; or if he has missing or extra limbs—one should remove him as well from that place. (3.232) "Servant" (*preṣya*) means a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*). By the word "even" (*api*), others as well—such as relatives who have arrived by chance—are to be removed; one should have them moved away from that location. "Lame" (*khañja*) means impaired in movement, such as those unable to walk. "One with missing or extra limbs" refers to eunuchs, those with deformed hands or feet, those suffering from elephantiasis, and so forth. (3.232)
When a Brāhmaṇa or even a mendicant has arrived for the purpose of food, he should, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, honor him according to his ability.

(3.233) A Brāhmaṇa who has come as a guest (*atithi*), or a mendicant (*bhikṣuka*) who seeks alms—even a Brāhmaṇa—he should honor according to his capacity, having been authorized by the Brāhmaṇas engaged in the meal. He should worship him appropriately with food or the giving of alms; for that day’s cooking is intended solely for that purpose. (3.233)
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have eaten.

The word *varṇa* should be understood here in the sense of "kind. Having brought together food of every kind accompanied by condiments, having combined it and moistened it with water, one should cast it forth—that is, scatter it—before those who have eaten and are satiated, immediately after they have said, "We are satiated. Not in a single spot, but rather scattered; not on the ground, but on the vessels. Even on the ground, it is not on clean ground, for he will later state: "The scattering [of food] is upon *darbha* grass" (MDh 3.235). Śaṅkha says: "One should perform the scattering once or thrice. (3.234)

The remnants of food and whatever scattering of grains (*vikiro*) is upon the *darbha* grass shall be the allotted portion for those who have died an unconditioned death and for women of noble family who have renounced the world. (3.235)

"[418] 'No fire-ritual (agnisaṃskāra) is to be performed for him'—this refers to those who have died before three years [of age] and have not been consecrated. The remnants of food remaining in the vessels and the scattering of food upon the *darbha* grass constitute their share (*bhāgadheya*). By the word *bhāgadheya*, only a 'share' is meant; for indeed, there is no benefit from the *śrāddha* for them. This refers to those who abandon teachers and others, or alternatively, to those who abandon women of the family—that is, wives of the family who have no visible fault. However, in the independent reading where it says 'women of the family' (*kulayoṣitām*), they explain that 'women of the family' refers to unmarried maidens. Therefore, the remnants of food should be assigned to them."

Nor should it be said, "How can that which is impure and remains from eating (ucchiṣṭa) be fit as a sacrificial portion? For by virtue of the scriptural injunction, there is no impurity, just as in the case of the remains of Soma. 3.235.
They declare that the food remaining on the ground after a meal is the portion for the group of servants who are upright and free from deceit;

this is the share they receive at a rite for the ancestors (pitr-śrāddha). The previous verse [3.235] described the disposal of what remains in the vessel; this verse states that the leavings which have fallen upon the ground are intended for the group of servants. "Upright" (ajihma) means not crooked; "free from deceit" (aśaṭha) means not lazy. Such is the share for that group of servants. Therefore, one should give an abundance so that some falls upon the ground as he eats.
Until the rite of sapindikarana for a deceased member of the twice-born caste has been performed, one should offer a śrāddha meal without an offering to the gods and present a single pinda. (3.237)

For a twice-born person who has passed away, the rite known as *sahapiṇḍakaraṇa* (the offering of the joint rice-ball) must be performed for one who died first, until that act is completed. The offering of the rice-ball together with the two previous ones must not be performed. How, then, should it be done? "And he should offer one rice-ball"—here the word *ca* (and) has the sense of *eva* (only/exclusively); therefore, he should offer one rice-ball to that deceased person alone. For a Brāhmaṇa guest should be fed for that very purpose.

In another Smṛti, a further specific procedure is recorded: "It is devoid of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa*" (YDh 1.251). By the term *agnaukaraṇa* here, the request for permission—namely, "I shall perform the offering in the fire"—is prohibited, but not the *homa* itself. For indeed, in the Gṛhya-sūtras, the *homa* is prescribed specifically with reference to the *preta-śrāddha*.

Regarding the time at which the rite should be performed and for how long, that must be sought from other Smṛtis: "The first [śrāddha] is on the eleventh day; it should also be performed on the anniversary of death, and every month for a year."
"And every year, the annual Śrāddha should indeed be performed, having the same purpose as the monthly ones. (YDh 1.256)

And so it is stated in the *Kaṭhaka*: "In this manner, [the rite] is performed annually. The mention of the eleventh day is intended as an indication for the cessation of impurity (*āśauca*), since it is heard in scripture: "Having become pure, one should offer to the ancestors. For the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* record that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony takes place at the end of the year. And this *śrāddha* is the *ekoddiṣṭa* type, and the offering (*nirvapaṇa*) is an ancillary part of it. As for the statement in the *Śrauta* tradition, "one should offer to the ancestors," which implies giving to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not yet been performed, such an offering here would not be appropriate; for a *smṛti* rule cannot override a *śruti* injunction. (3.237)
But once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the Dharma, the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by means of this very same procedure. (3.238)

But when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, then by this very procedure (*āvṛt*), according to the rules for the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, one should offer [the oblation] to three [ancestors]. *Āvṛt* refers to the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*). [424] One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha* beginning with the deities (*daivapūrva*); one should feed the ancestors (*pitṛn*) alone. [425] Here, however, one should not designate the deceased (*preta*). [426] And here, "the ancestors" refers to the grandfathers and others who, having been previously made *sapiṇḍa* and introduced into the group of ancestors, are now so called; one should feed them. In that case, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates that the deceased (*preta*) is to be invoked among those very same Brahmins, for his integration (*saṃsarga*) with all of them occurs there; that rite is for the purpose of effecting that integration.

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "One should feed Brāhmaṇas for the deceased, for the father of the deceased, for the grandfather of the deceased, and for the great-grandfather of the deceased" (ViDh 21.12), even here it is not heard [in the text] that one should feed them separately. In that regard, just as an oblation intended for many deities is offered once and as a single unit directed toward those many deities, so too a Brāhmaṇa may be fed while directed toward many [ancestors]; thus, nothing is illogical. For in this way, the scriptural statement [of Viṣṇu] is upheld, and in the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), an even number of Brāhmaṇas are not fed. This is to be understood in the same manner as the rule of those who hold: "One for each [side], or one for both" (MDh 3.115); according to their view, a single person is fed for the sake of all [the ancestors]. It should be viewed in this light.

But if this were the case, would it not follow from the rule "three for the ancestral rites" (MDh 3.115) that there is a collective reference to all the gods? In that instance, all [the gods] would be intended for each individual Brahmin, and even there, no separate mention is made.

How is it that [the vessel] does not exist? For it is recited in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "But certainly not one for all; this is explained by the *piṇḍas*" (*ĀśG* 4.7.4, 6). Furthermore, it says: "One should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*) for the sake of the *argha* offering" (cf. *YDh* 1.253). In that case, in the absence of the vessels prepared for the *āsanna* [ancestors], from which vessel would the water from the *preta*-vessel be poured for the *argha*? If it were from the combined [vessels], that is incorrect; for that [water] was prepared for the grandfather and others, not for the father. Nor is it logical for something intended for one purpose to be used for another purpose. If, on the other hand, one were to perform the pouring together (*saṃnayana*) after having already performed the *argha* offering, then the statement—"having performed the *argha*, one should pour [the water] for the sake of that [pouring] into the independent *argha*"—would be contradicted. By the method stated here, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Now, who is this one called a *preta*? It is because after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, no funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is offered to the great-grandfather, since [the deceased] has entered into those very ancestors. And so says the *Smṛti*: "He who joins a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed with a separate funeral cake becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is born as a slayer of his father."

For indeed, [the inheritance] is determined for him as distinct [from the others], and not as one [share] common to all; and the mantras express this very meaning, beginning with "Those who are equal" (MD 3.11.10).

To this it is replied: This word *preta* does not function through its connection with the verbal root √*i* ("to go"). This is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) meaning "the dead," as in "the deceased is now a *preta*. For one who has merely traveled a long distance is not called a *preta*. Furthermore, there is a connection with the action [of going] both generally for those previously deceased and for those recently deceased. Thus, the Śruti says: "Those who depart from this world [are] equal," which shows the use of the term *preta* regarding one whose death has not been long. Also: "Food for the *preta* for three days," referring to one who has just passed away. As for the statement "with a separate *piṇḍa*," this is its meaning: after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* should not be performed. Whenever a *śrāddha* is to be performed, it must then be performed for the three ancestors, specifically for the three ancestors on the anniversary of death, and not for the father alone. Likewise, by the phrase "it should be done according to this very procedure," the performance of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* is extended by analogy.

But surely, by the phrase "by this very [rite]," there is understood a reference to the subject under discussion, because pronouns denote what is proximate, and it is the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* that is proximate.

It is not so. For if, even after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the rite were to be performed for only one [ancestor], then the very mention of a distinction would be untenable. Furthermore, the word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction within the procedure under discussion: "This rule applies to the rite where there is no *sapiṇḍana*; however, once the *sapiṇḍana* rite has been performed, this [rule] is not to be considered applicable. Therefore, although it is separated [in the text], the *pārvaṇa* nature is extended by virtue of being present in the mind. Moreover, if the *ekoddiṣṭa* were to be performed when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, then what difference would there be between the rule "giving to three" and the rule "on the new moon day"? Would there not be the same meaning there as well—namely, that it refers to the rite where there is *sapiṇḍana*? Nor is another time-period recognized in the *Mānava-śāstra*, such as "every year on the anniversary of death," etc., by which this [text] could be explained as referring specifically to that. Consequently, due to the lack of distinction, *ekoddiṣṭa* rites would result everywhere. In that case, the statement from the *Mahābhārata* would be contradicted; for, concerning sacred bathing places (*tīrthas*), it is said: "He indeed formerly gratified his ancestors with the *śrāddha*."

As for another Smṛti text stating, "And every year, the *śrāddha* should indeed be performed like the monthly one" (YDh 1.256), even there, by the word "monthly" (*māsika*), the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) alone is intended, because that serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all *śrāddhas*; for it is in that [new moon *śrāddha*] that the specific ritual rules (*dharma*) are prescribed. It is not appropriate to designate the [annual *śrāddha*] mentioned in the verse "But every month for a year" by the term "monthly," for no specific rules are prescribed for it that would distinguish it [from other types]. Furthermore, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is found here as well—performed on the eleventh day for the first [anniversary], or on the thirteenth for a Kṣatriya, and so forth. Therefore, it is not appropriate to designate the *ekoddiṣṭa* by the term "monthly. Indeed, it is called "monthly" due to its connection with the time of a month; however, it does not have a connection with the month alone, as its connection with other times has also been shown. Since it may be performed after a month [of impurity] according to the rule "Having become pure, one should offer to the ancestors," yet it is not performed during the month itself, it cannot be designated by the term "monthly" here. On the other hand, since the new moon day is the point of origin [for the rite], and because the term "monthly" is heard in the context of the full moon rite (*paurṇamāsika*), and because the "monthly *śrāddha* of the rice-balls" is a fixed requirement, and because there is an absence of connection with other times and because it possesses specific ritual properties (*dharma*), the extension of those properties to it is appropriate.

The *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with uncooked food) also has the *pārvaṇa* as its archetype. Since it follows that archetype, although the offering to three ancestors would normally apply, the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* (rite for a single ancestor) is prescribed. Furthermore, there is this statement of Yājñavalkya:
"On the anniversary of death, however, [the śrāddha] should be performed every month for a year;
likewise annually, and the first [annual rite] on the eleventh day. (YDh 1.256)

In that case as well, such a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is prescribed. For there too, it is understood that the *Amāvāsya* [Śrāddha] alone is the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, even when the Ekoddiṣṭa is connected with the time of a month, it is not logical to extend its specific properties (*dharmātideśa*) elsewhere. Indeed, one beggar does not beg from another beggar; for that [Ekoddiṣṭa] is itself a modification (*vikāra*) of that [Amāvāsya].

Furthermore, there is only one *śrāddha*. Therefore, there is no evidence that the general term *māsika* refers specifically to the *ekoddiṣṭa*. The same applies to Yājñavalkya. If there were an immediate reference [to the preceding], then an extension (*atideśa*) of the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* would result; for this is heard immediately after that: having recited "This is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*" (YDh 1.254) and "Prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*" (YDh 1.255), what follows immediately thereafter is stated as "On the day of death," etc. (YDh 2.256).

Therefore, disregarding mere proximity, the reference is made to the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsya*) alone as being characterized by its specific ritual properties (*dharmavat*). Furthermore, the mantras clearly illuminate our position: "Be united with your former ancestors," where those who exist together with the former ancestors are addressed. The plural form in "be united" (*saṃsṛjyadhvam*) is used for honor. Thus says the author of the *Nirukta* regarding [the verse] "These very dawns" (*etā u tyā uṣasaḥ*, RV 1.92.1): "The phrase 'these very dawns' uses the plural for the sake of honoring that which is singular."

Now, those balls (*piṇḍa*) into which [the portion] is placed with the words "Be united" (*saṃsṛjyadhvam*) are being referred to; and that which is being placed [therein] is, as before, designated by the plural "with the ancestors" (*pūrvebhiḥ pitṛbhiḥ*). In this way, the plural "with the ancestors" will be used according to its proper application (*prāyogika*). Otherwise, if the plural were assumed to refer to the balls being placed there in the phrase "Be united," it would have to be considered figurative (*ayathārtha*) in both instances.

This too is of no consequence, because each individual *piṇḍa* is joined with a portion of the [original] *piṇḍa*. For it is said: "Having set aside the fourth *piṇḍa*, one should divide it into three parts and place them upon the *piṇḍas*. Therefore, there is no simultaneous expression of multiple substrates here by which a plural form could be justified. Since each is designated individually, how can the plural form in the word *saṃsṛjyadhvam* ("be joined")—which implies a collective connection—be understood as expressing something remote? Furthermore, since the word *pūrvaiḥ* ("by the former ones") refers to the *piṇḍas* being deposited, the designation *ebhiḥ* ("by these ones") would not be appropriate.

Furthermore, this mantra is not injunctive (vidhāyaka), such that we would strive to determine its meaning [as a prescription]. It is merely expressive (abhidhāyaka). And it expresses the quality [of the person] through its application (viniyoga). Application, moreover, is association, and it reveals that [association]. Here, the number is neither applied nor revealed; it is connected only by way of possibility. And its cognition occurs prior to [the cognition of] the mantra. As for those who say: "The word 'fourth' (caturtha) is more appropriately applicable as 'prior' (pūrva); for the father is first, and in relation to him, the great-grandfather is the fourth as being prior."

This also is not correct. Having set aside four previous *piṇḍas*, the fourth—which is full—is indeed the *piṇḍa* for the deceased (*preta*). Furthermore, this *śrāddha* ceremony begins with the ancestors (*pitr*), not with the deceased. For it is said: "One should feed the ancestors alone; one should not designate the deceased again. Even for one who follows the sequence where the first *piṇḍa* is for the deceased, then for his father, and so on, this rule has been established: it is prescribed that this division into three parts (*traidha*) and the placing [of the portion] among the *piṇḍas* applies specifically to that which is the fourth. For such is the meaning of that statement: "Having divided the fourth *piṇḍa* into three parts, one should cast it [aside]. In that context, because of proximity, the connection of the two terms "the fourth *piṇḍa*" and "should cast" is understood. However, regarding the phrase "having divided into three," when there is an expectation as to what is to be divided into three, the *piṇḍa* standing nearby is connected [with that action]. Since the sentence is rendered complete by that much alone, there is no evidence for connecting it with the word "fourth."
In that regard, when a division [of property] presents itself for anyone, the determination is made according to another Smṛti:
"Having offered four balls of rice, the giver of the balls, calling out each name individually,
should divide the first one into three parts with the two verses beginning 'Those who are common'."

The state of being "first" (ādyatva) is intended with respect to the act of giving (*dāna*), and not because of a connection to a primordial person (*ādipuruṣa*). For instance, the great-grandfather would be prior to the grandfather, and the grandfather would also be prior to the father; thus, due to this lack of finality (*anavasthāna*), there would be no definitive understanding. However, the state of being first is established through the fixed order of giving. And so, even though the ball of rice (*piṇḍa*) is qualified by the term "fourth," it is logical that the division of the first [ball] occurs according to the sequence of giving, based on the authority of other Smṛtis regarding all three rites. Therefore, as for what is stated in the *Kāṭhaka*: "The division of the one who has passed away previously is desired"—what is this "desirability"?

As for what was said—"For this very reason there is no giving to him, because he is already included"—that is of no consequence. It is not on account of the statement, "The fourth morsel does not go [to him]," nor likewise, "The morsel proceeds to three [ancestors]," that this is so. As for your own reading, "One should designate the deceased again," which you have explained as "prohibiting a further gift when the previous deceased is already included"—this reading does not exist at all for the purpose of prohibition; rather, the particle *ca* is read with the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Even if that reading were present, the interpretation regarding the prohibition of a separate *piṇḍa* in the passage "He who has been made a *sapiṇḍa*" is the one that should be understood here as well. As for those other statements...
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the son should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* annually; however, for the two parents, he should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite on other occasions.

Regarding such statements as these: if these sentences exist, then what is the use of proclaiming the name of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)? Furthermore, these sentences are not found in any of the well-known *smṛtis* accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭas*).

Therefore, there is no specific indicative mark (*liṅga*) by which we might conclude that the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) for those deceased previously are deposited [on the new moon]. Consequently, the established practice (*samācāra*) must not be abandoned. It has been shown that this very position is consistent with reason. Thus, due to differences of opinion and because of the principle of optionality (*apacchedataḥ*), some propose the view that the funeral cakes for the deceased ancestors are to be deposited [on the new moon].
For a twice-born man who has died, until the sapindikarana rite is performed, one should offer a śrāddha without a deity, feed the guests, and present a single pinda. (MDh 3.237)

In this regard [450], the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, when the father has died but the grandfather is still living, should be understood as optional (*pākṣika*). This is provided that one does not accept the rule: "One does not offer [the oblation] by bypassing one who is alive. However, when there is the alternative view that he (the grandson) should take precedence, then the grandfather is to be joined with the ancestors even by bypassing him. In the same way, for a deceased son, the father may perform the rite optionally; likewise, upon the death of a childless wife, this very same rule applies to one whose mother is still living: "Others should perform [the rites] for those who have been negligent, and they [should perform them] for those [others]."
"By sons" means by offspring; although the mention of "sons" includes others who stand in their place, provided there is no prohibition by their own specific name. 3.238.

He who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala*—that fool goes head-first to the Kālasūtra hell. (3.239) Although the mention of the fault applies to the one eating the *śrāddha*, this is nevertheless an instruction for the performer [of the rite]. Therefore, he should act in such a way that [the recipient] does not give [the leavings], just as there are rules regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). A *vṛṣala* is a *śūdra*. "Head-first" means with feet upwards. The term *śrāddha* is used so that it may not be understood as referring only to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite which is under discussion. (3.239)
If one who has eaten at a *śrāddha* ceremony approaches the bed of a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*) on that same day, his ancestors lie for that month in her excrement. (3.240)

They say that the term *vṛṣalī* is intended as an illustration for any woman in general. They provide an etymological derivation: she is called *vṛṣalī* because she "desires the bull" (*vṛṣasyati*), that is, she causes her husband to waver. And thus, whether she be a Brāhmaṇī or any other [woman], all are prohibited. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "On that day he should remain celibate and self-restrained" (GDh 15.23). By the word *talpa*, sexual union is meant; it is not merely a prohibition against ascending the bed. The mention of "the day" (*ahar*) is intended to indicate a full day and night (*ahorātra*); thus, the prohibition would apply even at night. The phrase "in feces" (*purīṣe*) is a deprecatory explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of inducing desistance. The "fathers" (*pitaraḥ*) are those who eat at his Śrāddha. This point, too, should be explained as before. However, this is more logical: that the rule applies to both [the giver and the eater]. This is an occasional duty (*naimittika-dharma*) of the eater, prescribed when the occasion of eating at a Śrāddha arises. And from the context, it also pertains to the ritual act itself. (3.240)
Having asked, "Was it well-tasted?", he should then cause those who are satisfied to rinse their mouths. Once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you all be happy. (3.241)

Having given water for sipping (*ācamanika*) and food and drink, they should be asked with the word, “Was it well-tasted? (*svaditam*). Furthermore, according to another Smṛti, this question should be made after taking up some of the food. For there is the nature of some people such that, although there is a desire for food, they do not seek it out due to restraint if it is not present, yet they take what is at hand. One should cause those who are satisfied to sip water. Others, however, say they should be asked with the words, “Are you satisfied? (*tṛptāḥ stha*). And having ascertained that they are satisfied, they should be gratified with the word, “It was well-tasted” (*svaditam*). As he will say: “Regarding the father, one should simply say, ‘It was well-tasted’” (MDh 3.244). And when they have sipped water, one should dismiss them with the words, “May you rest at ease” (*abhito ramyatām*). “At ease” (*abhitaḥ*) means on both sides; the meaning is: “May you remain as you wish, either right here or in your own homes. (3.241)
Immediately thereafter, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhāstu" (Let there be *svadhā*).

For in all rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarma*), the utterance of *svadhā* is the supreme benediction. (3.242) After they have eaten and been granted permission to depart for their homes, they should immediately say "Svadhā. The term *svadhākāraḥ* refers to the vocalization of the word *svadhā*. It is the highest benediction. This applies to all ancestral rites, whether the *śrāddha* involves cooked food or uncooked food. (3.242)
Then, once they have finished eating, he should offer them the remainder of the food.
He should act according to what they say, having been authorized by the twice-born.

(3.243) The food that has been eaten must be offered to them. They should be asked, "Is this [leftover] here? He should act according to what they say, having received their permission. Therefore, without being authorized, he must not employ it for any other purpose. (3.243)
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "it is well-eaten" (svadita); at a rite for cattle, "it is well-cooked" (suśṛta);
at a rite for prosperity, "it is excellent" (saṃpanna); and at a rite for the gods, "it is pleasing" (rucita).

Even by another person who has arrived at that appropriate time, they should be gladdened with these words. However, another says: "With these words, a request for permission should be made when proceeding to eat and so forth; therefore, the performer of the *śrāddha*, out of satisfaction, should speak thus: 'May you enjoy [the food]' (*svadadhvam*)," though it is not "enjoyed" (*svaditam*), or rather the reading is "may he enjoy" (*svadatu*). This explanation, which conveys this meaning, depends upon other *smṛtis* and established custom; therefore, those who have begun eating should be gratified by the performer of the *śrāddha* or by another in this manner. When the cows are standing in the cow-pen, one should say in certain places, "It is well-cooked" (*suśṛtam*). The word "let it be" (*astu*) is understood everywhere. In the case of the gods, one says "it is pleasing" (*rucitam*) or "it has been made pleasing" (*rocitam*). (3.244)

The afternoon, as well as *darbha* grass, the preparation of the site, sesame seeds, creation, purification, and eminent twice-born men—these are the perfections (*saṃpadaḥ*) in the rites of *śrāddha*. (3.245) The *śrāddha* should be performed in the afternoon; these are the perfections in the rites of *śrāddha*. These items are to be prepared. Although it is stated without qualification, [the rule regarding] the afternoon does not apply to all *śrāddhas*. For thus says another *smṛti*:
"Rites for the gods (*daivika*) are performed in the forenoon, those for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) in the afternoon;
the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhi-nimittaka*) is in the morning.

A "dwelling" (*vāstu*) is a house; its "preparation" (*saṃpādana*) consists of sweeping, plastering the walls with lime and the like, smearing the ground with cow dung, and ensuring it slopes toward the south. "Creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) means distribution; it refers to the giving of food and condiments without stinginess. "Purification" (*mṛṣṭi*) means cleansing; it is a specific refinement of the food.
Others, however, explain it thus: "This is the power of manifestation (vibhava-śakti), not that there is no creation in the absence of these [causes]. (3.245)

Darbha grass, the strainer, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food (haviṣya), as well as whatever purifying means were previously mentioned, should be understood as the requisites for the oblation. 3.246 (V3.256)

*Darbha* grasses are well known. *Pavitra* refers to sacred mantras. *Haviṣya* items are those suitable and fit for the oblation (*havis*); these will be described in the preceding verse [471]. *Pavitra* also means purifying, namely purity of conduct. And that which was mentioned previously [472]: the preparation of the site, the creation [of the altar], the cleansing, and the most excellent Brāhmaṇas endowed with learning and good character. *Havyasaṃpadaḥ*: *havya* refers to sacrifices and the like performed for the sake of the deities, as well as the feeding of Brāhmaṇas; the word *havya* indicates divine rites in general. (3.243)
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is not seasoned, and salt-free salt are by their very nature called sacrificial offerings (havis). 3.247 (V3.257)

The *muni* is one who dwells in the forest (*vānaprastha*); his foods are those of the wilderness, such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like. This is merely an illustration; it includes village-grown grains such as *vrīhi* as well. Thus, the term "all" is used in the subsequent verse. Furthermore, later on, having introduced the phrase "that sacrificial food which lasts for many nights" (MDh 3.256), there follows an enumeration of village-grown items as well: "with sesame, *vrīhi*, barley, and beans" (MDh 3.257). *Milk* (*payas*) means cow’s milk. Its derivatives, such as curds and so forth, are also included by virtue of both traditional law (*smṛti*) and established custom. *Soma* is a specific type of plant. *Unprepared* (*anupaskṛta*) means unadulterated and not forbidden. Meat from slaughterhouses and the like is "unprepared. It refers to salt that is not alkaline (*akṣāralavaṇa*). Regarding this, a doubt arises: is it a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) containing a copulative compound (*dvandva*), or is it simply a negative compound? Is it "non-alkaline and non-salt" (*akṣāralavaṇam*), or is it a specific kind of salt called "alkaline-salt" (*kṣāralavaṇa*), and thus something other than that is permitted? It is more appropriate for it to be simply "salt. For if it were a compound containing a copulative, two distinct grammatical operations (*vṛtti*) would have to be resorted to, and there would be a difference in the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with each member of the compound. That would be cumbersome. Since no specific distinction is relied upon regarding the nature of the sacrificial food (*havis*), this should be understood as sacrificial food in general. In general injunctions such as "he subsists on sacrificial food" (*haviṣyeṇa vartate*) or "he eats his morning meal of sacrificial food" (*haviṣyāt prātarāśād bhuṅkte*), that which is fit for sacrifice (*haviṣya*) is to be understood. (3.247)
Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-restrained, silent, and pure, and looking toward the southern direction, he should ask these boons of the ancestors: 3.248. V3.258.

The preceding verse was incidental; now he states the remainder of the subject at hand. Having dismissed—that is, granted leave for—the Brahmins to dwell as they please after they have finished eating, [the performer], immediately thereafter looking toward the southern direction, should entreat the ancestors for these boons, that is, for desired objects; he should pray to his own ancestors while meditating on them, requesting in this manner: "If you are pleased, may this be accomplished for us. (3.248)
What, then, are those boons that should be requested? To this he says:
"May our donors prosper, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (3.249)
This verse is to be recited as a mantra. 3.249

Having thus performed the offering of the funeral cakes (nirvapaṇa), immediately thereafter, one should have those cakes consumed by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire, or else cast them into water.

(3.250) Immediately thereafter—that is, after the request for the boon—one should have the cows and other recipients consume the cakes offered to the ancestors. "Consuming" here refers specifically to casting them into the fire. There is an alternative reading, "prāpayet" (one should cause [them] to reach). (3.250)

Some perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) only after [the meal]; others cause them to be eaten by birds, or cast them into fire or water. (3.251) After the feeding of the Brahmins—once the feeding of the Brahmins has been completed—some prepare the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Others have it eaten by birds, that is, by fowls. This is a more elaborate procedure than the former. "Fire" (*anala*) means the sacrificial fire (*agni*). This merely restates what was previously mentioned. Furthermore, this offering of the rice-balls is intended to take place in the vicinity of the food-leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*). (3.251)
Then, the lawful wife, devoted to her husband and intent on the worship of the ancestors, seeking a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*. (3.252) V3.262

This is the procedure for the first and last balls; as for the middle one, it is as follows: the lawful wife who desires a son should eat that which is the middle of those balls—she who has not been married out of lust, but whose rule is: "The husband alone is to be served by me, and no transgression must be committed even in thought"; she is a devoted wife (*pativratā*), faithful to her husband, intent upon the worship of the ancestors and rites such as the *śrāddha*, and she applies herself with effort to his propitiation and so forth. She should eat it properly, according to the rules for sipping water (*ācamana*) and other observances. (3.252)

She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence, wealthy, possessed of progeny, as well as virtuous and *sāttvika*. (3.253) Having consumed that *piṇḍa*, she gives birth—that is, produces—a son. *Medhā* is the power of comprehension; he is endowed with, or possessed of, that. *Sattva* is a quality well-known among the Sāṃkhyas, characterized by courage, energy, and so forth; he is endowed with that. (3.253)
Having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should provide food primarily for his kinsmen.

Having given respectfully to the kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives. (3.254) Once the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) have been presented, he should wash those two hands; thereafter, he should perform the rite of sipping water. He should provide that which "goes to" or "reaches" the kinsmen—that is, he should prepare food intended for them. He should give it to the kinsmen; having given them food with due honor, he should also give to the relatives. Kinsmen (jñātayaḥ) are those of the same lineage (sagotra); relatives (bāndhavāḥ) are those on the mother’s and father-in-law’s side.

To this it is replied: Regarding what was stated, "One should act according to what they say" (MDh 3.243), if they should say, "Let this food reach our own homes," then what would become of the Vaiśvadeva oblation and other rites? One would have to perform another cooking. Alternatively, the offering of the remainder of the food for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is enjoined as a constant duty. When it is said, "The remaining food," they should say, "To those [deities] we desire. And this [offering] would be merely occasional if they were to accept it. (3.254)
The remnants, however, should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
then one should perform the domestic *bali* offering—thus the law is established.

(3.255) Whatever remains stuck to the vessels used for eating or has fallen on the ground while they are eating, that must not be wiped away from that place until the Brahmins have departed. Then, once the *śrāddha* rite is completed, immediately thereafter the domestic *bali*, the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, and the daily feeding of guests and others must be performed; for the word "bali" is intended to indicate these [other offerings] as well.

Others, however, maintain that the term *bali* is more commonly established as referring specifically to the *bhūtayajña*; therefore, they argue that the offering into the fire (*agnau homa*) is not contradicted by what precedes it. Nor should it be said: "When a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya karma*) has already commenced, how can another rite be inserted within it? For just as performing the morning and evening fire-offerings (*sāyaṃprātar homa*) while Brahmins have been invited on the previous day is not contradictory in the case of a two-day *śrāddha* ritual, so too is the *vaiśvadeva* offering made with the domestic fire (*aupasadāgnika*). Consequently, the ritual elements subsequent to the *bhūtayajña* are postponed, but those preceding it are not.

To this it is replied: If the Vaiśvadeva oblation were performed in the fire prior [to the Śrāddha], and the Bali offering were made after the Śrāddha, then the Devayajña and Bhūtayajña would be separated; consequently, there would be a violation of the prescribed order. Furthermore, the time for the Vaiśvadeva would not be subverted, because the time for the ancestral Śrāddha would not be lost. Therefore, the performance of all the Mahāyajñas follows after the Śrāddha. (3.255)

I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, conduces both to long-lasting benefit and to infinity. (3.256) The word *cirarātra* signifies a long period of time. Regarding that which "conduces to infinity" (*ānantyāya kalpate*), meaning it results in satisfaction for a long duration—that is what I shall declare; this is stated for the purpose of establishing the intention [of the rite]. The word *kalpate* implies the sense of "it suffices" or "it is effective," and the term *preta* (departed ancestor) is to be supplied as the subject. (3.256)

By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits, the ancestors of men are satisfied for a month when given according to the prescribed rule. (3.257) The mention of sesame seeds and the other items is not intended to exclude other grains; rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the specific rewards resulting from those mentioned. When these are offered according to the rule, the ancestors are pleased for a month. The phrases such as "the ancestors of men" and so forth are reiterative statements (*anuvāda*) included merely to complete the meter. (3.257)

For two months [one may subsist] on fish-meat, for three months on the meat of the deer (*hāriṇa*), for four on that of the ram (*aurabhra*), and for five indeed on that of birds (*śākuna*). (3.258) *Urabhras* are rams; *śakunis* are wild birds such as chickens and the like; *matsyas* are fish such as the *pāṭhīna* and others. (3.258)
For six months [one lives] by means of goat meat, and for seven indeed by means of the meat of the spotted deer (pārṣata);

for eight [months] by means of the meat of the black antelope (eṇa), and for nine indeed by means of the meat of the ruru deer. (3.259) The terms *ruru*, *pṛṣata*, and *eṇa* are words denoting specific species of deer. In the forms *raurava*, *pārṣata*, and *aiṇeya*, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in the sense of a derivative product (*vikāra*). (3.259)

They are satisfied for ten months by the flesh of boars and buffaloes; however, by the flesh of hares and tortoises, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months. (3.260) A "boar" (*varāha*) refers to a wild pig. (3.260) V3.270.
But for one year, with cow’s milk and milk-rice, and with the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa, there is satisfaction lasting for twelve years. (3.261)

Because the connection of what is explicitly stated (*śruta*) is stronger than that which is inferred (*anumita*), the connection here is with "cow's milk" (*gavyena payasā*), and not with the meat mentioned in the context. Others, however, reading the word *ca* as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), explain it thus: [the offering is made] with cow's meat, cow's milk, or *pāyasa*; *pāyasa* is a modification of milk, such as curd and the like; rice cooked with milk is well known. A *vārdhrīṇasa* is an old goat. For it is recited thus in the *nigamas*:
"The three-drinker, whose senses are decayed, white, old, and uncastrated."
Sacrificial priests call that animal a vārdhrīṇasa in rites for the ancestors.

He who drinks such that three things—the two ears and the tongue—touch the water is one who "drinks with three," known as a *tripiba*. As for the penance prescribed by Śaṅkha for the eating of cow's flesh, it should be understood to apply to cases other than the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the eighth-day offerings (*aṣṭakā*), and funeral rites (*śrāddha*). (3.261)

Black potherb (*kālaśāka*), large-scaled fish (*mahāśalkāḥ*), the meat of the rhinoceros and the black goat, honey, and all kinds of food fit for sages (*munyanna*) are prescribed for the sake of infinity [of merit]. (3.262) *Kālaśāka* is a well-known superior vegetable; it refers either to a black variety of *vāstūka* or a black species of *vāstūka*. *Mahāśalkāḥ* are said to be porcupines; others, however, say they are scaled fish. *Khaḍga* is the rhinoceros. *Loha* is the black goat and the entirely red one. Thus says the *Purāṇa*:
A black goat, as well as a red one, leads indeed to infinity.

The word *loha* refers, by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its color, to a goat possessing that color. Iron is black and copper is red; thus the word *loha* is applied to both. Although this color may also occur in sheep and other animals, commentators explain that only the goat is intended here due to its well-known usage in another Smṛti. Others, however, say that a bird named "Red-back" (*lohitapṛṣṭha*) is indicated by a part of its name, just as Devadatta is called simply "Datta. Customary practice (*samācāra*) should be sought in both cases. *Madhu* means honey from bees. In all these instances, what is intended is the production of an excess of pleasure, rather than the literal time [of the seasons] itself. For if it were so, there would be a non-performance for twelve years; in that case, it would contradict the rule: "The ancestral rite (*pitrya*) must be performed until death" (MDh 3.269). || 3.262 ||
Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.

Whatever food is mixed with honey, on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā asterism—this is especially meritorious; at that time, it becomes truly inexhaustible. This is a conjunction of the season, the asterism, and the lunar day. However, according to the statement of Āpastamba, [the merit applies] even on the eighth and tenth days during the rains, and under the Maghā asterism even without the other two being specified. Thus he said: "And under the Maghā asterism, it is especially meritorious" (ĀpDh 2.19.20). 3.263.
"May there be born in our family one who would give us milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee on the thirteenth lunar day, when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east. (3.264)

This is said with reference to the present thirteenth day, which is endowed with the qualities of the year and so forth. Thus the ancestors express their hope: "May there be such a one born in our lineage—one of superior qualities—who might offer us milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey and clarified butter on the aforementioned thirteenth day. Likewise, regarding the "shadow of an elephant" (*kuñjarasya prākchāyām*): this means when the shadow has moved toward the eastern direction, that is, at a time other than the afternoon; for during the remainder of the day, the long shadow of the elephant falls toward the east. Alternatively, the reading is *prākchāyām*. Indeed, the Brahmins are fed in the shadow. As for the subsequent rite, if it cannot be performed in the shadow due to its smallness, it should be performed in another location near it. Since it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), when possible, the principal act (*pradhāna*) must be performed with all its parts complete in the shadow of the elephant itself.

As for what some explain—that an eclipse (*grahoparāga*) is called "elephant-shadow" (*hastichāyā*)—on the basis of the passage, "Svarbhānu the son of Asura, having become an elephant, pierced the sun with darkness" (cf.

PB 14.11.14), that is incorrect; for in that context, the application of the word "elephant" is figurative. Furthermore, in another Smṛti, "elephant-shadow" is mentioned as distinct from an eclipse: "The elephant-shadow and the eclipses of the moon and sun" (YDh 1.218). || 3.264 ||
Whatever one gives according to the rule, correctly and endowed with faith, that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the next world. (3.265)

The phrase "whatever" is used distributively (*vīpsā*) to authorize all food that is not prohibited. The expression "in accordance with the rule" (*vidhivat*) is a restatement for the sake of clarity. What is enjoined here is "endowed with faith" (*śraddhāsamanvita*); [the meaning is] that one should give with faith. Given in such a manner, it becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the other world. Alternatively, "infinite" (*ananta*) prohibits any limitation of time, while "inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*) expresses the absence of depletion in measure; it remains abundant at all times. (3.265)
In the dark fortnight, the lunar days beginning with the tenth—excluding the fourteenth—are recommended for the *śrāddha* ceremony, as these are superior and not like others.

(3.266) By the mention of the tenth and subsequent days, there arises an excellence of fruit. However, the rite should also be performed on other days provided that faith is present; yet, regarding the fourteenth day, there is simply a prohibition. (3.266)
By performing [the rites] on odd lunar days and under odd asterisms, one attains all desires;
but by performing them on even days, one obtains abundant progeny for all the ancestors.

The "odd" days (*yuñji dināni*) are the second, fourth, and so forth. The "odd" lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa*, *nakṣatra*) are those beginning with Bharaṇī. The lunar days (*tithi*)—the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth—are called "odd. The second, fourth, sixth, eighth, and tenth are "even. The same should be understood for the eleventh and subsequent days, as well as among the lunar mansions. "All desires" (*sarvān kāmān*): these desires are presented according to their distinctions in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. "Abundant offspring" (*puṣkalāṃ prajām*): "abundant" (*puṣkalā*) means nourished by wealth, knowledge, strength, and men. (3.267)

Just as the latter fortnight excels the former fortnight, so does the afternoon excel the forenoon for a *śrāddha* offering. (3.268) The "former fortnight" (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and the "latter" (*apara*) is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). According to the rule that "the months begin with the bright fortnight of Caitra," just as the dark fortnight excels the bright fortnight for a *śrāddha*—meaning it yields superior results—so too does the afternoon excel the forenoon, based on this specific statement. From this, it is understood that the rite may indeed sometimes be performed even during the forenoon.

But surely there ought to be an example that is well-known; and no distinction regarding the *śrāddha* has been stated for the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*) as compared to the proponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Some say: "It is understood from the rule, 'In the dark fortnight, on the tenth day and so forth' (MDh 3.266). However, we reply: according to the principle of "But [it is established] by direct statement, because it is not otherwise known" (PMS 3.5.21), even that which is not explicitly prohibited can serve as an example. Furthermore, the injunction itself can be understood precisely from the statement of the example. (3.268)
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the rites performed correctly in the counter-clockwise direction, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion.

Whatever pertains to the ancestral rites (*pitrya*), this is the rule for that ritual action. The constituent elements (*padārtha*) have been explained previously. By one who is untiring—that is, by one who is diligent and possesses faith—until death; the meaning is that this rule is to be observed throughout one's life. With *darbha* grass in hand. As it has been said: "The *darbha* grasses are the purifier" (MDh 3.246). That *pavitra* made of *darbha* grass, with its ends tied together, is so called. (3.269)

One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, for that time is declared to belong to the *rākṣasas*; nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only just risen. Now, one might ask: since the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is specifically prescribed, how could there be any possibility [of the rite being performed] at night and so forth? If it is argued that by means of this specific statement, it is indicated that the rite exists elsewhere as well—this is true. However, the general understanding arises that the specific statement, such as "the afternoon is superior to the forenoon" (MDh 3.168), applies only to that context with respect to which it was made.

Therefore, some say that "the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) refers to a specific time, while other times constitute the subsequent period (*uttarakāla*). Regarding the rule "during an eclipse of the moon or sun" (YDh 1.218), since this would apply even during the night and so forth in the case of lunar eclipses and the like, this [specification] is for the purpose of prohibiting such occasions. Consequently, because there is a prohibition against performing rites at twilight during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and because there is a positive injunction [for it] at night during a lunar eclipse, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two.
Others, however, say: the "midday" (*madhyāhnakāla*) is distinct from both the forenoon and the afternoon; by this very prohibition, it is made known that the rite must be performed even then.
And regarding the sun, because it is the time of the forenoon, the prohibition applies when the sun has first risen; "Rākṣasī" is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). || 3.270 ||
By this procedure, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the Pāñcayajñika rite daily.

One should perform the Śrāddha three times a year according to the previously mentioned rule and the full range of prescribed procedures, beginning with the invitation on the day before. To the question of in which months this is done, he says: "in the Hemanta, Grīṣma, and Varṣā seasons. The rule of performing it "month after month" (MDh 3.112) is an optional alternative to the rule of performing it three times a year. That which is recited among the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) as part of the fivefold sacrifice must be performed daily; for that, the procedure consists only of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), placing the sacrificial cord over the right arm (apasavya), and feeding Brāhmaṇas facing north. It is precisely for this purpose that it is mentioned again here. Thus, earlier commentators explain that the rule of performing it three times a year applies specifically to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni); however, they alone know what the authoritative proof for this is. (3.271)
The oblation belonging to the sacrifice for the ancestors is not prescribed to be performed in a common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha for a twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires without the Darśa sacrifice. (3.272)

The oblation that constitutes a part of the *pitr-yajña* is called *paitṛyajñika*; it is not prescribed for the common (*laukika*) or traditional (*smārta*) fire. That is to say, it is not enjoined by the scripture as something to be performed therein. Therefore, it must be performed three times a year by one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). Even though it is indeed accomplished when performed three times in the common fire, nevertheless, in relation to the requirement of the year, it remains as if unperformed. For just as one who is to eat a *prastha* is said to have "not eaten" if he eats less than that [as explained by the previous commentators as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)]. This [verse] is explained by the predecessors as a supplement to what precedes, serving as an explanatory remark.

This, however, is logical: if it is said that when a worldly fire (*laukika-agni*) has not been formally consecrated for marriage and the like, no oblation (*homa*) forming part of the *śrāddha* should be performed in it; and by the prohibition of the oblation, it is implied that other rites distinct from that must be performed. Otherwise, since even a consecrated fire is prescribed as a constituent of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, one who lacks a fire would have no entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* at all—just as a blind person has no entitlement to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) due to the inability to gaze upon the clarified butter (*ājya*). This being the case, it is made known that for one possessing a fire, the *śrāddha* is accompanied by the oblation, whereas for one without a fire, it is performed even without it. Thus, this very point constitutes the scope of the rule: "In the absence of fire" (MDh 3.202).

Those who also explain that the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is intended [here], and that the oblation (*homa*) performed therein is not in the worldly *smārta* fire—they too have not spoken correctly. Let it be so that for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is the rule "having cooked [the food], he should offer it," etc., regarding its obligatory nature. However, they say that there is no prohibition against the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*darśa*) or during eclipses and the like for one who has maintained the fires (*āhitāgni*). But this contradicts established practice (*samācāra*).

Others, however, read: "Not without the Darśa"—meaning that for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the monthly rite (*māsānumāsika*) must be performed, but not the rule of performing it three times a year. Others say that this reading does not exist at all. What, then, is its meaning? It means that for one who has established the fires, rites such as the *Maghā-śrāddha* and others do not necessarily occur apart from the *Darśa-śrāddha*; thus, for him, only the *Darśa* is obligatory. For one who has not established the fires, however, even those rites prescribed for the winter season and so forth are obligatory. (3.272)
