Whatever fruit the best of the twice-born obtains by performing the ritual of the ancestors (pitṛyajña), he attains that entire result simply by offering libations of water to the ancestors after bathing. (3.273) This verse states that the daily *śrāddha* consisting of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajñika*), which was previously mentioned as being performed every day, is optional. By performing the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) after bathing, one obtains the very fruit of the ancestral sacrifice. As for what was stated [in verse 3.73], "one should feed even a single person," there is no rule that this must necessarily be done; however, the water-libation must certainly be performed. (3.273)

"They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; such is this ancient revelation (śruti). [3.274] This is stated for the purpose of inducing the engagement of one who might not otherwise engage due to aversion toward the ancestors. The deities—the Vasus and others—who reside in the three worlds, are themselves the ancestors who partake of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa). Therefore, they should be regarded as deities. This is the revelation heard in the Veda; hence it is "ancient," because the Veda is eternal. [3.274]
One should always be an eater of vighasa, and always an eater of amṛta;
for vighasa is the remnant of what has been eaten, and likewise, amṛta is the remnant of the sacrifice.

By the first quarter of the verse, the eating of food that remains after guests and others have eaten—which was previously enjoined—is restated. Scriptures are renowned for concluding with auspiciousness because they are auspicious in nature. A rite dedicated to the gods (*daiva*) is more excellent than one dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*). "The remnant of a sacrifice" (*yajñaśeṣam*): by this, the eating of the remnants of oblations from the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices is declared to be equivalent to *vighasa*. With the second half-verse, he provides an explanation of the meaning of the Veda out of sheer friendliness. Since a prescription is seen in a certain recensional branch (*śākhā*) using these two terms, he removes any confusion. One who eats *vighasa* is a *vighasāśī*. One whose meal is nectar is an *amṛtabhojanaḥ*. "The remnant of servants" (*bhṛtyaśeṣam*) should be understood as what remains after the servants have eaten. If the reading is *bhuktaśeṣam*, it should be understood by implication as "what was eaten [by guests] and so forth."

Others, however, maintain that because of the context, this should be understood as the remains of the food eaten at a *śrāddha*. Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "He should eat what has been served to the ancestors" (YDh 1.249). Some say that this meal is an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha* rite;

others, however, say that this is a rule for eating intended for the benefit of the person (*puruṣārtha*), since the section on *śrāddha* no longer applies by virtue of the statement, "They call them the Vasus" (MDh 3.274). The phrase "remains of a sacrifice" (*yajñaśeṣa*) should be understood as the remains of substances used in a sacrifice. (3.275)
All this rule regarding the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now let the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born be heard. (3.276) V3.286

For previously, the concluding summary of the rules for the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) as "pertaining to the five sacrifices" (*pāñcayajñika*) was intended solely for the sake of auspiciousness. With the latter half of the verse, there is an introduction to a portion of the subject matter of the chapter to be explained hereafter; these two [halves] have the purposes already stated. "The chief of the twice-born" refers to the Brāhmaṇas; their "occupations" (*vṛtti*) are their means of livelihood, that is, their duties. Or, they are the "primary occupations of the twice-born. We shall demonstrate this further on, as is well known. (3.276)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The *Manusmṛti* is indeed venerable, for there exists a commentary on it by Medhātithi that is appropriate to it;
yet, by the power of fate, that [commentary] has been lost, since no manuscript of it can be found anywhere.
King Madana, together with the son of Araṇa, had the restoration of the work carried out by having manuscripts copied here and there from various regions.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi Svāmin, son of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Virasvāmin.
